adaptivity: question-level by the owner's algorithm: correct -> next question one level up, wrong -> one level down; RC: a whole passage by the current level (5 questions together); LL: 30/60/90 s clips, each by level within its length

items.context: A zoology lecturer talks about how camels live in the desert.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, clear and friendly university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 145 words per minute). Slight stress on 'but it's wrong' and on 'actually'; a natural rise on the question 'So where does the camel get its water?'; a short pause at [pause].
script: Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water. It's an idea that has proved remarkably tenacious, but it's wrong.   The hump is actually a store of fat. When food is hard to find, the camel slowly uses this fat for energy. So where does the camel get its water? Well, mostly it's very good at not losing any. Camels sweat very little, and their bodies lose far less water than ours do. That's how they survive long desert trips.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer say about a camel's hump?
options: It stores fat, which the camel uses when food runs short
It holds water that the camel uses on long trips across the desert
It holds food that the camel has swallowed but not yet digested
It helps the camel keep water in its body by sweating less

explanation.he: המילה **but** במשפט **but it's wrong** פוסלת את רעיון המים, והמשפט **The hump is actually a store of fat** (הדבשת היא בעצם מאגר שומן) מראה שהגמל משתמש בשומן כשאין מספיק מזון.
explanation.en: The lecturer calls the water idea **wrong**: **The hump is actually a store of fat**, which the camel uses **when food is hard to find**.

items.context: A neuroscience lecturer talks about the sense of touch.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: male, about 45, lively and slightly amused university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A natural rise on the opening question; a short pause at [pause]; slightly slower on 'the brain turns the signal down' and on the final sentence after 'In short'.
script: Why can't you tickle yourself? It may sound like a facetious question, but it tells us something important about the brain.   Research suggests that whenever you move, your brain predicts what that movement will feel like. When the touch then arrives exactly as expected, the brain turns the signal down. That's why your own fingers feel dull, while someone else's can feel intense: their touch can't be predicted. In short, the brain pays less attention to sensations it has already forecast.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, why does a person's own touch not tickle?
options: The brain shuts off touch signals whenever the body is moving
The brain expects the feeling and so reacts to it less
Other people tend to touch with more force than we use on ourselves
A person's own fingers press too lightly to set off a reaction

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **predicts what that movement will feel like** המוח צופה מראש את התחושה, ולפי המשפט **the brain turns the signal down** המוח מחליש את האות, ולכן מגע צפוי מורגש פחות.
explanation.en: The brain **predicts what that movement will feel like** and then **turns the signal down**; another person's touch feels intense only because it **can't be predicted**.

items.context: Two wildlife researchers discuss photos from cameras placed in a nature reserve.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female wildlife researcher, about 35, upbeat and confident at first, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male wildlife researcher, about 45, calm and doubtful, slightly slower, with stress on 'visits, not animals' and on 'hardly'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: The cameras in the new reserve recorded twice as many foxes this year. Surely that means the population is recovering.
B: I think you're conflating two things. A camera counts visits, not animals. If food has become scarce, the same few foxes may be roaming further and passing the cameras again and again.
A: But the reserve has plenty of prey, doesn't it?
B: That's what we assumed last year, too.   Until we can tell individual foxes apart, the photos are hardly a cause for jubilation.

questions.stem: What is the man's view of the camera results?
options: They point to a recovery, though a smaller one than the woman claims
They show that the foxes in the reserve are short of food
They would be reliable if the reserve had enough prey
They do not yet show whether the number of foxes has grown

explanation.he: המשפט **A camera counts visits, not animals** (מצלמה סופרת ביקורים, לא בעלי חיים) והצירוף **Until we can tell individual foxes apart** (עד שנבחין בין שועל לשועל) מראים שעדיין אין לדעת אם השועלים התרבו.
explanation.en: He says **A camera counts visits, not animals**, and he holds back any judgment **Until we can tell individual foxes apart**.

items.context: A biology lecturer talks about chili peppers.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 35, warm and lively university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Pronounce capsaicin as 'kap-SAY-uh-sin'. A natural rise on the two questions; a short pause at each [pause]; stress on 'however' and slightly slower on the last sentence after 'In other words'.
script: Let's talk about something many of you probably ate this week: chili peppers. Why do they feel hot?   The burning comes from a chemical called capsaicin. Inside your mouth there are nerve endings whose job is to warn you about dangerous heat. Capsaicin happens to switch on those very same nerve endings. So your brain gets the message 'fire', even though the temperature in your mouth hasn't changed at all. In fact, at the amounts found in food, capsaicin is fairly innocuous; it doesn't really burn or damage anything.   Now, why would a plant make such a chemical? One popular explanation looks at who eats the fruit. Mammals chew the seeds and destroy them, so the burning keeps them away. Birds, however, don't feel capsaicin at all. They swallow the seeds whole and spread them far and wide. In other words, the pepper's heat seems to choose its own customers.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, why do chili peppers feel hot?
options: They slightly raise the temperature of the tongue and the inside of the mouth
A chemical in them does mild damage to the skin inside the mouth
Something in them sets off the nerves that warn of high heat
Their seeds give off a chemical when they are chewed

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Capsaicin happens to switch on those very same nerve endings** החומר מפעיל את עצבי האזהרה מפני חום, והמשפט **the temperature in your mouth hasn't changed at all** מראה שאין חום אמיתי.
explanation.en: **Capsaicin happens to switch on those very same nerve endings** that warn of heat, **even though the temperature in your mouth hasn't changed at all**.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer say about birds?
options: They sense the burning but have learned to put up with it
They chew up the seeds, which is why the heat is meant to stop them
They spread the seeds, since the burning does not affect them
They avoid the fruit until the burning chemical breaks down

explanation.he: המילה **however** מסמנת ניגוד ליונקים: לפי המשפט **Birds, however, don't feel capsaicin at all** הציפורים אינן חשות בחומר, ולפי הצירוף **spread them far and wide** הציפורים מפיצות את הזרעים.
explanation.en: After **however**, the lecturer says birds **don't feel capsaicin at all**; they **swallow the seeds whole and spread them far and wide**.

items.context: A student visits her sociology professor during office hours to ask about a famous study of factory workers.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female undergraduate student, about 21, curious and a little doubtful, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male sociology professor, about 55, friendly and measured, slightly slower, with stress on 'far less clear' and on 'I wouldn't go that far'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: Professor, I wanted to ask about the Hawthorne studies. Our textbook says the factory workers became more productive whether the lights were made brighter or dimmer, simply because they knew they were being watched.
B: That's the classic story, yes. In management courses it's treated as practically incontrovertible. But what do you make of it?
A: Honestly, it seemed too neat. If anything you change makes people work harder, how could you ever test anything?

B: Good instinct.   When researchers later went back to the original records, the pattern was far less clear. In one group, two workers were replaced partway through, and the pay system changed as well. Either of those could explain the rise.
A: So the effect doesn't exist?
B: I wouldn't go that far. Being observed probably does change behavior somewhat. The trouble is that a vivid anecdote calcified into a law, and the messy evidence behind it was forgotten.

questions.stem: What is the professor's view of the famous finding?
options: It is exaggerated, since the evidence behind it is far from clear
It holds up well, since output rose whether the lights went up or down
It is wrong, since being watched does not really change how people work
It is doubtful, because the original records were lost long ago

explanation.he: המשפט **the pattern was far less clear** (הדפוס היה ברור הרבה פחות) והמשפט **I wouldn't go that far** (לא הייתי מרחיק לכת) מראים שהממצא אינו מופרך, אבל הראיות שלו חלשות מתדמיתו, כלומר הוא מוגזם (**exaggerated**).
explanation.en: He says **the pattern was far less clear**, yet answers **I wouldn't go that far** when asked if the effect doesn't exist: the evidence is weaker than the story.

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention the replaced workers and the new pay system?
options: To show how the researchers kept the working conditions the same
To argue that the better pay was probably the real cause
To explain why output dropped partway through the study
To point out other possible causes of the rise in output

explanation.he: המשפט **Either of those could explain the rise** (כל אחד מהשניים יכול להסביר את העלייה) מציג את שני השינויים כהסברים אפשריים לעלייה בתפוקה, ולא כסיבה ודאית אחת.
explanation.en: He concludes **Either of those could explain the rise**: the two changes are possible alternative causes, not one proven cause.

items.context: An art history lecturer talks about ancient Greek sculpture.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 50, thoughtful and quietly ironic university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A short pause at each [pause]; a natural rise on 'So why has the white ideal lasted so long?'; stress on 'not' and 'our' in the 'It's not that ... It's that' pair, and slightly slower on the final sentence.
script: When we picture ancient Greek sculpture, most of us imagine immaculate white marble. That image, it turns out, is largely our own creation.   Under ultraviolet light, many statues show faint traces of paint: blue eyes, red lips, clothing patterned in bright greens and yellows. Most of the color wore away over the centuries, and later collectors sometimes scrubbed off what little remained. So why has the white ideal lasted so long? Partly because Renaissance artists admired the bare stone they found and copied it, until whiteness came to stand for classical taste itself.   Today, when museums show painted reconstructions, visitors often find them garish, even slightly embarrassing. But notice what that reaction reveals. It's not that the Greeks lacked refinement. It's that our idea of refinement grew out of a misreading. Far from being timeless, the white ideal is a later habit of the eye.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the lecture?
options: Greek sculptors left their finest works unpainted so that the marble itself would shine
Our picture of white Greek statues comes from later taste, not from the Greeks
Most of the paint on Greek statues was lost because collectors scrubbed it away
Museum reconstructions use colors that are too bright to be accurate

explanation.he: הצירוף **largely our own creation** (במידה רבה יצירה שלנו) והמשפט **the white ideal is a later habit of the eye** (הרגל מאוחר של העין) מראים שהאידיאל הלבן הוא טעם מאוחר, לא מנהג יווני.
explanation.en: The white image is **largely our own creation**, and **Far from being timeless, the white ideal is a later habit of the eye**.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer suggest about visitors who dislike the painted reconstructions?
options: They are right that Greek artists used color with little skill
They will probably come to prefer the painted versions in time
They have spotted real errors in the way the colors were rebuilt
They are judging by an ideal that was built on a mistake

explanation.he: המשפט **It's not that the Greeks lacked refinement** שולל חוסר עידון אצל היוונים, והמשפט **our idea of refinement grew out of a misreading** (תפיסת העידון שלנו צמחה מטעות) מסביר את תגובת המבקרים.
explanation.en: **It's not that the Greeks lacked refinement**; rather, **our idea of refinement grew out of a misreading**, which explains the visitors' dislike.

items.context: Two psychology students plan a study for their research methods course.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female psychology student, about 21, energetic and practical, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male psychology student, about 22, friendly and thoughtful, slightly slower, with stress on 'the cards or the person' and on 'repeating isn't the same as understanding'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: So for our project, I was thinking we'd compare students who simply reread a chapter with students who practice with flashcards. We could just ask people in the library which method they use, and then give both groups a short quiz.

B: That's quick, but I see a problem. People who choose flashcards might be different to begin with. Maybe they're more careful students in general. Then we wouldn't know whether it's the cards or the person.
A: Fair point. So we decide the method for them instead of letting them choose?

B: Exactly. We flip a coin for each volunteer, so both groups get a fair mix of people. And everyone should study the same short chapter, so the material is identical. Otherwise, a harder chapter could make one method look worse than it really is.
A: Okay. What about the quiz, though? If we test them right after they study, the rereaders will probably do better, since they can repeat whole sentences almost verbatim.
B: True. But repeating isn't the same as understanding.   What if we give two quizzes, one right away and one a week later, with questions that ask people to explain ideas, not just repeat facts?
A: I like that. Then we'd see whether any advantage actually lasts.
B: And whether it comes from real understanding, or just from having the words still fresh in mind.

questions.stem: What problem does the man find in the woman's first plan?
options: Finding enough volunteers in the library would take far too long
The groups might differ in other ways besides their study method
Rereaders might repeat more of the chapter word for word
The quiz would come too late, after the students had forgotten the chapter

explanation.he: המשפט **People who choose flashcards might be different to begin with** (מי שבוחרים בכרטיסי שינון עשויים להיות שונים מלכתחילה) מראה שההבדל בין הקבוצות עלול לנבוע מהאנשים ולא מהשיטה.
explanation.en: He says **People who choose flashcards might be different to begin with**, so the result could reflect **the person**, not **the cards**.

questions.stem: What do the speakers decide to do about the quiz?
options: Give a single quiz right after studying, made up of factual questions
Let the students reread the chapter before the second quiz
Give two quizzes a week apart that ask students to explain ideas
Use a different chapter for each group to keep the comparison fair

explanation.he: ההצעה **two quizzes, one right away and one a week later** (שני מבחנים, מיד ואחרי שבוע) והצירוף **explain ideas, not just repeat facts** (להסביר רעיונות ולא רק לחזור על עובדות) מתקבלים בתשובה **I like that**.
explanation.en: He proposes **two quizzes, one right away and one a week later**, asking people to **explain ideas, not just repeat facts**, and she replies **I like that**.

items.context: A linguistics lecturer talks about how young children learn to talk about the past.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 40, warm and engaging university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Say the child's sentences in a light, childlike tone without changing voice; pronounce 'goed' as 'go-ed' (rhymes with 'showed'). A natural rise on 'has the child's English actually gotten worse?'; a short pause at each [pause]; slightly slower after 'In other words'.
script: Here's something that baffles a lot of new parents. A two-year-old says, 'I went to the park,' perfectly correctly. A few months later, the same child says, 'I goed to the park.' So has the child's English actually gotten worse?   Not at all. This little slip is in fact a sign of progress. At first, the child has simply memorized 'went' as a separate word, the way you'd memorize a name. Then something changes. The child notices that most verbs form the past by adding the same ending: walk, walked; play, played. Once that pattern clicks, the child applies it everywhere, even to verbs that don't follow it.   Now, notice what this tells us. Nobody taught the child to say 'goed.' Adults don't say it, so it can't be simple imitation. The child has worked out a rule alone, and is now using it a little too exuberantly. Researchers often describe this as a U-shaped curve: performance starts high, dips, and then recovers. Eventually, the child learns that a handful of verbs are exceptions, and 'went' comes back, this time as a known exception to a known rule. In other words, these errors aren't a step backward. They show that the child has stopped merely copying and started building a grammar.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point?
options: The child's new errors reveal that a general rule has been learned
Children learn the past tense mainly by copying the adults around them
Children learn rules first and memorize separate words afterward
Parents should correct errors like 'goed' before they become habits

explanation.he: התגובה **Not at all** והצירוף **a sign of progress** (סימן להתקדמות), יחד עם הסיכום **started building a grammar** (התחיל לבנות דקדוק), מראים שהטעות מעידה על כלל שנלמד.
explanation.en: The error is **a sign of progress**: it shows **the child has stopped merely copying and started building a grammar**.

questions.stem: Why does the lecturer point out that adults don't say 'goed'?
options: To show that the form was not learned from other speakers
To argue that adult speech has little effect on how children learn
To explain why the child later goes back to saying 'went'
To show that adults correct children who make this mistake

explanation.he: מיד אחרי העובדה שמבוגרים אינם אומרים את הצורה **goed** בא הצירוף **so it can't be simple imitation** (לכן אין זה חיקוי פשוט): הילד גיבש את הכלל בעצמו.
explanation.en: Because adults don't say it, **it can't be simple imitation**, so **the child has worked out a rule alone**.

items.context: A history lecturer talks about how clocks in different towns came to show the same time.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 55, composed and wry university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A short pause at each [pause]; stress on 'didn't lead' and 'followed' in 'Governments didn't lead this change; they followed it'; slightly slower on the last two sentences.
script: Today we take it for granted that every clock in a region shows the same time. But for most of history, time was local. Noon was simply the moment the sun stood highest, so a town a little to the west kept a slightly later noon than its neighbor.   For centuries, nobody minded. Travel was slow, and a difference of a few minutes was inconsequential to anyone on horseback. The railways changed that. A timetable that had to juggle dozens of local times, one for every station, was a recipe for confusion. So the railway companies did something rather bold: they simply chose a single standard and ran their trains by it. In Britain, most lines adopted London time in the eighteen-forties. In the United States, the railroads divided the country into a few broad time zones in eighteen eighty-three.   Now, here's the point I want you to notice. Governments didn't lead this change; they followed it. In both countries, the law made standard time official only decades later, after most people were already living by it. And not everyone was won over at once. Some towns kept their own time for years, and a few public clocks were fitted with two minute hands, one for local time and one for the railway. So standard time wasn't handed down by scientists or lawmakers. It was a commercial convenience that gradually became so entrenched that we now mistake it for something natural.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point?
options: Railway companies and governments worked together to replace local time
Standard time spread because people found it more natural than solar time
Local time disappeared soon after the railways chose a single standard
Standard time was a business tool that lawmakers accepted only later

explanation.he: המשפט **Governments didn't lead this change; they followed it** (הממשלות לא הובילו את השינוי אלא הלכו בעקבותיו) והצירוף **a commercial convenience** (נוחות מסחרית) מראים שהחוק אישר רק בדיעבד פתרון עסקי.
explanation.en: **Governments didn't lead this change; they followed it**, and standard time was **a commercial convenience** that the law made official **only decades later**.

questions.stem: Why does the lecturer mention clocks with two minute hands?
options: To show that some towns would not display railway time
To illustrate that local time lived on alongside the new standard
To illustrate how precise clocks had to become for train timetables
To suggest that the law had already made railway time official

explanation.he: הצירוף **one for local time and one for the railway** (אחד לזמן המקומי ואחד לזמן הרכבת) מראה ששני הזמנים התקיימו זה לצד זה, כדוגמה למשפט **not everyone was won over at once**.
explanation.en: The clocks had hands **one for local time and one for the railway**, an example of how **not everyone was won over at once**.

items.context: A biology lecturer talks about the eyes of some animals that are active at night.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, warm and lively university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, a slight stress on 'aren't making any light', a short pause at [pause], and a slower, firmer last sentence.
script: Have you ever pointed a flashlight into a dark garden and seen a cat's eyes glow back at you? It can look eerie, almost ghostly. But the eyes aren't making any light of their own. At the back of the eye, many night animals have a thin layer that works like a mirror. Light that passes through once is bounced back for a second chance to be detected.   So the glow is simply reflected light, and it helps these animals see in the dark.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer explain about the glow in a cat's eyes at night?
options: The eyes give off a faint light of their own in the dark
A mirror-like layer shields the eyes from bright lights
The glow is meant to make the animal look scary to enemies
A layer in the eye sends incoming light back through it

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **But the eyes aren't making any light of their own** (אבל העיניים אינן מפיקות אור משלהן) והמשפט **the glow is simply reflected light** (הזוהר הוא פשוט אור מוחזר), שכבה בעין מחזירה את האור.
explanation.en: **But the eyes aren't making any light of their own**: **the glow is simply reflected light**, bounced back by a layer in the eye.

items.context: An economics lecturer talks about coins that were made of precious metal.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: male, about 55, dry and slightly amused university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'Which one do people spend?', a short pause at [pause], stress on 'Not the good one' and on 'oddly enough'.
script: Here's a puzzle from the history of money. Suppose two coins carry the same face value, but one is pure silver and the other holds only a modicum of silver, mixed with cheaper metal. Which one do people spend?   Not the good one. They hold on to the silver coin, or melt it down, and pay with the poor one. So, oddly enough, the worse coin ends up being the one that circulates, while the better coin quietly disappears from the market.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what happens when a pure silver coin and a coin with less silver have the same face value?
options: The coin with less silver soon vanishes from everyday trade
The coin with less silver becomes the one that changes hands
People melt down the cheaper coins to recover the silver in them
Sellers refuse to accept the coin with less silver as payment

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **pay with the poor one** (משלמים במטבע הגרוע) והמשפט **the worse coin ends up being the one that circulates** (המטבע הגרוע הוא זה שעובר מיד ליד), המטבע הזול יותר הוא זה שנמצא בשימוש.
explanation.en: People **pay with the poor one**, so **the worse coin ends up being the one that circulates**.

items.context: Two archaeologists discuss pottery found at a dig.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female archaeologist, about 35, enthusiastic and confident, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male archaeologist, about 50, calm and skeptical, slightly slower, with stress on 'Pots travel far more easily than people' and on 'not that anyone moved'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: We've uncovered a smattering of coastal-style bowls at the inland site, maybe forty pieces in all. To me, that suggests coastal families settled there.
B: That seems a bit glib. Pots travel far more easily than people. Forty bowls could have come through trade alone.
A: So what would change your mind?
B: Signs that daily life itself changed, like coastal-style houses or cooking hearths.   Until then, the bowls show contact between the two regions, not that anyone moved.

questions.stem: What is the man's view of the bowls?
options: They indicate that the coastal families did not move to the inland site
They show that traders, not settlers, brought them inland
They reveal ties between the areas, not proof that settlers came
They are a sign that people from the coast settled inland

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the bowls show contact between the two regions, not that anyone moved** (הקערות מעידות על קשר בין האזורים, לא על כך שמישהו עבר), אין בהן הוכחה לכך שמתיישבים הגיעו.
explanation.en: He says **the bowls show contact between the two regions, not that anyone moved**, so they do not prove settlement.

items.context: A student visits his physics professor during office hours to ask about a simple test he tried.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: male university student, about 20, curious and a little puzzled, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: female physics professor, about 50, patient and clear, moderate pace, with stress on 'And they were', 'quickly' and 'slowly'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: Professor, I tried something after your lecture on heat. I left a metal spoon and a wooden spoon on my desk overnight, and in the morning the metal one felt much colder. But you said they'd be at the same temperature.
B: And they were. Both had settled at room temperature. What you felt wasn't the temperature of the spoons. It was how fast each one pulled heat out of your fingers.
A: So the metal takes heat away faster?

B: Exactly. Metal is a good conductor, so it carries heat away from your skin quickly, and your skin cools. Wood is a poor conductor, so heat leaves your fingers slowly.   That's why a metal railing feels so glacial on a winter morning, almost icy, while a wooden bench beside it doesn't.
A: Then my hand is really measuring heat flow, not temperature.
B: That's it. Your skin is a fairly poor thermometer.

questions.stem: What is the professor mainly explaining to the student?
options: Why equally warm objects can feel different to the touch
Why metal loses its heat faster than wood does overnight
How the skin can be used to compare the temperature of objects
Why a metal railing is colder than a wooden bench in winter

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Both had settled at room temperature** (שתיהן הגיעו לטמפרטורת החדר) והמשפט **What you felt wasn't the temperature of the spoons** (מה שהורגש לא היה הטמפרטורה), חפצים חמים באותה מידה מרגישים שונה במגע.
explanation.en: **Both had settled at room temperature**, and **What you felt wasn't the temperature of the spoons**, so she explains why equally warm objects feel different.

questions.stem: According to the professor, why does the metal spoon feel colder?
options: It is still a few degrees cooler than the room around it
It passes heat into the fingers more slowly than wood
It draws heat out of the skin faster than wood does
Skin is less sensitive when it touches a good conductor

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **it carries heat away from your skin quickly** (היא מוליכה חום הרחק מהעור במהירות), המתכת מושכת חום מהאצבעות מהר יותר מהעץ.
explanation.en: Metal **carries heat away from your skin quickly**, while with wood **heat leaves your fingers slowly**.

items.context: A geography lecturer talks about a famous world map.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 45, engaging and confident university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'So is the map simply wrong?', a short pause at [pause], stress on 'tool for sailors' and on 'the price', and a slower, firmer last sentence.
script: Take the world map most of us grew up with, drawn by Gerardus Mercator in the sixteenth century. On that map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. So is the map simply wrong? Not exactly.   Mercator wasn't trying to show the true size of countries. He was making a tool for sailors. On his map, a course that keeps the same compass direction appears as a straight line, so a navigator could plot a route with a ruler. To make that work, the map stretches places more and more toward the poles. That's why the lands near the poles look so swollen. In other words, the distortion isn't an aberration or a careless error; it's the price of a map built for steering ships. Every flat map has its flaws, because a round Earth can't be laid flat without distortion. The real question is which distortion suits your purpose.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point about the map?
options: Its size errors reflect the limited methods of its time
Its size errors are the cost of the job it was designed to do
Since flat maps are distorted anyway, the choice of map hardly matters
It is a poor guide for sailors because it stretches the lands near the poles

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the price of a map built for steering ships** (המחיר של מפה שנבנתה לניווט ספינות) והמשפט **He was making a tool for sailors** (הוא יצר כלי למלחים), העיוות נובע מייעוד המפה.
explanation.en: The distortion is **the price of a map built for steering ships**, since **He was making a tool for sailors**.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what made the map useful to sailors?
options: It showed each country at its true size relative to the others
Its straight lines marked the shortest way between two ports
It showed the lands near the poles in more detail than earlier maps
It turned a course on one compass heading into a straight line

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **a course that keeps the same compass direction appears as a straight line** (מסלול ששומר על אותו כיוון מצפן נראה כקו ישר), אפשר היה לשרטט מסלול בסרגל.
explanation.en: On the map, **a course that keeps the same compass direction appears as a straight line**, so routes could be drawn with a ruler.

items.context: An architecture lecturer talks about how some tall medieval buildings were built.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 50, clear and enthusiastic university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Stress on 'doesn't just press down' and 'pushes outward', a short pause at [pause], a slower delivery on 'Now, this is the key point', and a firm last sentence.
script: Today I want to look at a problem that medieval builders faced. Imagine you want a tall stone building with a high stone ceiling, what we call a vault. The trouble is that a heavy vault doesn't just press down. It also pushes outward, against the tops of the walls, and if nothing resists that push, the walls lean and the roof falls in. For centuries, the answer was to build very thick walls with only small windows, because every opening weakened the wall. The result was solid, but the inside was dark.   Then, in twelfth-century France, builders tried something different. Instead of making the wall carry the outward push, they moved the support outside the building. They built stone arms, called flying buttresses, that reach from the upper wall across to heavy columns of stone standing a little apart from it. Each buttress catches the push of the vault and carries it down to the ground outside. Now, this is the key point. Once the wall no longer had to hold up the roof on its own, it could be opened up. That's why Gothic cathedrals have those huge windows of colored glass, and why their interiors seem so ethereal, flooded with light and almost floating. So the buttresses we see on the outside aren't decoration. They're the reason the inside could be so bright.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How outside supports let builders open up the walls of tall buildings
Why medieval builders preferred thick walls with small windows
How colored glass was made strong enough for very large windows
Why stone arms were added mainly to decorate the outside of tall buildings

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **they moved the support outside the building** (הם העבירו את התמיכה אל מחוץ למבנה) והמשפט **it could be opened up** (אפשר היה לפתוח את הקיר), הקיר התפנה לחלונות גדולים.
explanation.en: Builders **moved the support outside the building**, so the wall **could be opened up** for huge windows.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what problem did a heavy stone vault create?
options: It pressed sideways on the walls as well as downward
It pulled the walls inward toward the center of the building
It pressed down so hard that the walls sank into the ground
It made the walls lean unless they were lightened by windows

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **doesn't just press down** (לא רק לוחץ כלפי מטה) והמשפט **It also pushes outward** (הוא גם דוחף החוצה), הקמרון לחץ גם הצידה על ראשי הקירות.
explanation.en: A heavy vault **doesn't just press down**; **It also pushes outward**, against the tops of the walls.

items.context: Two history students discuss a famous inscribed stone from ancient Egypt in a seminar.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent for both speakers. A: female graduate student, about 25, confident and quick, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male graduate student, about 27, thoughtful and measured, slightly slower, with stress on 'too much credit', 'stand for sounds' and 'starting point'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: I'd argue the Rosetta Stone is what unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs. The same text appears in hieroglyphs and in ancient Greek, which scholars could already read. If you can read one version, you can match it, word by word, against the other. That's a ready-made translation.

B: It's a famous story, but I think it gives the stone too much credit. Scholars had copies of the text for about twenty years before anyone could actually read the hieroglyphs. The problem wasn't a lack of texts; it was a paucity of good ideas.
A: Meaning what, exactly?

B: Well, for a long time people assumed each sign was a picture of an idea, not a sound. The real breakthrough came when Champollion showed that many signs stand for sounds, much like letters. It also helped that he knew Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language, so he could guess how the words were pronounced.
A: But without the Greek, he wouldn't have had a shred of evidence to test his guesses against.

B: Agreed, the stone gave scholars the impetus, a target and a way to check their work.   I'm only saying it was a starting point. The decoding itself depended on a new idea about how the script worked.
A: So, necessary, but not enough on its own.
B: That's how I'd put it.

questions.stem: What is the man's main point about the stone?
options: It provided a ready-made translation that by itself made reading the hieroglyphs possible
Its value lay in showing that each sign stands for an idea
Scholars needed twenty more years of texts before they could use it
It started the work, but rethinking the signs cracked the code

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **it was a starting point** (זו הייתה נקודת התחלה) והמשפט **The decoding itself depended on a new idea about how the script worked** (הפענוח נשען על רעיון חדש על הכתב), פריצת הדרך באה מהבנת הסימנים.
explanation.en: He calls the stone **a starting point** and says **The decoding itself depended on a new idea about how the script worked**.

questions.stem: According to the man, what did Champollion's knowledge of Coptic allow him to do?
options: Read the Greek part of the stone, which others could not
Make informed guesses about how Egyptian words sounded
Check his guesses against a second version of the text
Locate further copies of the text in other languages

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **he knew Coptic** (הוא ידע קופטית) והמשפט **he could guess how the words were pronounced** (הוא יכול היה לנחש איך הגו את המילים), הקופטית עזרה לו בהגייה.
explanation.en: Because **he knew Coptic**, **he could guess how the words were pronounced**.

items.context: A biology lecturer talks about how geckos climb.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, lively and clear university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'So what holds it there?', a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'almost nothing' and 'billions of them together'.
script: Geckos are nimble climbers. A gecko can run straight up a glass window, or even hang upside down from a ceiling. So what holds it there? It isn't glue, and it isn't suction.   Its toes are covered with millions of tiny hairs, and each hair splits into even finer tips. These tips get so close to the surface that very weak forces between molecules start to pull. A single tip holds almost nothing, but billions of them together can hold the whole animal.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what keeps a gecko attached to a glass window?
options: A sticky liquid that its toes leave on the glass
Air pushed out from under its toes, which holds them down
The grip of each tiny hair, which could support most of its weight
Many weak pulls that together add up to a strong hold

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **A single tip holds almost nothing, but billions of them together can hold the whole animal** (קצה בודד כמעט לא מחזיק, אבל מיליארדים יחד מחזיקים את כל החיה), האחיזה מצטברת ממשיכות חלשות רבות.
explanation.en: **A single tip holds almost nothing, but billions of them together can hold the whole animal**, so many weak pulls add up.

items.context: Two materials scientists discuss a piece of old window glass in their lab.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female researcher, about 30, curious and confident, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male researcher, about 45, calm and precise, slightly slower, with stress on 'doesn't hold up' and 'uneven'. A short pause at [pause]; A's 'Usually?' is a quick, surprised question.
script: A: Look at this pane from a seventeenth-century house. It's thicker at the bottom, so the glass must have been flowing down slowly for centuries.

B: That's the popular story, but it doesn't hold up. At room temperature, glass is far too stiff to sag like that, even over millions of years.   Old panes simply came out of the workshop uneven, and builders usually set the heavier edge at the bottom.
A: Usually?
B: Some old panes are lopsided the other way, with the thick edge on top.

questions.stem: According to the man, why is the old pane thicker at the bottom?
options: The glass has been creeping downward since it was put in place
It sagged over the centuries, though more slowly than people assume
It was uneven from the start and fitted heavy side down
Its maker shaped it thick at one end on purpose

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Old panes simply came out of the workshop uneven, and builders usually set the heavier edge at the bottom** (הזגוגיות יצאו לא אחידות, והצד הכבד הוצב למטה), העובי אינו נובע מזרימה.
explanation.en: **Old panes simply came out of the workshop uneven, and builders usually set the heavier edge at the bottom**; the glass did not flow.

items.context: A psychology lecturer describes a simple memory experiment.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: male, about 50, warm and friendly university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Read the three example words slowly, with a small gap after each. Rising intonation on 'Which words will they remember?', a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'first few', 'last few' and 'middle'.
script: Here's a simple test you can try on a friend. Read out a list of about fifteen mundane words, like chair, apple and window, and then ask your friend to write down as many as they can. Which words will they remember?   Most people recall the first few words best, because they had time to repeat them silently. They also recall the last few words, because those are still fresh in their minds when the list ends. It's the middle of the list that gets lost. Psychologists call this the serial position effect. Now, here's the interesting part. If your friend has to count backward for thirty seconds before writing, the last words fade away, but the first words stay. So the end of the list is held only for a short time, while the beginning has been stored more firmly. In other words, the start and the end of a list are remembered for different reasons.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How silently repeating words helps people memorize long lists
How a word's place in a list affects the chance of recalling it
Why the words at the start of a list are the first to be forgotten
How counting backward helps people remember new words

explanation.he: לפי הצירופים **the first few words** ו-**the last few words** (המילים הראשונות והאחרונות) והמשפט **It's the middle of the list that gets lost** (האמצע הולך לאיבוד), מיקומה של מילה ברשימה משפיע על הסיכוי שהמילה תיזכר.
explanation.en: The lecturer contrasts **the first few words** and **the last few words** with **the middle of the list that gets lost**.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, why do people recall the last few words on the list?
options: They were heard just before the friend started writing
There was enough time to repeat them silently in the head
They have been stored more firmly than the first words
A short count backward helps to keep them fresh

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **because those are still fresh in their minds when the list ends** (כי הן עדיין טריות בזיכרון כשהרשימה נגמרת), זוכרים את המילים האחרונות כי הן נשמעו ממש לפני הכתיבה.
explanation.en: People recall the last words **because those are still fresh in their minds when the list ends**.

items.context: A student visits her statistics professor during office hours to ask about her project data.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female undergraduate, about 21, puzzled at first and then quick and engaged, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male professor, about 55, patient and friendly, slightly slower, with stress on 'skill plus luck', 'doesn't carry over' and 'comparison group'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: Professor, I'm a bit flummoxed by my project data. I gave a reaction-time test twice, a week apart, and the students who did best the first time mostly did worse the second time. Did they just stop trying?

B: Probably not. Think of any score as two parts: skill plus luck. The people at the top on day one were probably skilled, but they were also having a lucky day.   Luck doesn't carry over, so the second time, their scores drift back toward the average.
A: And the weakest group should improve, then?
B: Exactly, for the same reason. It's called regression to the mean. It isn't that people changed; extreme scores are partly chance.
A: So if I'd trained the top group in between, I might have blamed the training.
B: And with the bottom group, you'd think it worked wonders. That's why you need a comparison group.

questions.stem: According to the professor, why did the top students do worse the second time?
options: They lost interest and made less effort in the second test
Their actual skill partly slipped back toward an average level
The weaker students practiced and caught up with them
Their first scores partly reflected luck that did not repeat

explanation.he: לפי המשפטים **Luck doesn't carry over** (המזל לא עובר הלאה) ו-**extreme scores are partly chance** (ציונים קיצוניים נובעים בחלקם ממקרה), הירידה נובעת ממזל שלא חזר.
explanation.en: **Luck doesn't carry over**, and **extreme scores are partly chance**, so the top scores fell back.

questions.stem: Why does the professor say that a comparison group is needed?
options: Training on its own would make the top group's scores fall
Changes due to chance could look like effects of training
The bottom group's scores could not rise without some training
It would show which students had simply stopped trying

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **you'd think it worked wonders** (אפשר היה לחשוב שהאימון עשה פלאים) ולפי המשפט שאחריו **That's why you need a comparison group** (לכן צריך קבוצת השוואה), שיפור מקרי עלול להיראות כהשפעת האימון.
explanation.en: Chance alone would lift the bottom group, so **you'd think it worked wonders**, which is **why you need a comparison group**.

items.context: A psychology lecturer tells the story of a famous horse.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 50, dry and engaging storytelling tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'So was Hans really counting?', a short pause at [pause], 'Not quite' said slowly, and stress on 'without knowing', 'reading people' and 'not at sums'.
script: In the early nineteen-hundreds, a horse in Berlin known as Clever Hans became famous for doing arithmetic. Ask him what three plus two was, and he would tap his hoof five times. Experts examined him and found no sleight of hand; his owner wasn't cheating anyone. So was Hans really counting?   Not quite. A young psychologist noticed that Hans got the answer right only when the questioner knew it and stood where Hans could see them. As the taps neared the right number, the questioner's face and posture changed very slightly, and Hans simply stopped tapping at that cue. The questioners had no inkling that they were giving the answer away; they were doing it without knowing. Now, the lesson here isn't that Hans was stupid. He was remarkably good at reading people, just not at sums. And that's why, today, careful studies keep the person running a test from knowing the expected answer.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point about Hans?
options: He was poor at arithmetic but highly alert to human signals
His owner was secretly signaling the answers to him
He could really count, but only when his questioner was in sight
He learned arithmetic by closely studying his questioners' faces

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **He was remarkably good at reading people, just not at sums** (הוא היה טוב במיוחד בקריאת אנשים, רק לא בחשבון), הסוס לא ידע לחשב, אלא קלט רמזים מהשואלים.
explanation.en: The lecturer says **He was remarkably good at reading people, just not at sums**, so he was reading cues, not counting.

questions.stem: What research practice does the lecturer link to the story?
options: Letting the animal see the questioner's face during a test
Checking that an animal's owner is not cheating
Making sure the tester does not know the expected result
Judging an animal's intelligence by more than its sums

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **careful studies keep the person running a test from knowing the expected answer** (מחקרים זהירים מונעים מעורך הבדיקה לדעת את התשובה הצפויה), הבודק אינו יודע מראש את התשובה הצפויה.
explanation.en: The lecturer says **careful studies keep the person running a test from knowing the expected answer**.

items.context: A botany lecturer talks about the Venus flytrap.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 40, energetic and clear university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'How does it tell the difference?', a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'once', 'a second time' and 'counting'.
script: Today, let's look at one of the best-known plants in the world, the Venus flytrap. It grows wild in only a small area of wetlands in the southeastern United States, where the soil is very poor in nutrients. The plant still makes its own food from sunlight, like other plants, but it gets nitrogen and other nutrients from the insects it catches. Now, here's the puzzle. Snapping shut takes a lot of energy, and reopening an empty trap can take many hours. So a flytrap can't afford to squander that effort on a raindrop or a falling leaf. How does it tell the difference?   Inside each trap are a few tiny trigger hairs. If something touches a hair once, nothing happens. But if the hairs are touched a second time within about half a minute, the trap closes. A raindrop usually strikes once, while a crawling insect keeps moving and touches the hairs again. In other words, the plant is counting. And it doesn't stop there. Even after the trap shuts, the plant is finicky about its meal. The trap seals tightly and starts to digest only when the insect keeps struggling and touches the hairs several more times. The edges also leave small gaps at first, so very tiny insects can escape, because they wouldn't be worth the cost. So a plant with no brain still makes something like a decision.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How a flytrap tells real prey apart from false alarms
Why flytraps grow only in soil that lacks nutrients
How flytraps make their food from insects instead of sunlight
Why very small insects are the flytrap's favorite prey

explanation.he: לפי השאלה **How does it tell the difference?** (איך הצמח מבחין בהבדל?) והמשפט **the plant is counting** (הצמח סופר), ההרצאה מסבירה איך המלכודת מבדילה בין טרף לאזעקת שווא.
explanation.en: The lecture asks **How does it tell the difference?** and answers that **the plant is counting** touches.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what makes the trap close?
options: A single firm touch on any one of its trigger hairs
Something heavy, such as a falling leaf, landing inside
An insect struggling and touching the hairs several more times
A second touch on the hairs soon after the first one

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **if the hairs are touched a second time within about half a minute, the trap closes** (אם נוגעים בשערות פעם שנייה תוך כחצי דקה, המלכודת נסגרת), מגע אחד אינו מספיק.
explanation.en: **If something touches a hair once, nothing happens**, but **if the hairs are touched a second time within about half a minute, the trap closes**.

items.context: Two developmental psychologists discuss a well-known test given to young children.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent for both speakers. A: female researcher, about 35, confident and quick, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male researcher, about 50, measured and careful, slightly slower, with stress on 'misgivings', 'sensible bet' and 'narrower'. A short pause at [pause]; A's 'Weaker, but not gone' is firm, and her last line is conceding.
script: A: It's one of the most lauded findings in psychology. Four-year-olds who could hold off eating one marshmallow to get two later went on to do better at school years afterward. That looks like a measure of self-control, plain and simple.

B: I have some misgivings about that last part. In a later study, children first dealt with an adult who either kept a small promise, like bringing better crayons, or broke it. Then came the marshmallow test, with the same adult. The kids who'd met the reliable adult waited about four times as long.
A: So waiting partly depends on whether the child believes the second treat will really come.

B: Exactly. For a child whose promises are often broken at home, eating now isn't weak will; it's a sensible bet.   And a larger follow-up, with a more varied group of children, found the link to later achievement much weaker, roughly half as strong, and smaller still once family background was taken into account.
A: Weaker, but not gone. Part of the link survives, so I wouldn't throw the test out.
B: Nor would I. My point is narrower. What the test measures is tangled up with the child's circumstances, so the story of pure willpower is overblown.
A: Fair enough. Self-control matters, but so does having a reason to trust.

questions.stem: What is the man's main point about the test?
options: It is a straightforward measure of how much self-control a child has
It should be set aside now that its link to success has disappeared
Its results blend self-control with a child's life situation
Children who eat the treat right away are showing weak will

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **What the test measures is tangled up with the child's circumstances** (מה שהמבחן מודד כרוך בנסיבות חייו של הילד), התוצאה אינה משקפת כוח רצון בלבד.
explanation.en: He says **What the test measures is tangled up with the child's circumstances**, so it is not pure willpower.

questions.stem: Why does the man describe the study with the adult who kept or broke a promise?
options: To suggest that children from unreliable homes plan poorly
To show that trust in the reward affects how long children wait
To show that reliable adults train children in self-control
To explain why a later study chose a more varied group of children

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **waiting partly depends on whether the child believes the second treat will really come** (ההמתנה תלויה בחלקה באמונה שהפרס השני יגיע), שהגבר מאשר במילה **Exactly**, הניסוי מראה את תפקיד האמון.
explanation.en: The man confirms (**Exactly**) that **waiting partly depends on whether the child believes the second treat will really come**.

items.context: A physics lecturer talks about hearing distant sounds after dark.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 50, clear and friendly university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, light stress on 'helps a little' and a firmer 'isn't the main reason', a short pause at [pause], and slower delivery on 'bends sound waves back down toward us'.
script: Have you ever noticed that a distant train sounds much closer at night? It's a perplexing effect, and most people assume the night is simply quieter. That helps a little, but it isn't the main reason.   After sunset, the ground cools quickly, so the air near it becomes cooler than the air above. Sound travels faster in warmer air, and this difference bends sound waves back down toward us. So instead of escaping upward, the sound stays near the ground.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what mainly makes a distant sound seem closer at night?
options: The night is quieter, so faint sounds are easier to pick out
Sound moves faster in the cool layer of air that forms near the ground
The cold ground soaks up less of the sound than it does in the daytime
Cool air below and warmer air above bend the sound back down

explanation.he: לפי המשפטים **the air near it becomes cooler than the air above** (האוויר ליד הקרקע קר מזה שמעליו) ו-**this difference bends sound waves back down** (ההבדל מכופף את הקול חזרה מטה), זו הסיבה העיקרית; השקט רק עוזר מעט.
explanation.en: The quiet only **helps a little**; the main reason is that **this difference bends sound waves back down toward us**.

items.context: Two linguists discuss a well-known claim about the vocabulary of some languages.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female linguist, about 35, brisk and a little skeptical, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute), with a rising, slightly teasing tone on 'by now?'. B: male linguist, about 50, calm and exact, slightly slower, with stress on 'Not bogus', 'badly framed' and 'how the grammar works'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: You've heard the old claim that Inuit languages have hundreds of words for snow. Surely that's been shown to be bogus by now?
B: Not bogus, just badly framed. Those languages build one long word out of many small parts, so a speaker can create endless words about snow, or about fish, or about anything else.
A: So counting them misses the point.
B: That's the crux.   A huge count tells you how the grammar works. It doesn't tell you that snow fills people's minds.

questions.stem: What is the man's view of the claim about words for snow?
options: It mistakes a grammar feature for a special interest in snow
It is simply false and is no longer worth discussing
It shows how much snow fills these speakers' thoughts
It holds for snow but not for other everyday subjects like fish

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **A huge count tells you how the grammar works** (מספר עצום מלמד על אופן פעולת הדקדוק), ולא על כך שהשלג ממלא את מחשבותיהם (**snow fills people's minds**).
explanation.en: He says **A huge count tells you how the grammar works**, not that **snow fills people's minds**.

items.context: A biology lecturer talks about how honeybees behave when they return to the hive.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, warm and lively university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, short pauses at [pause], clear stress on 'direction' and 'distance', and a slower, firmer delivery on the last two sentences.
script: How does a honeybee tell the other bees where to find flowers? Bees can't draw maps, and they can't point. For a long time, this was a real puzzle. The answer turned out to be a dance.   When a bee comes back to the hive from a good patch of flowers, she runs in a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she circles back and does it again, many times. The direction of that straight run shows the direction of the flowers, compared with the position of the sun. And the length of the run shows the distance. The longer she shakes, the farther away the food is.   The other bees stay close to her and pick up this information, and then they fly off to find the flowers. That's a staggering amount of information in a few seconds of movement. So the dance isn't a celebration. It's a set of directions.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: Why bees dance after a good day of collecting food
How bees let each other know where food can be found
How bees use the sun's position to find their way home
How bees build and move around on the honeycomb

explanation.he: השאלה **How does a honeybee tell the other bees where to find flowers?** (איך דבורה מראה לדבורים אחרות איפה הפרחים?) והמשפט **It's a set of directions** (זו מערכת הוראות דרך) מראים שהריקוד מוסר מקום מזון.
explanation.en: The lecture opens with **How does a honeybee tell the other bees where to find flowers?** and ends: **It's a set of directions**.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what does the length of the bee's straight run show?
options: Which way the other bees should fly to reach the flowers
How much food the patch of flowers can give the hive
How far away the flowers are
Where the sun is in the sky

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the length of the run shows the distance** (אורך הריצה מראה את המרחק), אורך הריצה מלמד כמה רחוקים הפרחים, ואילו הכיוון נקבע לפי כיוון הריצה.
explanation.en: The lecturer says **the length of the run shows the distance**: **The longer she shakes, the farther away the food is**.

items.context: A student visits his astronomy professor during office hours to ask about the seasons.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: male undergraduate, about 20, polite and a little puzzled at first, then relieved, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: female professor, about 50, patient and encouraging, slightly slower, with stress on 'don't support it', 'early January' and 'The tilt'. A short pause at [pause]; 'Two effects, one cause' is said slowly, as a summary.
script: A: Professor, I'm still confused about the seasons. I always thought summer comes when the Earth is closer to the Sun.

B: It's a natural guess, but the numbers don't support it. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, which is the middle of winter up here in the north. And the change in distance over the year is measly, only a few percent.
A: Then what does cause summer?

B: The tilt. Earth's axis leans, so for part of the year our half of the planet leans toward the Sun.   Here, try this makeshift model, a desk lamp and an orange. When the light hits the orange straight on, a small patch gets all of it. When the orange tips away, the same light is spread over a wider area, so each spot gets less.
A: So in summer the sunlight is more direct, and the days are longer, too.
B: Exactly. Two effects, one cause.

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention that Earth is closest to the Sun in early January?
options: To explain why it is winter in the north in January
To show that distance and tilt each cause one of the two effects
To show that the student's idea does not fit the facts
To point out how much the Sun's distance changes during the year

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **It's a natural guess, but the numbers don't support it** (זה ניחוש טבעי, אבל המספרים אינם תומכים בו), עובדת ינואר מפריכה את הרעיון של הסטודנט.
explanation.en: She calls his idea **a natural guess, but the numbers don't support it**, and the January fact is her evidence.

questions.stem: What does the professor use the lamp and the orange to show?
options: The orange warms up more when it is moved closer to the lamp
A tipped orange gets more light than one facing the lamp
Tipping the orange changes how far its surface is from the lamp
Slanted light is spread more thinly over the surface

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **When the orange tips away, the same light is spread over a wider area, so each spot gets less** (כשהתפוז נוטה, אותו אור מתפזר על שטח רחב יותר), ולכן אור שפוגע בזווית חלש יותר בכל נקודה.
explanation.en: The model shows that when the orange tips away, **the same light is spread over a wider area, so each spot gets less**.

items.context: An economics lecturer talks about using numbers to judge how well people do their work.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 55, thoughtful and measured university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Slight emphasis on 'once a measure becomes a target', short pauses at [pause], a light, almost amused tone on 'nobody here needs to be devious', and firm stress on 'isn't that numbers are useless' and 'the link'.
script: Here's a pattern that turns up in schools, hospitals and offices alike. A number starts out as a useful sign of something we care about. Then we reward people for raising that number, and it quietly stops telling us what we wanted to know. Economists sometimes put it this way: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.   Take a school judged mainly by its students' test scores. Teachers spend more time on test practice, scores rise, and yet the skills the test was meant to sample may barely move. Notice that nobody here needs to be devious. People are simply responding, quite sensibly, to what they're rewarded for.   So the lesson isn't that numbers are useless, or that we should stop measuring. It's that heavy pressure on a single figure is injurious to the link between that figure and the thing behind it. Keep several measures, and keep looking past them.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point?
options: Rewarding a figure can loosen its tie to the thing it tracks
Measurement tends to do more harm than good in public services
Targets tempt people to cheat, so the figures they produce become unreliable
Test scores are a poor way to judge what students have learned

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **heavy pressure on a single figure is injurious to the link between that figure and the thing behind it** (לחץ כבד על מספר יחיד פוגע בקשר בין המספר למה שמאחוריו), תגמול על מספר מחליש את הקשר הזה.
explanation.en: The point is not that **numbers are useless** but that **heavy pressure on a single figure is injurious to the link** with what it stands for.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer suggest about the teachers in his example?
options: They are bending the rules to make their school look better
They are reacting reasonably to the way they are rewarded
They now spend less time on test practice than before
Their students' skills improved along with the test scores

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **People are simply responding, quite sensibly, to what they're rewarded for** (אנשים פשוט מגיבים, באופן הגיוני למדי, למה שמתגמלים אותם עליו), המורים אינם מרמים.
explanation.en: The teachers are not cheating: **People are simply responding, quite sensibly, to what they're rewarded for**.

items.context: A literature lecturer talks about the early printed texts of a famous play.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 45, engaging and slightly wry university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Read the quoted line 'To be, or not to be, ay, there's the point' a little slower, as a quotation, with a brief pause before it. Short pauses at each [pause], light stress on 'though' and 'questioned', and a slower, firmer delivery on the last sentence.
script: Most of us picture a famous play as a single, fixed text, the words exactly as the author wrote them. With Shakespeare's Hamlet, that picture runs into trouble. The play survives in three early printed versions, and they don't agree.   The earliest one is much shorter than the other two. Some speeches are missing, some characters have different names, and even the most famous line comes out strangely: To be, or not to be, ay, there's the point. For a long time, scholars treated this first version as a botched copy, full of errors. The usual theory was that it had been cobbled together from memory by an actor who had played a small part, and then passed to a printer.   More recently, though, that confident story has been questioned. The short version moves quickly and works well on stage, so some scholars think it may record a version cut down for performance, or perhaps an early draft that the author later expanded. Nobody can settle the question for certain.   But here's what has changed. Instead of hunting for the one true Hamlet and throwing the rest away, some modern editions now print all three versions, and treat them as possible stages in the life of a play. In other words, the text may never have been fixed in the first place.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's main point?
options: The play may never have existed in one fixed, final form
The shortest version is the most faithful record of the play
An actor's poor memory may explain the gaps in the first version
Editors should search harder for the original wording

explanation.he: לפי המשפט המסכם **the text may never have been fixed in the first place** (ייתכן שהטקסט מעולם לא היה קבוע), העורכים מפסיקים לחפש גרסה אחת ואמיתית (**the one true Hamlet**).
explanation.en: Her summary: **the text may never have been fixed in the first place**, so editors stop **hunting for the one true Hamlet**.

questions.stem: What reason does the lecturer give for doubting the older theory about the first version?
options: Its famous lines turn out to be closer to the familiar wording
Its characters have the same names as in the later versions
The author is known to have written a first draft of the play
The short version runs smoothly when it is acted on a stage

explanation.he: אחרי המילה **though** בא הנימוק: **The short version moves quickly and works well on stage** (הגרסה הקצרה זורמת ועובדת היטב על הבמה).
explanation.en: After **though**, she gives the reason: **The short version moves quickly and works well on stage**.

items.context: Two primatologists discuss research on wild and captive chimpanzees in a seminar.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: male researcher, about 40, doubtful but fair-minded, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute), with a questioning rise on 'rather than learning?' and 'anything like that in chimps?'. B: female researcher, about 50, confident and precise, slightly slower, with stress on 'the same nuts and the same stones', 'just as well' and 'Not convincingly, no'. A short pause at [pause]; A's last line is relaxed and conciliatory.
script: A: I'm still not sure we should call it chimpanzee culture. Different groups do different things, sure, but that might just reflect where they live, different food, different materials lying around.

B: That was a fair worry once. But take nut cracking. In parts of West Africa, chimps crack hard nuts with stone hammers. In forests just across a river, the same nuts and the same stones are there, and the chimps there don't crack them.
A: Couldn't that be a fluke of history, or simply genes, rather than learning?

B: That's where the experiments come in.   In captive groups, researchers taught one chimp a way to open a puzzle box. Her method spread through her group. A neighboring group, started off with a different method, kept its own, even though the other method worked just as well. For me, that clinches it. These habits are picked up from others and passed along.
A: All right, I'll grant that they learn traditions socially. But human culture builds on itself. Each generation improves on what it inherited. Is there anything like that in chimps?
B: Not convincingly, no. Their tool-using prowess is real, but no group seems to have added improvements over many generations.
A: Then maybe we agree more than it seemed. Culture, yes, but not the kind that keeps growing.

questions.stem: Why does the woman describe the experiment with the puzzle box?
options: To show that chimps end up using whichever method works best
To explain how a river can keep neighboring chimp groups apart
To counter the idea that the differences are inborn, not learned
To show that habits spread faster in captivity than they do in the wild

explanation.he: הגבר שואל אם ההבדלים גנטיים (**simply genes, rather than learning**), והמשפט **That's where the experiments come in** (כאן נכנסים הניסויים) עונה לו: ההרגלים נלמדים מאחרים.
explanation.en: The experiments answer the question of **simply genes, rather than learning**: the habits **are picked up from others**.

questions.stem: What do the two speakers agree on by the end of the discussion?
options: Chimp traditions do improve, just more slowly than human ones
Chimps share learned habits, but these do not keep growing
Calling chimpanzee behavior a culture goes too far
Chimps copy one another's habits mainly when kept in captivity

explanation.he: המשפט **Culture, yes, but not the kind that keeps growing** (תרבות כן, אבל לא מהסוג שממשיך לגדול) מסכם את ההסכמה, אחרי המשפט **no group seems to have added improvements** (נראה שאף קבוצה לא הוסיפה שיפורים).
explanation.en: They end on **Culture, yes, but not the kind that keeps growing**, since **no group seems to have added improvements**.

items.title: Why Onions Make Us Cry
paragraphs: Many people cry when they cut onions, but their tears have nothing to do with sadness. The cause is a chemical change that takes place inside the onion as soon as a knife enters it.

An onion is made of many tiny cells. Inside each cell, two kinds of chemicals are kept apart. When a knife breaks the cells, the two chemicals mix and quickly turn into a new gas. When this gas rises and reaches our eyes, it makes them burn, so the eyes produce tears to wash it away.

Scientists believe that the gas helps the onion protect itself. Onions grow under the ground, where many small animals dig for food. If an animal bites into an onion, the gas stings its eyes and nose, so the animal may leave the onion alone and look for other food.

Cooks have found simple ways to cry less. A cold onion helps, because the two chemicals mix more slowly when they are cold. A sharp knife also helps. It cuts cleanly through the onion, but a dull knife crushes it and breaks many more cells. Heat, on the other hand, destroys one of the two chemicals, so no new gas can form in an onion that is being cooked.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain why onions bring tears and how cooks can reduce them
To describe how onions protect themselves from hungry animals
To describe the chemical changes that happen in food when it is cooked
To warn cooks that cutting raw onions can harm their eyes

explanation.he: משפטי הנושא עוברים מהסיבה לדמעות, הצירוף **a chemical change**, אל המשפט **Cooks have found simple ways to cry less**, ולכן המטרה היא להסביר למה בצל מביא דמעות ואיך מפחיתים אותן (הצירוף **reduce them**).
explanation.en: It explains the **chemical change** behind the tears, then says **Cooks have found simple ways to cry less**, so it covers the cause and the cure.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what happens when a knife breaks the cells of an onion?
options: A gas that was stored in the cells escapes into the air.
The cells fill with water and the onion becomes soft.
Two chemicals that were separate join and form a gas.
Tears inside the onion wash the chemicals away.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **two kinds of chemicals are kept apart** והצירוף **the two chemicals mix and quickly turn into a new gas**, שני חומרים שהיו נפרדים (הצירוף **were separate**) מתערבבים ויוצרים גז חדש.
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says the chemicals **are kept apart** until the cells break, and then they **mix and quickly turn into a new gas**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, how does the gas help the onion?
options: It may help the onion take in water from the ground.
It may cause animals to stop eating it.
It warns nearby plants that an animal is coming.
It makes the onion taste sweeter to small animals.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the animal may leave the onion alone and look for other food**, הגז גורם לבעלי חיים לעזוב את הבצל, כלומר להפסיק לאכול אותו (הצירוף **stop eating it**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 says the gas stings an animal, so **the animal may leave the onion alone and look for other food**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "crushes" is closest in meaning to
options: slices neatly through
cools
heats
presses and damages

explanation.he: המילה **but** יוצרת ניגוד בין סכין שחותכת נקי לבין סכין קהה ששוברת הרבה יותר תאים, לפי הצירוף **breaks many more cells**, ולכן פירוש המילה **crushes** הוא מועכת (הצירוף **presses and damages**).
explanation.en: The word **but** contrasts a knife that **cuts cleanly** with one that **breaks many more cells**, so **crushes** means presses and damages.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about onions that are frying in a hot pan?
options: They might lose most of their smell and taste.
They may sting the cook's eyes more than raw onions do.
Their cells become harder while they are cooking.
They will not bring tears to the cook's eyes.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **no new gas can form in an onion that is being cooked**, בבצל שמתבשל לא נוצר גז, והגז הוא שגורם לדמעות, ולכן בצל במחבת לא מביא דמעות לעיני מי שמבשל (הצירוף **bring tears**).
explanation.en: No gas means no tears: **no new gas can form in an onion that is being cooked**, so frying onions will not make the cook cry.

items.title: A Pencil Without Lead
paragraphs: Most people call the dark center of a pencil its "lead." In fact, a pencil contains no lead at all. Lead is a heavy metal that can harm our health. The center of a pencil is made of graphite, a soft black material, mixed with clay.

The wrong name is about five hundred years old. In the 1500s, people in England found a large amount of graphite. It left dark marks on paper, just as lead did, so they believed it was a kind of lead. Scientists later learned the truth, but the old name stayed.

At first, people wrapped thin sticks of graphite in string, because graphite breaks easily and makes fingers dirty. Later, the sticks were placed inside wood. Pure graphite was scarce, however: only a few places had good supplies of it. In the late 1700s, pencil makers found a new method. They mixed graphite powder with clay and baked it. This needed much less pure graphite, so pencils could be made in many more countries.

The clay also let makers control the line. More clay makes the center harder, so it leaves a light, thin line. More graphite makes it softer, and the line becomes darker. That is why many pencils carry letters such as H, for hard, and B, for black.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How the tools that people write with have changed since ancient times
What pencil centers are really made of and how they developed
Why lead is dangerous for people who use pencils
How people in England first found graphite

explanation.he: משפטי הנושא עוברים מהטענה **a pencil contains no lead at all**, דרך מקור השם, אל התערובת של גרפיט וחימר, ולכן הקטע עוסק במה שיש באמת במרכז העיפרון ואיך הוא התפתח (הצירוף **how they developed**).
explanation.en: It begins with **a pencil contains no lead at all**, then explains the old name and the clay mix: what pencil centers are and how they developed.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why did people in the 1500s believe that graphite was lead?
options: It was as heavy as the metal called lead.
Scientists of that time told them it was lead.
It made the same kind of marks on paper.
It was found in the same places as lead.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **It left dark marks on paper, just as lead did**, הגרפיט השאיר על הנייר סימנים כהים כמו עופרת, כלומר אותו סוג של סימנים (הצירוף **the same kind of marks**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says **It left dark marks on paper, just as lead did, so they believed it was a kind of lead**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, why did people wrap graphite sticks in string?
options: The sticks were easy to snap and left marks on fingers.
It made the lines on paper darker and thinner.
There was not yet enough wood in England to cover the sticks.
It kept the graphite from mixing with the clay.
