explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **because graphite breaks easily and makes fingers dirty**, המקלות נשברו בקלות ולכלכו את האצבעות, כלומר היה קל לשבור אותם (הצירוף **easy to snap**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 gives the reason after **because**: **graphite breaks easily and makes fingers dirty**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the word "scarce" is closest in meaning to
options: hard to find
easy to break
soft and black
dangerous to use

explanation.he: לפי ההסבר שאחרי הנקודתיים, הצירוף **only a few places had good supplies of it**, היה גרפיט טהור רק במקומות מעטים, ולכן פירוש המילה **scarce** הוא נדיר, קשה להשיג (הצירוף **hard to find**).
explanation.en: The words after the colon, **only a few places had good supplies of it**, show that **scarce** means hard to find.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about a pencil marked H?
options: It probably makes darker lines than a B pencil does.
Its center probably contains more clay than a B pencil's.
It contains a small amount of lead mixed with the graphite.
It was probably made before the late 1700s.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **More clay makes the center harder** והצירוף **H, for hard**, בעיפרון שמסומן באות **H** יש כנראה יותר חימר (הצירוף **more clay**) מאשר בעיפרון שמסומן באות **B**.
explanation.en: **More clay makes the center harder**, and H stands for **hard**, so an H pencil probably has more clay than a B pencil.

items.title: Liking What We Know: The Mere-Exposure Effect
paragraphs: Most people believe that they like a song, a face or a brand because of its qualities. Research in psychology suggests that something simpler is often involved: people tend to like things more after they have seen or heard them several times, even when the things themselves have not changed. This is known as the mere-exposure effect.

In a typical experiment, volunteers are shown unfamiliar shapes or made-up words. Some items appear once, while others appear many times. Later, the volunteers rate how much they like each one, and the items shown more often usually receive higher ratings. Remarkably, this can happen even when the images flash by too quickly to be remembered.

One common explanation is that familiar things are easier for the brain to process. Because this ease feels pleasant, people may mistake it for genuine liking. Another possible reason is that, for early humans, things met often without harm were probably safe.

The effect has limits, however. It works best for things that people feel neutral about at first; repeated contact with something disliked may only deepen the dislike. Too many repetitions can also turn pleasure into boredom, as when a catchy song becomes cloying after it has been played a hundred times.

The effect may even shape how we see ourselves. In one study, people were shown two photographs of their own face: a normal one and a reversed one, like the image in a mirror. Most preferred the reversed photograph, while their close friends preferred the normal one.

glossary.he: מתקתק ומעיק, נעים מדי עד שנמאס
glossary.en: so sweet or pleasant that it becomes unpleasant

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: People usually prefer a reversed photograph of their own face.
People's tastes are shaped by many different forces, such as culture, age and personal experience.
Meeting something again and again can make it more appealing, up to a point.
People soon grow bored with the things they see or hear many times.

explanation.he: משפטי הנושא עוברים מהאפקט עצמו, הצירוף **the mere-exposure effect**, אל המשפט **The effect has limits, however**, ולכן הרעיון המרכזי הוא שמפגש חוזר מגביר חיבה, אבל רק עד גבול מסוים (הצירוף **up to a point**).
explanation.en: The text presents **the mere-exposure effect** and then says **The effect has limits, however**, so repeated contact raises liking only up to a point.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, the items that were shown more often
options: were easier for the volunteers to recognize and remember
were mostly made-up words rather than shapes
made the volunteers feel bored after a while
were given more favorable scores by the volunteers

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the items shown more often usually receive higher ratings**, הפריטים שהוצגו יותר פעמים קיבלו דירוג גבוה יותר, כלומר ציונים חיוביים יותר (הצירוף **more favorable scores**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says **the items shown more often usually receive higher ratings**, so the volunteers gave them more favorable scores.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what is one common explanation for the effect?
options: Liking something makes the brain process it more easily.
Familiar things remind people of happy times in their past.
People are taught from an early age to trust familiar things.
People confuse the comfort of easy processing with liking.

items.title: Why English Spelling Breaks Its Own Rules
paragraphs: English spelling has long bedeviled learners and native speakers alike. One sound can be written in several ways, as in "blue," "shoe" and "through," while the letters "ough" sound different in "though," "tough" and "cough." Many people assume that the system is simply random, but most of its oddities have historical causes.

The most important cause is timing. Printing reached England in the late 1400s, and over the next two centuries, printers and teachers gradually settled on fixed spellings. Speech, however, kept changing. Between about 1400 and 1700, the pronunciation of many vowels shifted greatly, and some letters stopped being sounded; the "k" and "gh" in "knight" were once both pronounced. As a result, many modern spellings record the way English sounded centuries ago.

Other oddities were added on purpose. In the 1500s, some scholars who admired Latin wanted English words to display their Latin roots. They therefore put a "b" into "debt" and "doubt," which had been spelled without one, because the Latin words contained a "b." English speakers never pronounced the new letter.

Many people have suggested making spelling match sound, but such plans have rarely succeeded. One reason is that writing words exactly as they sound would obscure the links between related words. The silent "g" in "sign," for instance, shows its connection to "signature," where the "g" is heard. In addition, English is spoken with many different accents, so no single spelling could suit them all.

items.title: Why We Get Goosebumps
paragraphs: Most people know the small bumps that rise on their arms on a cold morning. Goosebumps also appear unbidden at other moments, such as during a frightening film or a moving song. They may seem unimportant, but they tell an interesting story about our past.

Every hair grows from a tiny opening in the skin, and a small muscle is attached to its base. When this muscle tightens, it pulls the hair upright and pushes up the skin around it, forming a bump. People cannot produce goosebumps by choice, because these muscles are controlled by the part of the nervous system that works automatically, the same part that makes the heart beat faster under stress.

In furry animals, this reaction is clearly useful. When the hairs stand up, they trap a thicker layer of air close to the skin, which keeps the body warm. Raised fur also makes an animal look larger and may scare away an enemy, as anyone who has seen an angry cat knows. Humans, however, have lost most of their body hair, so the bumps on our skin provide almost no warmth and frighten no one.

For this reason, many scientists describe goosebumps as a leftover from hairy ancestors. Yet recent studies on mice suggest the story is not over: the same nerves and muscles seem to help new hair grow after a cold spell. If this is also true for people, the reflex may still do a modest job for us, though nothing like the important one it does for furry animals.

items.title: Lichens: Tough Partners with a Weak Spot
paragraphs: On old stone walls, tree trunks and rooftops, it is common to see crusty patches of gray, yellow or pale green. Most people pass these unassuming growths without a second glance, or take them for moss. In fact, a lichen is not a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and a tiny green alga that live together as one body.

Each partner supplies what the other lacks. The alga, like a plant, uses sunlight to make sugars, which feed the fungus. The fungus, in turn, forms the body of the lichen, holding water and sheltering the alga from strong light and drying winds. Because of this arrangement, lichens can survive where neither partner could live alone, from desert rock to the edges of polar ice. Many can dry out for months and recover within minutes of rain.

Yet lichens thrive mainly where the air is pristine. The very habit that lets them live on bare rock, where there is no soil, leaves them exposed to dirty air. Lichens have no roots and no protective outer layer, so they absorb water and minerals directly from rain, fog and the air, across their whole surface. Along with what they need, they take in whatever pollutants the air carries, and they have no way to filter these out. Sulfur dioxide, a gas released by burning coal, is especially harmful; in many nineteenth-century industrial cities, lichens almost completely vanished from trees.

This sensitivity has turned lichens into useful tools. Because species differ in how much pollution they can survive, researchers can judge the air in a place by recording which lichens grow there. Leafy and bushy types tend to disappear first, while some flat, crusty ones persist even in fairly polluted streets. Such surveys cost far less than electronic monitors, and since many lichens grow only a few millimeters a year, they reflect the air over many years rather than on a single day. As sulfur pollution has fallen in many places, lichens have been slowly returning to city trees.

items.title: Mine Is Worth More: The Endowment Effect
paragraphs: Imagine being handed a humdrum coffee mug, the kind sold in any campus store. Within minutes, you may refuse to sell it for a price you would happily have paid for it a moment earlier. Economists call this the endowment effect: people tend to value an object more highly simply because it belongs to them. From the point of view of traditional economics, this is puzzling, since a mug's worth should not depend on who happens to be holding it.

The effect has been shown in many experiments with a similar design. Half of the participants receive a mug, and the others receive nothing. Owners are asked for the lowest price at which they would sell; non-owners, for the highest price they would pay. Because the mugs were handed out at random, the two groups should value them about equally. Yet owners typically ask for roughly twice as much as buyers are willing to offer, and as a result, far fewer trades take place than economists would predict.

The most common explanation is that people feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size. For an owner, selling the mug means losing something, whereas for a buyer, getting it is merely a gain. Since the pain of the loss outweighs the pleasure of the gain, owners demand more to give the mug up. Ownership may also create a kind of attachment: once an object is "mine," it can quickly become part of how people see themselves.

The effect is not universal, however. Some studies suggest that it is much weaker among experienced traders, such as dealers who buy goods in order to resell them, perhaps because they see those goods as things to exchange rather than to keep. Businesses, meanwhile, appear to understand the effect well. Free trials and generous return policies let customers take a product home, where it soon begins to feel like their own, and when the time comes to decide, many find it surprisingly hard to give back.

items.title: Where Does a Word End? How Infants Find Words in Speech
paragraphs: In written English, spaces show exactly where each word begins and ends. Speech offers no such help. In ordinary conversation, words run into one another with few pauses, which is why a foreign language often sounds like one long, unbroken stream. Infants face this problem in every language, and they must begin to solve it before they know a single word.

How they do it is still being studied, but one clue seems to be which sounds appear together. Within a word, syllables tend to follow one another in a predictable order, while across word boundaries the order is far less fixed. In the phrase "pretty baby," for example, "pre" is very often followed by "ty," because the two belong to the same word. By contrast, "ty" can be followed by many different syllables, since "pretty" can come before almost any word. A listener who notices which syllables usually go together can therefore guess where words probably end.

In a widely cited experiment, eight-month-old infants heard four made-up words, such as "mekosa," joined together without pauses for about two minutes. The only clue to where each word ended was how reliably one syllable followed another. Because infants tend to pay more attention to sounds they have not heard before, the researchers then measured how long the babies listened to short sequences. The infants listened longer to sequences that crossed the edges of the made-up words than to the words themselves, as if those sequences were relatively novel. Without any instruction, they had become unwitting statisticians.

These results do not mean that statistics alone explain how children learn words. Real speech is far messier than this artificial stream, and infants also rely on other clues, such as the rhythm of stressed syllables and words they often hear on their own, like their names. Still, the infants proved deft at the task, and the same skill appears in surprising places: similar learning has been reported when the stream consisted of musical tones rather than syllables, and even in some monkeys.

items.title: Islands of Heat: Why Cities Stay Warm After Dark
paragraphs: On a sultry summer evening, a person driving out of a large city may notice the air growing cooler with almost every kilometer. This pattern, known as the urban heat island, has been measured in cities around the world. Surprisingly, the gap between city and country is often small at midday. It tends to widen after sunset, and on calm, clear nights a city center can stay several degrees warmer than the farmland around it.

The main cause is the materials that cities are built from. Dark roads and roofs absorb much of the sunlight that falls on them, and stone, brick and concrete store this heat during the day. Whereas open fields lose their warmth soon after sunset, these materials give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by blocking the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away. Cities also have far fewer plants than the countryside. Plants release water through their leaves, and as this water evaporates, it takes heat from the surrounding air.

The extra heat is more than a matter of comfort. Unremitting warmth at night gives the body less chance to recover from a hot day, and heat speeds up the chemical reactions that form some air pollutants. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for air conditioning. Because air conditioners pump heat out of buildings and into the street, while their motors add heat of their own, this response compounds the very problem it is meant to ease.

Several remedies have been proposed. Roofs painted white or covered with pale materials reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it, and they can be installed within weeks. Trees act more slowly, since a young tree may need years to cast much shade. Once grown, however, trees both shade the ground and cool the air through the water they release, so many planners regard them as the better long-term choice.

glossary.en: hot and humid in an unpleasant way

glossary.he: בלתי פוסק, שאינו נרגע או נחלש
glossary.en: never stopping or becoming less strong

explanation.en: The passage moves from the effect (**It tends to widen after sunset**) to its causes, costs and **remedies**: cities stay warmer after dark, causing problems that can be reduced.

explanation.en: Plants release water, and **as this water evaporates, it takes heat from the surrounding air**.

explanation.en: Air conditioners add heat (**while their motors add heat of their own**), so the response **compounds**, or makes worse, the problem.

items.title: One Insect, Two Lives: How Locusts Form Swarms
paragraphs: For most of its existence, the desert locust is an unremarkable grasshopper. Living alone in the deserts between West Africa and India, it is green or sandy brown, flies mainly at night and keeps aloof from others of its kind. Under certain conditions, however, this retiring insect joins a swarm that may contain billions of individuals and can cover hundreds of kilometers in a few days.

So different are the two forms that for a long time they were classified as separate species. Not until the 1920s did researchers establish that they were one and the same animal, capable of switching between a solitary phase and a swarming phase. The swarming form is not only drawn to its neighbors but also strikingly marked: young swarming locusts are a gaudy black and yellow, a pattern that, some studies suggest, may warn birds and lizards that the insects are unpleasant to eat.

What sets off the change is crowding. After heavy rains, desert plants spring up and locust numbers rise quickly; as the land dries out again, the insects are pushed together onto the few green patches that remain. Repeated contact appears to be the decisive signal, in particular the touching of the hind legs by neighbors. In laboratory studies, merely stroking these legs for a few hours was enough to make solitary locusts start seeking out company. The chemical messenger serotonin seems to play a central part, since locusts in which it was blocked did not change.

The shift in behavior takes only a few hours, whereas the full change in color and body shape builds up over several generations. This difference has practical consequences. Once a ravenous swarm has formed, it can strip farmland of its crops over wide areas, and spraying it from the air is costly and only partly effective. Control programs therefore watch the breeding areas, where plant life is normally sparse, for the sudden growth that follows unusual rains, and try to treat the first crowded groups of young locusts before they can fly.

glossary.en: keeping apart from others; distant
too bright and showy in color
extremely hungry; eager to eat a great deal

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?

explanation.en: Its purpose is to explain how crowding (**What sets off the change is crowding**) turns a lone insect into a swarming one, and why this matters for control.

explanation.en: The pattern **may warn birds and lizards that the insects are unpleasant to eat**, so it tells predators the insects taste bad.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **merely stroking these legs for a few hours was enough**, כמה שעות של מגע ברגליים האחוריות הספיקו כדי שארבה בודד יחפש חברה.
explanation.en: In the lab, **merely stroking these legs for a few hours was enough to make solitary locusts start seeking out company**, so lone locusts became sociable.

explanation.he: הצירוף **normally sparse** מנוגד לצמיחה הפתאומית אחרי גשמים (הצירוף **the sudden growth that follows unusual rains**), ולכן המילה **sparse** פירושה דליל (**thinly scattered**).
explanation.en: Plant life that is **normally sparse** contrasts with **the sudden growth that follows unusual rains**, so **sparse** means thinly scattered.

explanation.he: ההתנהגות משתנה תוך שעות (הצירוף **only a few hours**) והצבע לאורך דורות (הצירוף **over several generations**), ולכן ארבה חברותי שעדיין ירוק נמצא כנראה בתחילת השינוי.
explanation.en: Behavior changes in **only a few hours**, color **over several generations**, so a sociable but still green locust is probably early in the change.

items.title: Smarter Than Their Grandparents? The Puzzle of Rising Test Scores
paragraphs: Over much of the twentieth century, average scores on intelligence tests rose in many countries, by roughly three points every ten years. The rise long went unnoticed because of the way such tests are scored. A test's average is set at 100 on a large sample group, and every few decades the test is restandardized on a new group. Only when researchers compared the two sets of results did the pattern become clear: people taking an older version of a test scored well above 100 on its original standards.

Genes cannot change fast enough to explain gains on this scale, which appeared within two or three generations, so the causes must lie largely in the conditions people grow up in. A further clue comes from the shape of the gains. Scores on tests of vocabulary and arithmetic rose only a little, whereas the gains were concentrated in tasks of abstract reasoning, such as finding the rule behind a series of shapes or explaining how two things are alike.

Some proposed explanations are prosaic. Children today are, on average, better fed and healthier than their grandparents were, and they spend more years in school. Another view holds that modern life has trained people to think in a particular way. Asked what a bee and a flower have in common, a person schooled in this way will answer that both are living things; someone from an earlier era might have replied, quite sensibly, that bees feed on flowers. Tests reward the first kind of answer, and the practice of sorting things into abstract classes has spread with schooling.

In recent decades, however, the rise appears to have waned in several wealthy countries, and in a few, scores have even begun to fall. The fall shows up even when younger brothers are compared with their own older brothers, a finding that points away from genetic explanations and toward changes in how children grow up. What those changes might be, whether in schooling, reading or the use of screens, remains a matter of debate.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **people taking an older version of a test scored well above 100 on its original standards**, הנבחנים בגרסה ישנה הצליחו הרבה יותר מקבוצת המקור.
explanation.en: The pattern became clear when **people taking an older version of a test scored well above 100 on its original standards**.

options: Children are now better fed and healthier than their grandparents were.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **Genes cannot change fast enough**, העלייה הופיעה בתוך שניים או שלושה דורות (הצירוף **within two or three generations**), זמן קצר מדי לשינוי גנטי.
explanation.en: **Genes cannot change fast enough** to explain gains that **appeared within two or three generations**: the time was too short.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "concentrated" is closest in meaning to

explanation.he: מילת הניגוד **whereas** מעמידה עלייה קטנה (הצירוף **rose only a little**) מול המשימות המופשטות, ולכן המילה **concentrated** פירושה כאן נמצא בעיקר (**found mostly**).
explanation.en: **whereas** contrasts scores that **rose only a little** with abstract tasks, so **concentrated** means found mostly in those tasks.

questions.stem: What does the author imply about the answer that bees feed on flowers?
options: It reflects a different way of thinking, not a lack of intelligence.

explanation.he: המחבר מכנה את התשובה הגיונית (הצירוף **quite sensibly**) ומייחס את ההבדל לאימון (הצירוף **trained people to think in a particular way**), ולכן היא דרך חשיבה אחרת ולא חוסר אינטליגנציה.
explanation.en: The author says it was given **quite sensibly** and that modern life **trained people to think** differently, so it reflects another way of thinking.

items.title: Stuck with QWERTY? The Debate over a Keyboard
paragraphs: Most keyboards for English still use a layout known, after the first six letters of its top row, as QWERTY. Designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters, machines that have long since vanished, it survives on computers and even on phone touchscreens. It was purportedly arranged to slow typists down, a story repeated far more often than it is checked. The real history is more complicated, and the layout has become a test case in a debate about why weaker designs survive.

In early typewriters, each key moved a metal arm that swung up to strike the paper. When two arms that sat close together were used in quick succession, they could collide and jam. The designers therefore separated many letter pairs common in English, so that their arms would come from different parts of the machine. The aim, in other words, was to keep the machine running smoothly rather than to hold the typist back.

Not until the 1930s did a serious rival appear: a layout that placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, where the fingers rest. Its inventor reported that typists trained on it worked far faster. Yet it never caught on. To some economists, the reason was plain: by then, millions of typists had learned QWERTY, employers expected it, and manufacturers built machines for it. Each of these choices supported the others, so that a standard born of happenstance became almost impossible to dislodge, even, in their view, once a better one existed.

Critics dismiss this account as a fable. Much of the evidence for the rival's superiority, they note, came from studies run by its own inventor, and later comparisons by others found the difference in speed to be small. If so, sticking with a familiar layout is not a trap but a reasonable choice, since retraining millions of typists would cost far more than it could save. The rival still has ardent users, some of whom report less strain on their fingers, but they remain few.

glossary.he: לכאורה, כפי שנטען (אך לא בהכרח נכון)

explanation.en: Neighboring arms used in quick succession **could collide and jam**, so the letters were split up to keep them apart.

explanation.en: Typists had learned it, employers expected it and makers built for it, and **Each of these choices supported the others**.

items.title: Why Flying East Feels Worse: Jet Lag and the Body Clock
paragraphs: Much of the misery travelers feel after a long flight has little to do with cramped seats or dry cabin air. Its main source is a timekeeper in the brain, a small cluster of cells that runs the body on a roughly daily cycle and tells us when to grow sleepy. At home this clock stays in step with the local day; after a rapid crossing of several time zones it does not, and the resulting mismatch is what we call jet lag.

The clock is not fixed, however. Light, especially in the morning, nudges it each day, so a traveler gradually shifts to local time, often at about one time zone per day. Not until it catches up does the body abandon its old routine. Meanwhile, the traveler lies awake at night, feels bleary in the morning and struggles to concentrate. Even meals may sit uneasily, since digestion keeps the old timetable too.

Curiously, direction matters. Most people find a westward trip far easier than an eastward one across the same number of zones. The explanation seems to lie in a quirk of the clock: left without daylight cues, it tends to complete its cycle in a little more than twenty-four hours. Because it already leans toward a later schedule, it can be cajoled into delaying, which is what a flight west demands, with little effort. Flying east requires the opposite. The clock must be advanced, so that the traveler becomes sleepy hours before the body is ready, and this it resists.

This logic shapes common advice. Westbound travelers are often told to spend the late afternoon outdoors, which helps delay the clock. After a long eastward trip, the guidance is less obvious. Light reaching the eyes late in the body's night shifts the clock earlier, but light during its evening shifts it later. Since a traveler's internal evening may fall in the destination's early morning, bright sunshine soon after arrival can push the clock the wrong way, prolonging the very lassitude travelers hope it will cure.

glossary.he: עייף ומטושטש, בעיקר בעיניים, כמו אחרי שינה מעטה
glossary.en: tired and unable to see or think clearly, as after too little sleep

explanation.he: הקטע מגדיר את התופעה כאי-התאמה (**the resulting mismatch**) ומראה שהכיוון משנה, ולכן הרעיון: השעון הפנימי יוצא מהתאמה לשעה המקומית, וכיוון הטיסה קובע כמה קל לתקן זאת (**how readily this is put right**).
explanation.en: Jet lag is **the resulting mismatch** between the inner clock and local time, and since **direction matters**, which way one flies affects how readily it is put right.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following can happen before the inner clock has caught up with local time?
options: The traveler may sleep soundly at night but feel drowsy during the day.

delayed

items.title: Why Old Films Seem to Hurry
paragraphs: Anyone who has watched a film from the early silent era knows the effect. Pedestrians hurry along at an ungainly trot, and crowds move with the jerky haste of wind-up toys. It is tempting to conclude that early filmmakers lacked skill, or even that life itself once moved faster. Neither conclusion holds up. The hurry is, for the most part, an accident of the way these films are shown today.

Early cameras had no motor. An operator turned a crank by hand, usually producing sixteen to twenty frames, or still pictures, per second, though the rate could turn wayward as the arm tired. Operators sometimes cranked slowly on purpose, so that a chase would look faster on screen. Projectors were often hand-cranked as well, and projectionists did not always match the speed at which a film had been shot; some theaters ran films fast to squeeze an extra show into the evening. Audiences seldom objected, since motion looks natural across a fairly wide range of speeds.

The arrival of sound in the late 1920s ended this freedom. Because the sound was locked to the pictures, any change in speed would alter the pitch of voices and music, and the ear, unlike the more forgiving eye, notices even slight changes of that kind. The industry therefore settled on a fixed rate of twenty-four frames per second, which remains the usual standard today. When a film shot at sixteen frames per second is run on equipment built for twenty-four, each second of action is squeezed into two-thirds of a second, and the figures on screen rush accordingly.

Careful restorers now try to recover each film's original pace, often by repeating some frames so that it plays correctly on modern equipment. The results can be striking: walkers stroll, dancers turn graceful, and scenes that once seemed risible regain their intended mood. Such work suggests that our picture of the early twentieth century as a frantic, comic age owes more to machinery than to the people who lived in it.

glossary.en: awkward and clumsy in movement

glossary.he: הפכפך, לא צפוי, סוטה מהמסלול הרצוי
glossary.en: unpredictable; not keeping to the expected course

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To show that the rush in early films comes largely from how they are screened today
To describe how the coming of sound fixed film speed at twenty-four frames per second
To argue that early filmmakers often sped up their scenes to make audiences laugh
To trace how film technology developed from cameras turned by hand to the equipment in use today

explanation.he: פסקה 1 טוענת שהחיפזון הוא תאונה (**for the most part, an accident**) ושאר הפסקאות מסבירות זאת, ולכן המטרה: להראות שהחיפזון בסרטים הישנים נובע בעיקר מאופן ההקרנה היום (**how they are screened today**).

Projectionists obeyed guidelines that arrived with each film.

explanation.en: Because the sound was tied to the pictures, a speed change **would alter the pitch of voices and music**, which the ear notices.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "forgiving" is closest in meaning to
options: willing to excuse the mistakes of others
quick to spot small changes
quickly worn out by effort
not troubled by small differences

explanation.he: העין מנוגדת לאוזן שמבחינה בכל שינוי קטן (הצירוף **notices even slight changes**), ולכן המילה **forgiving** פירושה כאן סלחנית לשינויים, לא מוטרדת מהבדלים קטנים.
explanation.en: The eye is contrasted with an ear that **notices even slight changes**, so **forgiving** means not troubled by small differences.

questions.stem: The author would most likely say that modern viewers who laugh at the hurried figures in a silent film are

explanation.en: The hurry is **for the most part, an accident**, and at the right pace scenes **regain their intended mood**, so the laughter is mostly at an unintended effect.

items.title: The Winner's Curse: When Winning an Auction Means Losing
paragraphs: Winning an auction usually calls for celebration, yet economists have long suspected that the exultant winner is often the bidder who erred most. The suspicion seems to have arisen among engineers studying auctions for the right to drill for oil beneath the sea: winning companies, they noticed, tended to earn disappointing returns, as if victory itself carried a penalty. The pattern became known as the winner's curse.

The curse arises when an item is worth roughly the same to every bidder but no one knows exactly how much, as with an oil field of unknown size. Suppose a dozen firms make honest estimates: some will guess too high, some too low, and on average they may be about right. Yet the highest bidder is, almost by definition, the one whose estimate lay furthest above the truth. Far from signaling superior judgment, then, victory is evidence of overestimation, and a winner who bids the full estimate will, on average, pay too much.

The cure is to bid less than one's estimate, which carries a surprising corollary. Seldom is a crowded field seen as a reason for caution, yet here it is one: the more rivals there are, the further above the truth the highest estimate is likely to lie, so a sensible bidder should shade the bid further as the field grows. Canny bidders appear to grasp this, at least in part. Yet in classroom auctions of coin-filled jars, the average bid often falls below the jar's value while the winning bid exceeds it, sometimes even when participants have been warned.

Not every auction carries this danger. When someone wants an item for purely personal reasons, such as a painting that recalls a childhood home, its value is not an estimate of some hidden quantity, and winning reveals nothing new. The risk lies wherever value is shared but uncertain: companies bidding for rival firms, publishers competing for a promising manuscript and sports teams courting a sought-after player have all, by some accounts, ended up as rueful winners.

glossary.en: very happy and proud because of a success

glossary.he: ממולח, נבון ופיקח, בעיקר בענייני כסף ועסקים
glossary.en: clever and careful, especially in money or business matters
showing regret about something one has done
too confident or proud; excessive

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Companies bidding for offshore drilling rights have often paid more than the oil they found was worth.
Since auction winners usually pay too much, companies would do better to stay away from items whose worth is uncertain.
The price an auction reaches tends to depend on how many people take part and on how much they know.
Where an item's true worth is much the same for all bidders but uncertain, winning often means having overestimated it.

explanation.he: הניצחון מעיד על הערכת יתר (**victory is evidence of overestimation**) כשהערך משותף ולא ודאי, ולכן הרעיון: במצב כזה הזוכה לרוב העריך יתר על המידה (**winning often means having overestimated it**).
explanation.en: When value is **shared but uncertain**, **victory is evidence of overestimation**: winning often means having overestimated the item.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what first led observers to suspect that winning an auction could be costly?
options: Classroom auctions in which the winners of coin-filled jars lost money
The weak earnings of companies that had secured undersea drilling rights

explanation.en: Engineers studying drilling rights saw that **winning companies, they noticed, tended to earn disappointing returns**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is the highest bidder likely to have overestimated the item?
options: Each bidder tends to inflate the estimate on purpose in order to win.
Most estimates of something whose worth is uncertain turn out to lie well above the truth.
The winning offer tends to come from the guess that overshot by the most.
The winner usually has less information than the companies that lose.

explanation.he: כל מציע מציע לפי הערכתו, ולכן ההצעה הגבוהה ביותר באה ממי שהערכתו חרגה יותר מכולם (הצירוף **the one whose estimate lay furthest above the truth**).
explanation.en: The highest bidder is, **almost by definition, the one whose estimate lay furthest above the truth**.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "shade" is closest in meaning to
options: trim somewhat
partly conceal from rivals
drive upward
mimic closely

explanation.he: הפתרון הוא להציע פחות מההערכה (הצירוף **bid less than one's estimate**), ולכן המילה **shade** פירושה כאן להוריד מעט את ההצעה ככל שמספר המתחרים גדל.
explanation.en: The cure is to **bid less than one's estimate**, so to **shade** the bid means to trim it somewhat.

questions.stem: The results of the classroom auctions described in the passage suggest that
options: adding more bidders to the room would have raised the average bid above the jar's value
a winner can overpay even when the typical bid is below the item's worth
warning bidders about the curse is enough to prevent it

explanation.he: ההצעה הממוצעת נמוכה מהשווי אך ההצעה הזוכה גבוהה ממנו (הצירוף **the winning bid exceeds it**); מכאן שהזוכה יכול לשלם ביתר גם כשרוב ההצעות נמוכות.
explanation.en: Since **the average bid often falls below the jar's value while the winning bid exceeds it**, a winner can overpay even when typical bids are low.

items.title: Teaching to Learning Styles: A Popular Idea Put to the Test
paragraphs: Few ideas in education are as widely held as the notion that each student has a preferred learning style, whether visual, auditory or hands-on, and learns best when lessons are pitched to it. In surveys conducted in several countries, a large majority of teachers have said they espouse the idea, and questionnaires that sort pupils into types are sold to schools and parents alike. Its appeal is easy to understand: it honors individual differences and seems to explain why a lesson that delights one child leaves another cold.

Testing the idea, however, is harder than it first appears. It is not enough to show that people have preferences, which they plainly do, or that some method works well for learners in general. An unimpeachable test would first sort learners by style, then teach some of each type in a matching way and others in a mismatched way. Only if visual learners did better with pictures while auditory learners did better with spoken explanations could the theory claim support.

When reviewers went looking for studies of this kind, they found surprisingly few, and most of those failed to show the predicted pattern. Learners who described themselves as visual, for example, did not reliably remember pictures better than words. Critics do not quibble with the existence of preferences; their point is that preferences seem to be a poor guide to how people actually learn. Hardly any of the well-designed studies has borne out the central claim.

What appears to matter more is the material itself. A map shows the layout of a region better than any description, and the sound of a language is best learned by listening, whatever a student's supposed type. Many researchers therefore warn that such pigeonholing may do quiet harm, steering pupils away from the very methods a subject demands. That the theory survives at all, they suggest, says more about its intuitive charm than about the evidence.

glossary.he: לאמץ רעיון או עמדה ולתמוך בהם
glossary.en: to adopt or support an idea or cause
so reliable that it cannot be doubted
to argue about small, unimportant details

glossary.he: תיוג וסיווג נוקשה ומצמצם של אנשים

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?

To argue that teachers should stop taking their students' differences into account

explanation.en: Support requires that **visual learners did better with pictures while auditory learners did better with spoken explanations**.

explanation.en: Self-described visual learners **did not reliably remember pictures better than words**; the answer restates this without going further.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the phrase "borne out" is closest in meaning to

questions.stem: Why does the author mention a map and the sound of a language?

items.title: Costly Signals: Why a Peacock's Train Can Be Trusted
paragraphs: Few sights in nature seem as wasteful as the peacock's sumptuous train. Its long, eye-spotted feathers take months to grow, can slow the bird when it flees and make it easy for predators to spot. Natural selection is expected to weed out traits that hamper survival, yet this one has persisted. Part of the answer is that peahens favor males with larger, more elaborate trains. But that merely moves the puzzle back a step: why should females prefer an ornament that serves no practical purpose?

One influential explanation holds that the cost is not a flaw in the signal but the very source of its value. Carrying a heavy train is hard even for a healthy male; a sickly one bearing the same load would soon fall prey to a predator. Because only a vigorous male can maintain such a display, the display becomes reliable evidence of vigor. Far from being hoodwinked by a pretty ornament, then, a female who chooses by tail size is in effect judging a quality she cannot observe directly.

The logic becomes clearer when costly signals are compared with cheap ones. A signal that costs nothing to produce can be sent by anyone, so it carries little information: if a weak male could grow a splendid train as easily as a strong one, females would gain nothing by attending to it. Costly signals resist such subterfuge, since a display that taxes a strong animal would ruin a weak one.

When the idea was proposed in the 1970s, many biologists were incredulous: it seemed to imply that evolution would favor waste. Later mathematical models suggested that the principle can work, though under narrower conditions than its supporters had first claimed; a signal may also stay honest without being especially costly, as long as cheats are detected and punished. Few researchers today regard cost as the only route to honesty, yet the core insight has survived: what makes a signal believable is less what it says than what it would cost a liar to say it.

glossary.en: splendid and expensive-looking; lavish
tricked or deceived
a trick or dishonest method used to hide the truth or get one's way
unable or unwilling to believe something

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

explanation.en: The passage explains a wasteful ornament: **the cost is not a flaw in the signal but the very source of its value**, since only a strong male can bear it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which explanation of the peacock's train does no more than shift the puzzle to a new question?

explanation.en: The females' preference for big trains **merely moves the puzzle back a step**: it raises the new question of why they prefer a useless ornament.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a peahen that selects a mate by the size of his train is actually assessing

how many months he has spent growing his long feathers

the beauty of a pretty ornament that serves no practical purpose

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **a quality she cannot observe directly** (תכונה שהיא אינה יכולה לראות ישירות), הנקבה בודקת למעשה את החיוניות של הזכר (**vigor**), כלומר את בריאותו וכוחו.
explanation.en: The female is **in effect judging a quality she cannot observe directly**: the male's **vigor**, that is, his health and strength.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "taxes" is closest in meaning to
options: wins admiration for
sets apart from rivals
puts heavy demands on

explanation.he: לפי ההמשך **would ruin a weak one** (הייתה הורסת בעל חיים חלש), הפועל **taxes** מתאר עומס כבד, כלומר הצירוף **puts heavy demands on** (מעמיס דרישות כבדות, מתיש).
explanation.en: Since the same display **would ruin a weak one**, **taxes** must mean puts heavy demands on, not anything positive or financial.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the idea's early supporters
options: overstated the range of cases in which it holds
lost faith in it once mathematical models were built
were themselves incredulous when it was first proposed

explanation.en: Models showed it works **under narrower conditions than its supporters had first claimed**, so the supporters overstated its range.

items.title: Sealed Before It Was Understood: The Early Years of Canned Food
paragraphs: For most of history, the chief ways to keep food from turning putrid were to dry, salt, smoke or pickle it, each of which altered its taste. Around 1800, a Paris confectioner found an alternative. He packed cooked food into thick glass bottles, sealed them tightly with cork and wax, and then heated them in boiling water for hours. Food treated in this way could last for months, sometimes years, and still taste nearly fresh. What he could not do was say why.

The usual explanation of the day held that air was the agent of decay, and that heating somehow expelled or altered whatever air remained inside. The theory was mistaken, yet the steps it recommended worked. Unbeknownst to anyone, the heat was killing the microbes that make food rot, while the tight seal kept new ones from entering. Not until the 1860s did experiments show that living organisms, rather than air itself, were responsible for spoilage.

Because the real cause was unknown, failures remained unaccountable. Some batches spoiled while others prepared in the same way did not, and cans sometimes swelled as gas built up inside. Larger containers failed more often, it was eventually realized, because heat took longer to reach their centers. Manufacturers working without a theory could adjust heating times only by trial and error, and those who shortened them to save fuel sometimes paid for it with spoiled stock. Only once the role of microbes was established could heating times be calculated rather than guessed.

The container, too, developed in an unexpected order. Within a few years, English makers had replaced fragile glass with cans of iron coated in tin, which were lighter and did not shatter. Yet these early cans were so thick that opening one was an irksome business, usually done with a hammer and chisel. A tool designed for the purpose seems to have appeared only decades later, once thinner cans had come into use. Like its science, the convenience of canned food trailed well behind the method itself.

glossary.en: decaying and smelling very bad
without someone knowing
impossible to explain
annoying and tiresome

questions.stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: how English makers soon replaced glass bottles with cans of tin-coated iron
how early food makers came to realize that air is what makes food decay
the many different methods that people have used over the centuries to stop food from rotting

explanation.he: הממציא לא ידע להסביר למה השיטה עובדת (**What he could not do was say why**), ולכן הרעיון: שיטת שימור שעבדה הרבה לפני שהובנה או נעשתה נוחה (**worked long before it was understood or made convenient**).
explanation.en: The method worked before anyone could **say why**, and its convenience **trailed well behind the method itself**: the method worked long before it was understood or made convenient.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the method succeeded despite a mistaken theory because
options: the steps it called for happened to deal with the true cause of decay
the confectioner himself rejected the usual explanation of his day
the heat drove out the air that had been left inside the sealed bottles
experiments in the 1860s showed how long the food needed to be heated

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the heat was killing the microbes** (החום המית את החיידקים) והצירוף **the tight seal kept new ones from entering**, הצעדים עצמם טיפלו בגורם האמיתי למרות ההסבר השגוי.
explanation.en: The steps worked because **the heat was killing the microbes** and **the tight seal kept new ones from entering**, even though the theory was wrong.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why were larger containers more likely to fail?
options: Their seals let in more of the air than the seals of smaller ones did.
Manufacturers heated them for a shorter time in order to save fuel.
The heat needed more time to penetrate to the middle of the food.
Gas built up inside them more quickly than in smaller ones.

explanation.he: הצירוף **because heat took longer to reach their centers** (כי לחום לקח יותר זמן להגיע למרכזם) מסביר את הכישלון: מרכז המכל הגדול לא התחמם מספיק.
explanation.en: Larger containers failed **because heat took longer to reach their centers**, so the middle of the food was not heated enough.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word "it" in "paid for it" refers to
options: the fuel that the manufacturers wanted to save
the choice to cut heating times short
the method of trial and error
the theory that the manufacturers lacked

explanation.he: בצירוף **those who shortened them to save fuel sometimes paid for it**, מי שנשא במחיר הוא מי שקיצר את החימום, ולכן המילה **it** מציינת את ההחלטה לקצר את זמני החימום.
explanation.en: In **those who shortened them to save fuel sometimes paid for it**, the price was paid for the shortening, so **it** is the choice to cut heating times.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the last paragraph?

To suggest that the earliest cans were often unsafe to eat from
To show how the discovery of microbes changed the way cans were made
To add a further case in which canning's progress followed a surprising sequence

explanation.he: הפסקה נפתחת במשפט **The container, too, developed in an unexpected order** (גם המכל התפתח בסדר לא צפוי), והמילה **too** מסמנת מקרה נוסף של אותו פער.
explanation.en: The paragraph opens with **The container, too, developed in an unexpected order**; **too** marks a second example of the same gap.

items.title: Shared Pastures: Must Common Resources Be Ruined?
paragraphs: A well-known argument holds that a resource left open to untrammeled use is bound to be ruined. Picture a pasture on which every villager may graze cattle. Each herder who adds an animal gains the full benefit of it, while the harm that one more animal does to the grass is spread among everyone. Reasoning this way, each herder keeps adding animals until the pasture is grazed bare. The remedy seemed equally clear: shared land must either be divided into private plots or placed under the control of a government.

The argument proved influential, but later field research painted a more complicated picture. Investigators who studied mountain meadows, village forests, irrigation canals and coastal fisheries found communities that had drawn on such resources for generations, sometimes centuries, without exhausting them. Many of these groups had neither split their land into private holdings nor surrendered it to outside authorities. They had instead devised rules of their own.

The rules varied with local conditions, yet certain features recurred. Who might use the resource was clearly defined, so that outsiders could be kept away. The users themselves usually helped make and revise the rules, and they policed one another rather than relying on distant officials. Penalties tended to escalate: a first offense might bring a small fine or a warning, while repeated violations brought heavier ones. Such a scheme deters persistent cheats without turning a contrite neighbor who erred once into an enemy.

In hindsight, the original argument described not shared ownership as such but a resource that no one controls, used by people who cannot communicate or enforce an agreement. Real herders are seldom so hamstrung. Even so, the field studies offer no universal cure. The arrangements they describe tend to work best for small, stable groups with clear boundaries, and grow far harder to sustain when users are numerous, anonymous or scattered, as on the open ocean. The gloomy prediction, then, is less a law of nature than a warning about what happens when rules are absent.

glossary.en: not limited or restricted in any way
feeling sorry for having done something wrong
severely limited and unable to act effectively

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Herders who share a pasture tend to add animals until the grass is gone, because each herder pays just part of the cost.
Field studies show that shared resources are best managed by local communities rather than by governments or by private owners of land.
Shared resources need not be ruined, since their overuse tends to reflect a lack of workable rules rather than sharing itself.
How people use land and water tends to vary from one society to another.

explanation.he: המשפט המסכם קורא לתחזית אזהרה ולא חוק טבע (**less a law of nature than a warning**), ולכן הרעיון: משאב משותף אינו חייב להיהרס, כי השימוש המופרז נובע מהיעדר כללים (**a lack of workable rules**) ולא מהשיתוף עצמו.
explanation.en: The closing sentence calls the prediction **less a law of nature than a warning about what happens when rules are absent**, so shared resources need not be ruined.

questions.stem: According to the argument described in the passage, why does each herder keep adding animals?
options: He fears that unless he acts first, the other herders will take the grass for their own herds.
He reaps the whole benefit of an extra cow but bears only a share of the harm.
The government has set no limit on the number of cattle he may keep.
He fails to notice that the grass is slowly being grazed bare.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **gains the full benefit of it** (מקבל את כל התועלת) והצירוף **is spread among everyone** (מתחלק בין כולם), הרועה מרוויח הכול ונושא רק בחלק מהנזק.
explanation.en: Each herder **gains the full benefit of it**, while the harm **is spread among everyone**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the users of these resources typically
options: left the enforcement of their rules to officials who lived far away
admitted outsiders who agreed to respect local customs
punished first offenses as severely as repeated ones
had a hand in drawing up and changing the rules

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **The users themselves usually helped make and revise the rules** (המשתמשים עצמם עזרו בדרך כלל לקבוע ולשנות את הכללים), הם היו שותפים לניסוח הכללים.
explanation.en: The passage says **The users themselves usually helped make and revise the rules**, so they had a hand in drawing them up and changing them.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "policed" is closest in meaning to
options: kept watch over and disciplined
reported their misdeeds to the authorities
protected from outsiders
taught the rules to

explanation.he: המילה **policed** באה בניגוד לצירוף **rather than relying on distant officials** (במקום להסתמך על פקידים רחוקים), ולכן פירושה לפקח ולהעניש (**kept watch over and disciplined**).
explanation.en: Users **policed one another rather than relying on distant officials**: they kept watch over and disciplined each other themselves.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the original argument
options: has been refuted by studies of fisheries and forests
rested on an assumption about people that rarely holds in practice
was intended mainly as a description of mountain meadows
was eventually accepted as sound by most of the researchers who went into the field

explanation.he: הטיעון הניח אנשים שאינם יכולים לתקשר או לאכוף הסכם (הצירוף **cannot communicate or enforce an agreement**), אבל לפי המשפט **Real herders are seldom so hamstrung** רועים אמיתיים כמעט אינם כבולים כך.
explanation.en: The argument assumed people who **cannot communicate or enforce an agreement**, yet **Real herders are seldom so hamstrung**.

items.stem: Ben went to bed early on Friday because he was very tired.
options: Ben went to bed early on Friday, so he was very tired.
On Friday, Ben felt very tired, so he went to bed early.
Ben went to bed early on Friday.
Ben went to bed late on Friday because he was very tired.

explanation.he: המילה **because** (כי, בגלל ש-) מציגה את הסיבה: בן היה עייף מאוד, ולכן הלך לישון מוקדם, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הקשר הזה בעזרת המילה **so** (לכן).
explanation.en: **Because** gives the reason: Ben was very tired, so he went to bed early, and the correct answer keeps this link with **so**.

items.stem: Our neighbor's dog was found by two children near the river.
options: Two children lost our neighbor's dog near the river.
Two children found a dog by the river.
Near the river, our neighbor's dog found two children.
Near the river, two children found our neighbor's dog.

explanation.he: המבנה **was found by two children** (נמצא על ידי שני ילדים) אומר שהילדים הם אלה שמצאו את הכלב, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על התפקידים האלה במשפט פעיל, בצירוף **two children found** (שני ילדים מצאו).
explanation.en: **Was found by two children** means that the children did the finding, and the correct answer keeps this in the active form **two children found**.

items.stem: If it rains on Saturday, we will play basketball in the gym.

explanation.en: The condition **If it rains on Saturday** says when they play in the gym, and the correct answer keeps it as **if the weather is rainy**.

items.stem: Most of the students in my class bring lunch from home, but a few buy food at school.
options: In my class, most students bring their lunch from home, while a small number buy food at school.
Most of the students in my class bring lunch from home, but a few forget it at school.

In my class, a small number of students bring lunch from home, and most buy food at school.

explanation.he: הצירוף **Most of the students** (רוב התלמידים) והצירוף **a few** (מעטים) קובעים מי מביא אוכל מהבית ומי קונה בבית הספר, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם בצירוף **most students** ובצירוף **a small number** (מספר קטן).
explanation.en: **Most of the students** and **a few** show who brings lunch and who buys food, and the correct answer keeps both as **most students** and **a small number**.

items.stem: Many cities now have bike lanes, and cyclists say that the lanes make them feel safer.
options: Cyclists report feeling safer thanks to the bike lanes that many cities now have.
Drivers report that bike lanes make them feel safer, and many cities now have them too.

explanation.en: **Make them feel safer** describes only a feeling of the cyclists, and the correct answer keeps it, while the option about removing the danger exaggerates.

items.stem: Mia could not hear the teacher because the room was very noisy.
options: The room was noisy, but Mia could hear the teacher.

The room was very noisy, so Mia could not hear the teacher.

explanation.he: המילה **because** (כי) מסמנת שהרעש הוא הסיבה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הקשר הזה בעזרת המילה **so** (לכן) אחרי הצירוף **the room was very noisy**.
explanation.en: **Because** makes the noise the reason, and the correct answer keeps this link with **so** after **the room was very noisy**.

items.stem: Our school was visited last year by a famous writer, who read stories to the younger children.

items.stem: Although the ferry ride takes longer than the bridge, many commuters prefer it because the tickets are cheaper and the seats are more comfortable.
options: Although the tickets are cheaper and the seats are more comfortable on the ferry, many commuters prefer the bridge because the ferry ride takes longer.
Despite taking longer than the bridge, the ferry is preferred by many commuters for its cheaper tickets and more comfortable seats.
Many commuters choose the ferry over the bridge, since the tickets are cheaper and the seats are more comfortable.

explanation.he: המילה **Although** (אף על פי ש-) מציגה ניגוד: המעבורת איטית יותר ובכל זאת נוסעים רבים מעדיפים אותה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הניגוד הזה בצירוף **Despite taking longer** (למרות שהנסיעה בה ארוכה יותר).
explanation.en: **Although** sets up a contrast: the ferry is slower, yet many commuters prefer it, and the correct answer keeps this with **Despite taking longer**.

items.stem: Most of the trees along the street survived the dry summer, but some of the younger ones died.
options: Most of the older trees along the street died during the dry summer, while the younger ones survived.

More than half of the street's trees lived through the dry summer, though some of the younger ones did not.

explanation.he: הצירוף **Most of the trees** (רוב העצים) והצירוף **some of the younger ones** (חלק מהצעירים) קובעים כמה שרדו וכמה מתו, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת עליהם בצירוף **More than half of** (רוב) ובצירוף **some of the younger ones**.
explanation.en: **Most of the trees** survived and **some of the younger ones** died; the correct answer keeps both amounts as **More than half** and **some of the younger ones**.

items.stem: The map of the old harbor was drawn by a sailor who had learned the coastline from a local fisherman.
options: A sailor drew the map of the old harbor after he had taught a local fisherman the coastline.

A local fisherman who had learned the coastline from a sailor drew the map of the old harbor.
After a local fisherman had taught him the coastline, a sailor drew the map of the old harbor.

explanation.en: **Was drawn by a sailor** names the mapmaker and **from a local fisherman** names the teacher, and the correct answer keeps both roles in the active form.

items.stem: Glass has been used for windows for many centuries because it is made from sand, which is cheap and easy to find.
options: Glass has served as a window material for many centuries, because the sand it is made from is cheap and easy to find.

explanation.he: הסיבה **made from sand, which is cheap and easy to find** (עשויה מן החול, שהוא זול וקל למצוא) כוללת שלושה חלקים, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שלושתם.
explanation.en: The reason **made from sand, which is cheap and easy to find** has three parts, and the correct answer keeps all three.

items.stem: When the bell rang, the students were already sitting at their desks, so the lesson started on time.
options: The students were not sitting at their desks when the bell rang, so the lesson started a little late.

explanation.he: הצירוף **were already sitting** (כבר ישבו) מראה שהישיבה קרתה לפני הצלצול, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הסדר הזה בצירוף **had already sat down** (כבר התיישבו) ובצירוף **before the bell rang** (לפני שהפעמון צלצל).
explanation.en: **Were already sitting** puts the sitting before the bell, and the correct answer keeps that order with **had already sat down** and **before the bell rang**.

items.stem: Researchers believe that regular exercise may help older adults remember things more easily, although the evidence is still limited.
options: Although the evidence is still limited, researchers believe that regular exercise may help older adults remember things for longer.

Older adults who remember things more easily may exercise regularly, researchers believe, although the evidence is still limited.

explanation.he: הצירוף **may help** (אולי יעזור) והצירוף **still limited** (עדיין מוגבלות) מראים זהירות, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם, ואילו האפשרות עם הצירוף **have proved** (הוכיחו) מגזימה.
explanation.en: **May help** and **still limited** show caution, and the correct answer keeps both, while **have proved** exaggerates.

items.stem: Even though lightning appears to strike at random, tall and pointed objects are hit far more often than flat ground, which is why many buildings are fitted with metal rods.
options: Although lightning looks random, it hits tall, pointed objects so much more often than flat ground that it rarely reaches level land, which is why many buildings are fitted with metal rods.

explanation.he: המילים **Even though** (אף על פי ש-) מציגות ויתור, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת עליו בעזרת המילה **yet** (ובכל זאת) ושומרת גם על הסיבה למוטות המתכת בעזרת הצירוף **this is the reason**.
explanation.en: **Even though** sets up a concession, and the correct answer keeps it with **yet** and keeps the reason for the metal rods with **this is the reason**.

items.stem: Few of the office staff in the study walked to work, but those who did took noticeably fewer sick days than colleagues who drove.
options: A small proportion of office staff in the study walked to work, but these walkers took noticeably fewer sick days than colleagues who drove.
Most of the office staff in the study walked to work, but those who did took noticeably fewer sick days than colleagues who drove.

explanation.he: המילה **Few** (מעטים) קובעת שרק מיעוט קטן הלך ברגל לעבודה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הכמות בעזרת הצירוף **a small proportion of** (חלק קטן מ-) ועל התוצאה בעזרת הצירוף **noticeably fewer sick days**.
explanation.en: **Few** means that only a small group walked, and the correct answer keeps this quantity with **a small proportion of** and the result with **noticeably fewer sick days**.

items.stem: Although many people believe that they work better under pressure, a survey of project teams suggests that tight deadlines usually lower the quality of the final product.
options: Although many people believe that they work better under pressure, a survey of project teams clearly shows that tight deadlines seriously damage the quality of the final product.

A survey of project teams suggests that people who believe they work better under pressure usually lower the quality of the final product by setting tight deadlines.

explanation.he: המילה **suggests** (מרמז) והמילה **usually** (בדרך כלל) מרככות את הטענה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת עליהן בעזרת המילה **indicates** והמילה **typically**, בלי להגזים ובלי להפוך את הכיוון.
explanation.en: **Suggests** and **usually** soften the claim, and the correct answer keeps both softeners with **indicates** and **typically**, without exaggerating or reversing the direction.

items.stem: The first exam was written by the university's lecturers, but its questions were reworded by a testing company, which also marked the answers.
options: The first exam was written by a testing company, and the university's lecturers then changed the wording of its questions and marked the answers.
The university's lecturers wrote the first exam, but it was a testing company that reworded its questions and also marked the answers.
The first exam, written by the university's lecturers, had its questions reworded and its answers marked by a testing company, which was paid an exiguous fee.
The university's lecturers marked the answers to the first exam, which they had written, while a testing company reworded its questions.

explanation.he: הצירוף **which also marked the answers** (שגם בדקה את התשובות) מראה שהחברה, ולא המרצים, בדקה את התשובות, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על התפקידים בעזרת המבנה **it was a testing company that**.
explanation.en: **Which also marked the answers** gives the marking to the testing company, not the lecturers, and the correct answer keeps every role with **it was a testing company that**.

items.stem: Although the new battery charges in just ten minutes, it lasts fewer hours than older models and must be replaced after roughly two years of regular use.
options: The new battery charges in just ten minutes but lasts fewer hours than older models.
The new battery runs for a shorter time than older models because it is smaller, and it must be replaced after roughly two years of regular use, although a full charge takes just ten minutes.
Because the new battery must be replaced after roughly two years of regular use, it charges in just ten minutes and lasts fewer hours than older models.
The new battery needs just ten minutes to charge, yet it does not run as long as older ones, and it has to be replaced after roughly two years of regular use.

explanation.he: כדאי לפרק את המשפט לשלוש יחידות: טעינה מהירה (**charges in just ten minutes**), חיי סוללה קצרים (**lasts fewer hours**) והחלפה אחרי כשנתיים (**replaced after roughly two years**), והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שלושתן.
explanation.en: The original has three units, **charges in just ten minutes**, **lasts fewer hours** and **must be replaced**, and the correct answer keeps all three and adds nothing.

items.stem: Unless farmers near the lake use less fertilizer, the algae that have spread over its surface in recent summers will probably keep growing.
options: As long as farmers near the lake use less fertilizer, the algae that have left its water turbid over the past few summers will probably keep growing.
