items.stem: Once all but extinct in the wild, the antelope now roams several reserves, though not every herd released into them has survived without the rangers' ministrations.
options: Once all but extinct in the wild, the antelope now roams several reserves, and every herd released into them has survived without the rangers' ministrations.
The antelope, which had nearly vanished from the wild, now lives in several reserves, though some of the herds set free there have been unable to survive without rangers' care.
Having almost died out in the wild, the antelope can now be found in several reserves, but most of the herds released into them have had to rely on the rangers to keep them alive.
Herds of the antelope roamed several reserves until all but a few of them died out, so rangers now care for every herd that is released into the wild.

explanation.he: הצירוף **all but extinct** פירושו כמעט נכחד, והצירוף **not every herd** פירושו שחלק מהעדרים לא שרדו בלי עזרה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם בצירופים **nearly vanished** ו-**some of the herds**.
explanation.en: **All but extinct** means almost extinct, and **not every herd** means some herds needed help; the correct answer keeps both with **nearly vanished** and **some of the herds**.

items.stem: Were it not for the heat trapped by gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide, the average temperature at Earth's surface would be well below freezing, a climate inimical to most life.
options: The heat that gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide trap is what keeps the average temperature at Earth's surface well below freezing, a climate inimical to most life.

If Earth's atmosphere lacked water vapor, carbon dioxide and the other gases that trap heat, its surface would freeze solid from the poles to the equator, and hardly any form of life could survive there.
Gases like water vapor and carbon dioxide trap heat, and without that heat Earth's average surface temperature would drop far below freezing, producing conditions hostile to most life.
Gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide trap so much heat that the average temperature at Earth's surface stays well above freezing, a climate inimical to most life.

explanation.he: המבנה **Were it not for** פירושו 'אלמלא', כלומר בלי החום שהגזים לוכדים הטמפרטורה הייתה נמוכה בהרבה מנקודת הקיפאון, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על כך בצירוף **without that heat** (בלי החום הזה).
explanation.en: **Were it not for** means without, so the trapped heat keeps Earth from being well below freezing, and the correct answer keeps this with **without that heat**.

items.stem: Much to the chagrin of the professional astronomers who had predicted its return, the comet was first spotted not by any of them but by an amateur with a homemade telescope.
options: An amateur with a homemade telescope sighted the comet before any of the professional astronomers who had forecast its return did, and this greatly annoyed them.
Much to the chagrin of an amateur with a homemade telescope, the comet whose return he had predicted was first spotted by professional astronomers.
The comet was spotted by an amateur with a homemade telescope before the professional astronomers had even predicted its return, which left them deeply embarrassed.
The professional astronomers who had predicted the comet's return were chagrined to learn that an amateur had built a better homemade telescope than any of theirs.

explanation.he: הצירוף **not by any of them but by an amateur** אומר שהחובב ראה את השביט לפני המקצוענים שחזו את חזרתו, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על כך בצירוף **before any of the professional astronomers** (לפני כל אחד מהמקצוענים).
explanation.en: **Not by any of them but by an amateur** means the amateur saw the comet before the professionals who predicted it, and the correct answer keeps these roles.

items.stem: No article in an openly edited online encyclopedia is safe from vandalism, but errors on its most-viewed pages are, as a rule, expunged within minutes, whereas those on obscure pages may linger for months.
options: Although any article in an openly edited online encyclopedia can be vandalized, errors on most of its pages are usually corrected within minutes, whereas those on obscure pages may linger for months.

Vandalism can strike any of the articles in an openly edited online encyclopedia, and although errors on its most-viewed pages are quickly expunged, its obscure pages are riddled with mistakes that linger for months on end.
Vandals who target the most-viewed pages of an openly edited online encyclopedia are, as a rule, caught within minutes, whereas those who target obscure pages may go unnoticed for months.

Any article in a freely editable online encyclopedia may be vandalized; still, mistakes on the pages people read most are usually removed within minutes, while those on little-known pages can stay for months.

explanation.he: הצירוף **its most-viewed pages** מגביל את התיקון המהיר לדפים הנצפים ביותר והמילה **may** מסייגת, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם בצירופים **the pages people read most** ו-**can stay** (עלולות להישאר).
explanation.en: **Its most-viewed pages** limits the quick fixes and **may** hedges the delay, and the correct answer keeps both with **the pages people read most** and **can stay**.

items.stem: Unable to write down every word, students who take lecture notes by hand must reduce what they hear to pithy summaries, which may help them remember the material better than classmates who type.
options: Students who take lecture notes by hand remember the material better than classmates who type, which might be why they can reduce what they hear to pithy summaries instead of writing down every word.
Students who handwrite their lecture notes cannot record everything that is said, so they have to sum it up briefly, and this might give them an advantage in recall over classmates using a keyboard.
Unable to write down every word, students who take lecture notes by hand must reduce what they hear to pithy summaries, which makes them remember the material far better than classmates who type.
Classmates who type their lecture notes can write down every word, so they remember the material better than students who must boil what they hear down to short summaries by hand.

explanation.he: הצירוף **Unable to write down every word** הוא הסיבה לסיכום והמילה **may** מסייגת את היתרון, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם בצירופים **so they have to sum it up** ו-**might give them an advantage** (עשוי לתת להם יתרון).
explanation.en: **Unable to write down every word** gives the cause of the summaries and **may** hedges the memory gain, and the correct answer keeps both with **so** and **might**.

items.stem: Far fewer onlookers notice a sartorial blunder than the person who made it tends to imagine, though it would be rash to conclude that such a blunder goes entirely unnoticed.
options: Those who make a fashion mistake usually think many more people see it than really do, but it would be unwise to assume that nobody sees it.
Usually only a handful of onlookers notice a sartorial blunder, though it would be rash to claim that it passes entirely unnoticed.
Onlookers notice a blunder in someone's clothing far less often than the person who made it tends to fear, and it would be rash to assume that anyone notices it.
People who commit a sartorial blunder tend to imagine that far fewer onlookers notice it than actually do, though it would be rash to say it goes entirely unnoticed.

explanation.he: הצירוף **Far fewer ... than ... tends to imagine** אומר שמי שטעה מגזים בהערכה, והאזהרה **rash to conclude ... entirely unnoticed** אומרת שיש רואים, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שניהם בצירוף **many more ... than really do**.
explanation.en: **Far fewer ... than ... tends to imagine** means the wearer overestimates, and **rash to conclude ... entirely unnoticed** means some do notice; the correct answer keeps both.

items.stem: Ben forgot his keys, so he could not ________ the front door.
options: wash
carry
open
paint

explanation.he: הצירוף **forgot his keys** (שכח את המפתחות) מראה שבן לא יכול היה להיכנס, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **open** (לפתוח).
explanation.en: **Forgot his keys** is the cause, and **so** gives the result: without keys, Ben could not **open** the front door.

items.stem: My sister likes loud music, but I like ________ music.
options: quiet
cheap
funny
famous

explanation.he: המילה **but** (אבל) מסמנת ניגוד ל-**loud music** (מוזיקה רועשת), ולכן הדובר אוהב מוזיקה **quiet** (שקטה).
explanation.en: **But** signals a contrast with **loud music**, so the speaker likes **quiet** (not loud) music.

items.stem: Doctors say we should avoid ________ drinks, such as cola, because they contain a lot of sugar.
options: thick
useful
cold
sweet

explanation.he: הדוגמה **such as cola** (כמו קולה) והסיבה **a lot of sugar** (הרבה סוכר) מראות שהרופאים מזהירים ממשקאות **sweet** (מתוקים).
explanation.en: The example **such as cola** and the reason **a lot of sugar** show that doctors warn against **sweet** drinks.

items.stem: Josh broke the window, but he decided to tell his teacher the ________.
options: joke
truth
dream
lie

explanation.he: המילה **but** (אבל) מסמנת ניגוד לשבירת החלון (**broke the window**), והצירוף הקבוע **tell the truth** (לומר את האמת) הוא מה שג'וש החליט לעשות.
explanation.en: **But** contrasts with **broke the window**, and the fixed phrase is to **tell the truth**.

items.stem: The market was so ________ on Saturday that it was hard to walk between the tables.
options: clean
familiar
crowded
colorful

explanation.he: המבנה **so ... that** (כל כך ש...) מראה שהתוצאה, **hard to walk between the tables** (קשה ללכת בין השולחנות), נובעת מכך שהשוק היה **crowded** (צפוף).
explanation.en: The pattern **so ... that** gives a result, **hard to walk between the tables**, that comes from a **crowded** market.

items.stem: Although days in the desert are dry and extremely hot, the nights can be surprisingly ________.
options: calm
scorching
dusty
chilly

explanation.he: המילה **Although** (למרות ש...) מסמנת ניגוד לימים החמים מאוד (**extremely hot**), ולכן הלילות הם באופן מפתיע **chilly** (קרירים).
explanation.en: **Although** signals a contrast with the **extremely hot** days, so the nights are surprisingly **chilly** (cold).

items.stem: The new teacher was very ________: she explained each idea several times, and she never lost her temper when students asked the same question again.
options: strict
patient
honest
creative

explanation.he: הנקודתיים מסבירים את המילה החסרה: מורה שמסבירה כל רעיון כמה פעמים ואינה כועסת (**never lost her temper**) היא **patient** (סבלנית).
explanation.en: The colon explains the blank: a teacher who explains ideas several times and **never lost her temper** is **patient**.

items.stem: Because the instructions were so ________, many customers could not build the bookshelf and called the shop for help.
options: confusing
polite
convenient
attractive

explanation.he: המילה **Because** (כי) והתוצאה **could not build the bookshelf** (לא הצליחו להרכיב את הכוננית) מראות שההוראות היו **confusing** (מבלבלות).
explanation.en: **Because** introduces a cause, and the result, **could not build the bookshelf**, shows that the instructions were **confusing**.

items.stem: Unless the weather becomes ________ before Friday afternoon, the school festival will take place outdoors as planned.
options: severe
dry
warm
pleasant

explanation.he: המילה **Unless** (אלא אם כן) מראה שהתוכנית לקיים את הפסטיבל בחוץ (**outdoors as planned**) תשתנה רק אם מזג האוויר יהיה **severe** (קשה, חמור).
explanation.en: **Unless** means 'if not': the festival stays **outdoors as planned** unless the weather becomes **severe** (very bad).

items.stem: Although the first version of the software was praised for its speed, users soon found it ________: it crashed whenever they opened more than three files at once.
options: complex
unreliable
efficient
unnecessary

explanation.he: המילה **Although** (למרות ש...) מסמנת ניגוד לשבחים על המהירות, והסבר הקריסות (**it crashed**) מראה שהתוכנה **unreliable** (לא אמינה).
explanation.en: **Although** contrasts the praise for speed with a problem, and **it crashed** shows the software was **unreliable** (not dependable).

items.stem: Despite being drawn with great care by a skilled artist, the map was ________ in many details: rivers appeared in the wrong places and two of the towns did not exist.
options: precise
decorative
inaccurate
detailed

explanation.he: המילה **Despite** (למרות) מסמנת ניגוד לציור הקפדני (**with great care**), וההסבר אחרי הנקודתיים (**in the wrong places**) מראה שהמפה הייתה **inaccurate** (לא מדויקת).
explanation.en: **Despite** contrasts the great care with the errors, and **in the wrong places** shows the map was **inaccurate** (not correct).

items.stem: While her novels sell millions of copies every year, the author herself is famously ________: she rarely gives interviews and avoids public events.
options: wealthy
garrulous
talented
reclusive

explanation.he: הנקודתיים מסבירים את המילה החסרה: מי שכמעט אינה נותנת ראיונות ונמנעת מאירועים ציבוריים (**rarely gives interviews and avoids public events**) היא **reclusive** (מתבודדת).
explanation.en: The colon explains the blank: someone who **rarely gives interviews and avoids public events** is **reclusive** (keeps away from people).

items.stem: Although the patient looked perfectly healthy, he had to ________ several tests before the doctors allowed him to leave the hospital.
options: deliver
undergo
request
resolve

explanation.he: הצירוף הקבוע **undergo tests** (לעבור בדיקות) מתאים למטופל שנבדק לפני שהרופאים מתירים לו ללכת (**before the doctors allowed him to leave**).
explanation.en: The fixed phrase is **undergo tests**: a patient is examined **before the doctors allowed him to leave** the hospital.

items.stem: Although news reports tend to focus on sudden disasters, many environmental hazards, such as slow poisoning from polluted water or years of lung damage from dust, are ________ and therefore easy to overlook.
options: dramatic
accidental
gradual
beneficial

explanation.he: הדוגמאות **slow poisoning** ו-**years of lung damage** מתארות נזק איטי, והמילה **Although** מנגידה אותו לאסונות פתאומיים (**sudden disasters**), ולכן הסכנות הן **gradual** (הדרגתיות).
explanation.en: The examples **slow poisoning** and **years of lung damage** describe slow harm, which **Although** contrasts with **sudden disasters**, so the hazards are **gradual**.

items.stem: Although the manager's speech was ________, listing every complaint in detail, it offered no practical way to solve any of them.
options: thorough
constructive
vague
brief

explanation.he: הצירוף **listing every complaint in detail** (רישום מפורט של כל תלונה) מתאר נאום **thorough** (יסודי), והמילה **Although** מנגידה אותו לחוסר פתרון מעשי.
explanation.en: **Listing every complaint in detail** describes a **thorough** speech, and **Although** contrasts it with the lack of a practical solution.

items.stem: Although donations to the animal shelter rose sharply after its televised appeal, they soon began to ________, and within a year the monthly total was smaller than it had been before the broadcast.
options: plateau
burgeon
accrue
dwindle

explanation.he: המילה **Although** מסמנת ניגוד לעלייה החדה, והסוף **smaller than it had been before the broadcast** מראה ירידה של ממש, ולכן התשובה היא **dwindle** (להצטמצם, להתמעט).
explanation.en: **Although** contrasts with the sharp rise, and **smaller than it had been before the broadcast** shows a real decline, so the answer is **dwindle** (shrink gradually).

items.stem: After a decade without a serious flood, residents of the bucolic river valley had grown ________, leaving drainage channels uncleared and sandbags rotting in storage, so last spring's storm caught them almost entirely unprepared.
options: resigned
lax
vigilant
prosperous

explanation.he: עשור בלי שיטפון (**After a decade without a serious flood**) הוביל להזנחה (**leaving drainage channels uncleared**), ולכן התשובה היא **lax** (רשלני, לא מקפיד).
explanation.en: A decade with no flood led to **drainage channels uncleared** and an unprepared town, so residents had grown **lax** (careless about precautions).

items.stem: Doctors advise against flying, however propitious the timing, until a patient's fever has begun to ________, that is, until the temperature has stayed below 38 degrees Celsius for a full day.
options: linger
spike
abate
fluctuate

explanation.he: הצירוף **that is** מסביר שהחום נשאר מתחת ל-38 מעלות יממה שלמה (**stayed below 38 degrees Celsius for a full day**), ולכן התשובה היא **abate** (לשכוך, להיחלש).
explanation.en: **That is** explains the blank: the temperature **stayed below 38 degrees Celsius for a full day**, so the fever has begun to **abate** (become less strong).

items.stem: Small farmers who grow ________ crops, such as strawberries, lettuce and fresh herbs, must sell them within days of the harvest and therefore have little power to hold out for a better price.
options: perishable
seasonal
verdant
subsidized

explanation.he: הדוגמאות (**strawberries, lettuce and fresh herbs**) והחובה למכור בתוך ימים (**must sell them within days of the harvest**) מצביעות על יבול שמתקלקל מהר, ולכן התשובה היא **perishable** (מתכלה).
explanation.en: The examples and **must sell them within days of the harvest** point to crops that spoil fast, so the answer is **perishable** (likely to go bad quickly).

items.stem: When the school trip was canceled, a clause buried in the contract's turgid small print meant that the tour operator, not the parents, had to ________ the bill for the unused hotel rooms.
options: split
dodge
pass
foot

explanation.he: הצירוף הקבוע **foot the bill** (לשאת בתשלום) מתאים לחובה שהסעיף הטיל (**had to**) על צד אחד בלבד (**the tour operator, not the parents**), ולכן התשובה היא **foot**.
explanation.en: **Foot the bill** means pay it, and the clause made one side pay alone, **the tour operator, not the parents**, so the answer is **foot**.

items.stem: Amid the welter of events at the university's open day, three introductory lectures are ________, so visitors must choose between biology, history and economics, all of which begin at ten o'clock.
options: concurrent
concordant
contiguous
discursive

explanation.he: החלקים **con** (יחד) ו-**cur** (לרוץ) נותנים 'רצים יחד', כמו בהסבר **all of which begin at ten o'clock**, ולכן התשובה היא **concurrent** (מתקיים בו-זמנית).
explanation.en: **Con** (together) plus **cur** (run) gives 'running together', which matches **all of which begin at ten o'clock**, so the answer is **concurrent**.

items.stem: Heavy snow did not stop the town's intrepid delivery drivers, but it did ________ their progress, so that a route that usually takes an hour took nearly five.
options: halt
hamper
chart
expedite

explanation.he: הצירופים **did not stop** ו-**but it did** אומרים שהשלג לא עצר אבל כן הפריע, והתוצאה **took nearly five** מראה האטה, ולכן התשובה היא **hamper** (לעכב, להכביד).
explanation.en: The snow **did not stop** the drivers, **but it did** slow them (**took nearly five**), so the answer is **hamper** (make progress slow and difficult).

items.stem: Sailors long regarded a ring around the moon as a ________ of storms: the ring itself does nothing to stir up the wind, but it often appears a day or so before bad weather arrives.
options: catalyst
remnant
harbinger
consequence

explanation.he: הטבעת אינה גורמת לרוח (**does nothing to stir up the wind**) אבל מופיעה לפני מזג האוויר הרע (**before bad weather arrives**), ולכן התשובה היא **harbinger** (מבשר, סימן מקדים).
explanation.en: The ring **does nothing to stir up the wind** yet comes **before bad weather arrives**, so it is a **harbinger** (an early sign of something coming).

items.stem: Far from being the ________ genius of later legend, the composer kept meticulous accounts, answered every letter within a week and rarely missed a rehearsal.
options: tormented
impecunious
feckless
unkempt

explanation.he: המבנה **Far from being** דורש את ההפך מן הפרטים שבהמשך, ומי שניהל חשבונות בקפדנות וענה לכל מכתב (**kept meticulous accounts, answered every letter**) היה אחראי, ולכן התשובה היא **feckless** (חסר אחריות).
explanation.en: **Far from being** demands the opposite of someone who **kept meticulous accounts, answered every letter**, so the answer is **feckless** (irresponsible and disorganized).

items.stem: The popular claim that people use only ten percent of their brains is not a scientific finding but a ________: a baseless story repeated so often that many accept it without question.
options: canard
misnomer
truism
platitude

explanation.he: ההסבר שאחרי הנקודתיים מגדיר את החסר כסיפור חסר בסיס שחוזר שוב ושוב (**a baseless story repeated so often**), ולכן התשובה היא **canard** (שמועת שווא, בדותה).
explanation.en: The colon defines the blank as **a baseless story repeated so often** that people believe it, so the answer is **canard** (a false, widely spread story).

items.stem: Even Victorian novels praised for their verisimilitude rely heavily on ________: the long-lost heir who turns up in the final chapter, for example, or the letter that arrives at exactly the moment the plot requires.
options: foreshadowing
contrivance
allegory
satire

explanation.he: הדוגמאות, כמו מכתב שמגיע בדיוק כשהעלילה צריכה אותו (**exactly the moment the plot requires**), הן פתרונות מאולצים, ולכן התשובה היא **contrivance** (תחבולה מלאכותית).
explanation.en: The examples, like a letter arriving at **exactly the moment the plot requires**, are artificial devices, so the answer is **contrivance** (an obviously planned, unnatural device).

items.stem: Plans for a second runway have been in ________ since the airline that was to use it went bankrupt: they remain unchanged and uncanceled, but no work will start until a new tenant is found.
options: arrears
perpetuity
flux
abeyance

explanation.he: הצירוף הקבוע **in abeyance** (מוקפא, מושהה זמנית) מתאים לתוכניות שלא בוטלו (**unchanged and uncanceled**) אבל מחכות (**until a new tenant is found**), ולכן התשובה היא **abeyance**.
explanation.en: **In abeyance** means suspended for now, matching plans that remain **unchanged and uncanceled** but wait **until a new tenant is found**.

items.stem: Teachers once dismissed disruptive pupils as ________, convinced that no amount of discipline or advice would change their conduct, yet later studies found that most embraced real responsibility with alacrity.
options: infallible
insolvent
incorrigible
incorruptible

explanation.he: החלקים **in** (לא), **corrig** (לתקן) ו-**ible** (ניתן) נותנים 'שאי אפשר לתקן', כמו בהסבר **no amount of discipline or advice would change their conduct**, ולכן התשובה היא **incorrigible** (חסר תקנה).
explanation.en: **In** (not) + **corrig** (correct) + **ible** (able) gives 'cannot be corrected', matching **no amount of discipline or advice would change their conduct**, so the answer is **incorrigible**.

items.stem: The village's sleepy appearance, all shuttered cottages and torpid cats, ________ its history: for nearly three centuries it was the busiest port on the coast, crowded with ships from a dozen countries.
options: betrays
presages
embodies
belies

explanation.he: המראה המנומנם (**sleepy appearance**) סותר את העבר כנמל העמוס ביותר בחוף (**the busiest port on the coast**), ולכן התשובה היא **belies** (נותן רושם כוזב).
explanation.en: A **sleepy appearance** gives a false picture of **the busiest port on the coast**, so the answer is **belies** (gives a false impression of).

items.stem: The philosopher was ________ rather than ascetic: he drank a single glass of wine with dinner and ate sparingly, but he never denied himself the pleasures of good company, music or travel.
options: abstemious
sybaritic
abstinent
puritanical

explanation.he: כוס יין אחת ואכילה במשורה (**a single glass of wine with dinner and ate sparingly**) מראות מתינות ולא התנזרות, ולכן התשובה היא **abstemious** (מתון באכילה ובשתייה).
explanation.en: Drinking **a single glass of wine** and eating **sparingly** shows moderation, not total refusal, so the answer is **abstemious** (moderate in eating and drinking).

items.stem: It was a very hot day, so we went to the ________ and swam all afternoon.
options: kitchen
station
pool
garage

explanation.he: הפועל **swam** (שחינו) מראה שהלכו למקום שבו אפשר לשחות, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **pool** (בריכה).
explanation.en: The word **swam** shows they went to a place for swimming on a **very hot day**, so the answer is **pool** (a place built for swimming).

items.stem: Our new neighbor is very ________; she smiles and says hello to everyone.
options: noisy
hungry
terrible
friendly

explanation.he: ההסבר שאחרי הנקודה-פסיק, **she smiles and says hello to everyone**, מתאר אדם נחמד, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **friendly** (ידידותית).
explanation.en: What follows the semicolon, **she smiles and says hello to everyone**, explains the blank, so the neighbor is **friendly** (kind and open to people).

items.stem: Rita was ________ for school today because her bus broke down on the way.
options: late
sorry
proud
afraid

explanation.he: המילה **because** (כי) מסבירה את התוצאה: האוטובוס התקלקל בדרך (**her bus broke down on the way**), ולכן ריטה הגיעה באיחור, **late** (מאחרת), לבית הספר.
explanation.en: The word **because** links the result to its cause: **her bus broke down on the way**, so Rita was **late** (not on time) for school.

items.stem: If you walk in the rain without a coat, you may ________ a cold.
options: hold
catch
throw
pull

explanation.he: הצירוף הקבוע **catch a cold** (להצטנן) הוא היחיד שמתאים לשם העצם **a cold**, וההליכה בגשם בלי מעיל (**walk in the rain without a coat**) מסבירה למה זה קורה.
explanation.en: The fixed phrase **catch a cold** (to become ill with a cold) fits **a cold**, and walking **in the rain without a coat** explains why it can happen.

items.stem: Some chemicals are ________; for example, strong cleaning liquids can burn the skin.
options: harmful
important
natural
invisible

explanation.he: הצירוף **for example** (למשל) מביא דוגמה: נוזלי ניקוי חזקים יכולים לשרוף את העור (**can burn the skin**), ולכן המילה החסרה היא **harmful** (מזיק).
explanation.en: **For example** introduces an instance: strong cleaning liquids **can burn the skin**, so some chemicals are **harmful** (able to hurt people).

items.stem: Even though Carlos had studied English for only one year, his speaking was already ________, and many visitors thought he was a native speaker.
options: hesitant
formal
fluent
local

explanation.he: הצירוף **Even though** (אף על פי ש) מעמיד את שנת הלימוד היחידה (**only one year**) מול התוצאה, ולכן הדיבור של קרלוס היה כבר **fluent** (שוטף), עד שחשבו שהוא דובר שפת אם.
explanation.en: **Even though** he had studied for **only one year**, his speaking was already **fluent** (smooth and easy), so visitors thought he was a **native speaker**.

items.stem: The rule was ________ because it allowed only some students to enter the competition.
options: unclear
unsafe
unknown
unfair

explanation.he: המילה **because** (כי) מסבירה מה הבעיה בכלל: הוא איפשר רק לחלק מהתלמידים להשתתף (**allowed only some students**), ולכן הוא **unfair** (לא הוגן).
explanation.en: Because the rule **allowed only some students** to enter, it treated people differently, so it was **unfair**: **un-** means not, and **fair** means equal and just.

items.stem: Whereas a cup of strong coffee keeps most people awake, a warm bath in the evening often makes them feel ________.
options: energetic
sleepy
thirsty
cheerful

explanation.he: המילה **Whereas** (ואילו) מציבה את הרחצה החמה מול הקפה שמעיר אנשים (**keeps most people awake**), ולכן היא גורמת להם להרגיש **sleepy** (מנומנמים).
explanation.en: **Whereas** sets the warm bath against coffee that **keeps most people awake**, so the bath makes them feel **sleepy** (ready for sleep).

items.stem: Students who study in a ________ place, such as a quiet library, usually remember more than those who study next to a loud television.
options: modern
unfamiliar
peaceful
private

explanation.he: הצירוף **such as** (כמו) מביא דוגמה, ספרייה שקטה (**a quiet library**), והמשפט מעמיד אותה מול טלוויזיה רועשת, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **peaceful** (שליו, שקט).
explanation.en: **Such as** gives an example, **a quiet library**, set against a **loud television**, so the blank means **peaceful** (quiet and calm).

items.stem: Although the school committee was ________ to change its old timetable, a flood of complaints from parents finally persuaded its members to try a new one.
options: reluctant
eager
powerless
qualified

explanation.he: הצירוף **Although** (למרות ש) והמילה **finally** (לבסוף) מראים שהוועדה התנגדה בתחילה והתלונות שיכנעו אותה (**finally persuaded**), ולכן המילה החסרה היא **reluctant** (לא ששה, חסרת רצון).
explanation.en: **Although** and **finally persuaded** show that the committee first resisted change, so it was **reluctant** (unwilling) to change its timetable.

items.stem: Although the experiment was carried out with great care, it produced ________ results: when repeated three times, it gave a different answer every time.
options: accurate
satisfactory
encouraging
inconsistent

explanation.he: הנקודתיים מסבירים את החסר: כשחזרו על הניסוי התקבלה בכל פעם תשובה שונה (**a different answer every time**), ולכן התוצאות היו **inconsistent** (לא עקביות), למרות הזהירות הרבה.
explanation.en: The colon explains the blank: repeating it gave **a different answer every time**, so despite the great care (**Although**) the results were **inconsistent** (not the same).

items.stem: Although the two companies had disagreed about prices for months, they finally ________ an agreement after one last night of talks.
options: broke
reached
rejected
threw

explanation.he: שם העצם **an agreement** קובע את הצירוף הקבוע **reach an agreement** (להגיע להסכמה), והצירוף **Although** עם **finally** מראה שאחרי חודשי ויכוח (**disagreed about prices for months**) הגיעו להסכמה.
explanation.en: **Reach an agreement** is a fixed phrase, and **Although** with **finally** shows that after months of disagreement the companies at last **reached** one.

items.stem: Although the earliest electric buses could run for only an hour between charges, ________ models, built over the next ten years, managed a full day.
options: original
occasional
previous
subsequent

explanation.he: הצירוף **built over the next ten years** מראה שהדגמים נבנו אחרי הראשונים, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **subsequent** (מאוחרים יותר), והצירוף **Although** מעמיד את הדגמים האלה מול האוטובוסים הראשונים.
explanation.en: **Built over the next ten years** shows these models came after the earliest ones, so the blank is **subsequent** (coming later), which **Although** contrasts with **the earliest** buses.

items.stem: Although many people believe that a large vocabulary makes someone a good writer, great authors often use ________ words, choosing the simplest term that expresses their meaning.
options: florid
foreign
ordinary
scientific

explanation.he: הצירוף **Although** (למרות ש) מציג אמונה נפוצה על אוצר מילים גדול, וההמשך, **choosing the simplest term**, מראה שסופרים גדולים משתמשים במילים פשוטות, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **ordinary** (רגילות).
explanation.en: **Although** introduces a common belief about a large vocabulary, and **choosing the simplest term** shows that great authors use **ordinary** (everyday) words.

items.stem: Although many trees, such as oaks and maples, lose all their leaves each autumn, others, such as pines and firs, are ________.
options: deciduous
evergreen
tropical
ancient

explanation.he: הצירוף **such as** (כמו) נותן דוגמאות לעצים שמאבדים את עליהם (**oaks and maples**), והמילה **others** מעמידה מולם עצים אחרים, **pines and firs**, ולכן המילה החסרה היא **evergreen** (ירוקי עד).
explanation.en: **Such as** gives examples of trees that **lose all their leaves**, and **others** sets different trees against them, so pines and firs are **evergreen** (they keep their leaves).

items.stem: Because the signal from the probe, now far beyond Pluto, was ________, arriving in brief bursts separated by long stretches of silence, the mission's dogged engineers needed weeks to piece together a single image.
options: faint
intermittent
uninterrupted
distorted

explanation.he: הצירוף שאחרי החסר מתאר אות שמגיע בפרצים קצרים עם שתיקות ארוכות ביניהם (**brief bursts separated by long stretches of silence**), ולכן התשובה היא **intermittent** (לסירוגין, מקוטע).
explanation.en: A signal **arriving in brief bursts separated by long stretches of silence** keeps stopping and starting, so it is **intermittent** (on and off).

items.stem: Unlike its predecessor, which fined shops heavily for every peccadillo, the new consumer agency is relatively ________, preferring warnings to fines; yet it is not careless: it inspects every store twice a year.
options: remiss
draconian
impartial
lenient

explanation.he: המילה **Unlike** מציבה את הסוכנות מול קודמתה, שקנסה בכבדות, והיא מעדיפה אזהרות (**preferring warnings to fines**) אך אינה רשלנית, ולכן התשובה היא **lenient** (מקל, סלחני).
explanation.en: **Unlike** a predecessor that fined heavily, the agency prefers **warnings to fines** yet **is not careless**, so it is **lenient** (mild in punishing).

items.stem: For the impoverished mountain village, the sale of a rocky hillside it had long considered worthless was a genuine ________, an unexpected fortune that paid for a new school and a clinic.
options: windfall
royalty
bequest
endowment

explanation.he: הצירוף שאחרי החסר מגדיר אותו כהון לא צפוי (**an unexpected fortune**) ממכירת אדמה שנחשבה חסרת ערך, ולכן התשובה היא **windfall** (רווח פתאומי ובלתי צפוי).
explanation.en: The phrase **an unexpected fortune**, from land the village had **long considered worthless**, defines a **windfall** (a sudden, unexpected gain).

items.stem: Although ________ technologies such as the pager and the fax machine have all but vanished from most offices, many hospitals keep them as stalwart backups for when the network fails.
options: wireless
bulky
obsolete
cutting-edge

explanation.he: הדוגמאות **the pager and the fax machine** הן מכשירים ישנים שכמעט נעלמו מן המשרדים (**have all but vanished**), ולכן התשובה היא **obsolete** (מיושן, שעבר זמנו).
explanation.en: The examples **the pager and the fax machine**, which **have all but vanished from most offices**, are **obsolete** (out of date) technologies.

items.stem: Delays of an hour or more are ________ for the course on the island's ramshackle single-track railway, so locals rarely complain and simply bring a book.
options: matter
obstacle
par
collision

explanation.he: המילים **for the course** והעובדה שהתושבים כמעט אינם מתלוננים (**locals rarely complain**) מובילות לביטוי **par for the course** (דבר רגיל וצפוי), ולכן התשובה היא **par**.
explanation.en: **For the course** and **locals rarely complain** point to the idiom **par for the course** (normal and expected), so the answer is **par**.

items.stem: The poet won no prizes and sold few books during her lifetime; her fame was entirely ________, arriving only decades after her death, when a scholar found her notebooks moldering in an attic.
options: posthumous
premature
postnatal
pseudonymous

explanation.he: התהילה הגיעה רק עשרות שנים אחרי מות המשוררת (**arriving only decades after her death**), ולכן התשובה היא **posthumous** (שלאחר המוות), עם התחילית **post-** (אחרי).
explanation.en: Fame **arriving only decades after her death** is **posthumous** (coming after death); **post-** means 'after'.

items.stem: Rather than banning skateboards outright and facing a deluge of complaints, the town fitted its benches and low walls with small metal studs, which ________ skaters without preventing anyone from sitting down.
options: prohibit
deter
lure
reprimand

explanation.he: הבליטות באות במקום איסור (**Rather than banning**) ואינן מונעות מאיש לשבת (**without preventing anyone from sitting down**), ולכן התשובה היא **deter** (להרתיע).
explanation.en: The studs work **Rather than banning** and **without preventing anyone from sitting down**, so they **deter** (discourage) skaters.

items.stem: In the 1830s the art of photography was still ________: a single portrait demanded minutes of perfect stillness, and few people yet imagined that it might one day rival painting.
options: imitative
outmoded
tedious
nascent

explanation.he: המילים **still** ו-**yet** וההסבר שאחרי הנקודתיים מתארים אמנות בתחילת דרכה, עם חשיפות ארוכות ועתיד שעוד לא נראה, ולכן התשובה היא **nascent** (מתהווה, בראשית דרכו).
explanation.en: **Still**, **yet** and the details after the colon describe an art just beginning, so photography was **nascent** (newly forming).

items.stem: On the eve of the competition final, the young pianist seemed almost ________ — not reckless, for she had practiced every piece for months, but untroubled, chatting with friends while her rivals paced the corridor.
options: foolhardy
indolent
despondent
insouciant

explanation.he: המבנה **not reckless ... but untroubled** מגדיר את החסר כשלווה חסרת דאגה של מי שהתכוננה היטב, ולכן התשובה היא **insouciant** (שליו וחסר דאגה, קליל).
explanation.en: The frame **not reckless ... but untroubled** describes calm, carefree ease, so she seemed **insouciant** (relaxed and unconcerned).

items.stem: The medieval town's rapacious growth all but ________ its Roman core: its houses were torn down for their stone, and only some paving beneath a few cellars survives.
options: obliterated
enshrined
encompassed
dwarfed

explanation.he: הצירוף **all but** פירושו כמעט לגמרי, ורק מעט ריצוף שרד (**only some paving beneath a few cellars survives**), ולכן התשובה היא **obliterated** (נמחה, הושמד כליל).
explanation.en: The phrase **all but** means almost completely, and **only some paving beneath a few cellars survives**, so the core was almost entirely **obliterated** (destroyed).

items.stem: Though often handsome, with grand town halls, nineteenth-century factory towns were notoriously ________ places to live, with conditions such as coal smoke, open sewers and drinking water drawn from polluted rivers.
options: unprepossessing
unwholesome
idyllic
provincial

explanation.he: הדוגמאות שאחרי הצירוף **such as**, עשן פחם, ביוב פתוח ומי שתייה ממקור מזוהם, הן כולן סכנות לבריאות, ולכן התשובה היא **unwholesome** (לא בריא, מזיק לבריאות).
explanation.en: The examples after **such as** (**coal smoke, open sewers and drinking water drawn from polluted rivers**) all harm health, so the towns were **unwholesome** (unhealthy).

items.stem: Cheap smartphones brought about a ________ change in how travelers find their way: within a decade, the folding paper map, once a fixture of every glove box, had become a mere curio.
options: cosmetic
loose
sea
climate

explanation.he: שינוי שבתוך עשור הפך את מפת הנייר לחפץ נדיר (**had become a mere curio**) הוא **a sea change** (שינוי עמוק ויסודי), ולכן התשובה היא **sea**.
explanation.en: A change that, **within a decade**, turned the paper map into **a mere curio** is **a sea change** (a deep, complete transformation), so the answer is **sea**.

items.stem: Although the novel's narrator is a lugubrious village doctor speaking in the first person, she is curiously ________, reporting the private thoughts of strangers and knowing how each of their lives will end.
options: omnipresent
omniscient
omnivorous
omnipotent

explanation.he: היא מדווחת על מחשבות של זרים ויודעת איך יסתיימו חייהם (**knowing how each of their lives will end**), כלומר יודעת הכול, ולכן התשובה היא **omniscient** (יודע-כל: **omni-** = כל, **sci** = לדעת).
explanation.en: Reporting **the private thoughts of strangers** and **knowing how each of their lives will end** means knowing everything: **omniscient** (all-knowing).

items.stem: A good referee, however vociferous the home crowd, must be ________: she may care deeply about the sport itself, but she must have no stake in which team wins.
options: uninterested
unflappable
self-interested
disinterested

explanation.he: לפי ההסבר שאחרי הנקודתיים, מותר לה לאהוב את הספורט, אבל אסור שיהיה לה אינטרס בתוצאה (**no stake in which team wins**), ולכן התשובה היא **disinterested** (חסר פניות, ללא אינטרס אישי).
explanation.en: She **may care deeply about the sport itself** but must have **no stake in which team wins**, so she must be **disinterested** (impartial, with no personal interest).

items.stem: Even the historian's most persistent critics offered ________ praise for her new edition of the chronicle: they still disputed her conclusions, but conceded that no one had ever assembled the evidence so carefully.
options: fulsome
obligatory
grudging
belated

explanation.he: המבקרים עדיין חלקו על מסקנותיה אבל הודו (**still disputed her conclusions, but conceded**) שאיש לא אסף ראיות בקפידה כזאת, ולכן התשובה היא **grudging** (שניתן בחצי פה, בחוסר רצון).
explanation.en: Critics who **still disputed her conclusions, but conceded** her care give praise unwillingly, so it was **grudging** (given reluctantly).

items.context: A zoology lecturer talks about an unusual feature of the octopus.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, warm and lively university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'Why so many?', a short pause at [pause], and slower, firmer delivery on 'aren't spares' and the last sentence.
script: We have one heart, and so do cats, birds and fish, so you might be surprised to learn that an octopus has three. Why so many? Well, two of them are small, and they have one job: pushing blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen. The third heart then sends that fresh blood around the rest of the body.   So the extra hearts aren't spares in case one fails. Each heart simply handles a different part of the trip.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer say about the three hearts of an octopus?
options: Two are spares that take over if the main heart fails
The third serves the gills while the two small ones serve the body
The three of them pump blood through the gills to gain oxygen
Each of them moves blood along its own section of the journey

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Each heart simply handles a different part of the trip** (כל לב פשוט אחראי על חלק אחר של המסלול), כל לב מזרים את הדם בקטע משלו: שני הלבבות הקטנים לזימים, והשלישי לשאר הגוף.
explanation.en: The two small hearts serve the gills and the third serves the body, so **each heart simply handles a different part of the trip**.

items.context: Two botany students look at the seedlings they have been growing in their lab.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female undergraduate, about 21, surprised and excited at first, then thoughtful, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male undergraduate, about 22, calm and explanatory, slightly slower, with stress on 'Taller, yes, but', 'searching for it' and 'instead of'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: Look at the seedlings we kept in the dark cupboard. They're taller than the ones on the windowsill!
B: Taller, yes, but look how pale they are, and those frail stems can barely hold them up.
A: So why grow so fast without light?
B: Because they're searching for it. A seedling in the dark spends its energy stretching upward, hoping to reach the light, instead of building strong stems and green leaves.
A: So the height is a sign of trouble, not health.

questions.stem: According to the man, why did the seedlings in the cupboard grow taller?
options: They were in better health than the seedlings left on the windowsill
The dark cupboard kept them warmer than the seedlings near the window
They put their growth into height in an attempt to find light
Their stems were already sturdy, which left energy for height

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Because they're searching for it** (כי הנבטים מחפשים את האור) והצירוף **spends its energy stretching upward** (משקיע את האנרגיה בגדילה כלפי מעלה), הנבטים גבהו כדי להגיע אל האור.
explanation.en: The seedlings grew tall **because they're searching for** light: each one **spends its energy stretching upward**.

items.context: A chemistry lecturer talks about an early version of the periodic table.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 50, engaging and confident university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A short pause at [pause], a lift in energy on 'Now, this is the bold part', and slower, firmer delivery on 'Instead, he left a gap' and on the last sentence.
script: When chemists first tried to arrange the elements in a table, they kept running into the same problem: the pattern didn't quite work. In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev found a way around it. He lined the elements up by weight and put those that behaved alike in the same column. But where the pattern broke down, he didn't force an element into the wrong place. Instead, he left a gap.   Now, this is the bold part. Mendeleev was adamant that those gaps were not mistakes. He insisted they belonged to elements that nobody had found yet, and he even described what those elements would be like. Not everyone was convinced. Then, over the next twenty years or so, three of them were discovered, and they matched his descriptions closely. So the gaps turned out to be the table's greatest strength. They showed that it could predict, not just organize.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what did Mendeleev do where the pattern broke down?
options: He kept a place empty rather than squeeze an element into it
He put the nearest element there and simply marked it as uncertain
He moved those elements to a separate list at the end
He stopped the table at the point where the pattern ended

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Instead, he left a gap** (במקום זאת, הוא השאיר משבצת ריקה), מנדלייב לא דחק יסוד למקום שאינו מתאים לו, אלא השאיר את המקום פנוי.
explanation.en: Where the pattern broke down, **he didn't force an element into the wrong place**; **instead, he left a gap**.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer see as the greatest strength of the table?
options: It sorted elements that act alike into neat groups
It foretold elements that had not yet been detected
It corrected mistakes that earlier chemists had made
It gave exact weights for the elements known then

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **They showed that it could predict, not just organize** (הרווחים הראו שהטבלה יכולה לחזות, ולא רק לסדר), כוחה הגדול של הטבלה היה בחיזוי יסודות שהתגלו רק מאוחר יותר.
explanation.en: The gaps **showed that it could predict, not just organize**: the elements he described were found later.

items.context: A student visits his psychology professor during office hours to ask about a study from class.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: male undergraduate, about 20, curious and openly surprised, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: female psychology professor, about 50, friendly and clear, slightly slower, with stress on 'About half', 'that's the point', 'store very little' and 'not of vision'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: Professor, can I ask about the study you mentioned in class? The one where a stranger stops someone to ask for directions.
B: Sure. While they're talking, two workers carry a large door between them. Behind the door, the stranger is swapped for a different person.
A: And people really didn't notice?
B: About half of them didn't. They kept giving directions to a completely new person, utterly oblivious to the change.
A: That's hard to believe. Weren't they looking right at him?

B: They were, and that's the point. We feel as if we take in every detail of a scene, but we actually store very little.   Our brains keep only what seems important at the moment, like the fact that this person needs help, and fill in the rest.
A: So it's not that their eyesight was poor.
B: Not at all. It's a limit of attention and memory, not of vision.

questions.stem: According to the professor, what did about half of the people in the study do?
options: They stopped giving directions once they saw a new face
They went on helping a new person without realizing it
They noticed the change but were too polite to mention it
They helped the two workers carry the door down the street

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **They kept giving directions to a completely new person** (הנבדקים המשיכו לתת הוראות דרך לאדם חדש לגמרי), כמחצית מהנבדקים המשיכו לעזור בלי לשים לב להחלפה.
explanation.en: **About half of them didn't** notice: **they kept giving directions to a completely new person**.

questions.stem: How does the professor explain the result of the study?
options: Their eyesight was weaker than they themselves believed
They kept looking away from the stranger while they were giving directions
Their minds kept the general sense of the scene but few details
The first and second strangers looked almost exactly like each other

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **we actually store very little** (בפועל אנחנו שומרים מעט מאוד), המוח שומר רק את מה שנראה חשוב ברגע זה ומשלים את השאר, ולכן הנבדקים זכרו את התמונה הכללית בלבד.
explanation.en: **We actually store very little**: **our brains keep only what seems important at the moment** and fill in the rest.

items.context: A geology lecturer talks about how caves form in a common kind of rock.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 45, calm and clear university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, a short pause at each [pause], stress on 'But in most limestone caves', 'very weak acid' and 'the same water also builds things', and slower, firmer delivery on the last two sentences.
script: Today I want to answer a question that visitors to large caves often ask: what dug out all this space? It's natural to imagine an underground river roaring through the rock and grinding it away. But in most limestone caves, the real work was done much more quietly, by rainwater.   Here's how it happens. As rain soaks down through the soil, it picks up carbon dioxide. That turns the water into a very weak acid, not strong enough to hurt your skin, but strong enough to dissolve limestone, slowly. The water seeps into small cracks in the rock, and over thousands of years it widens them, little by little, into passages and chambers. In the end, a whole subterranean world of tunnels can lie beneath an ordinary-looking field. Now, the same water also builds things. When a drop hanging from the roof of a cave loses some of its carbon dioxide into the air, it can no longer hold all of the limestone it dissolved, so it leaves a tiny ring of mineral behind. Drop after drop, ring after ring, those deposits grow into the long, icicle-shaped stalactites that hang from cave roofs.   So a limestone cave is really the work of chemistry rather than force. The water first takes the rock away, and then, in the very same cave, it slowly gives some of it back.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, how are most limestone caves formed?
options: Underground rivers rush through the rock and grind it away over many years
A strong acid stored deep inside the rock burns tunnels through it
Movements of the ground crack the rock open and leave wide empty spaces
Rain that absorbs a gas in the soil slowly eats the rock away

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the real work was done much more quietly, by rainwater** (העבודה האמיתית נעשתה בשקט רב יותר, בידי מי הגשם), המערות נוצרות ממי גשם שקולטים פחמן דו־חמצני מהקרקע וממיסים את הסלע.
explanation.en: **But in most limestone caves, the real work was done much more quietly, by rainwater**, which **picks up carbon dioxide** and dissolves the rock.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, why does a drop hanging from a cave roof leave mineral behind?
options: Some of the gas it carries escapes into the air of the cave
It picks up extra carbon dioxide from the rock of the cave roof
The cold air in the cave turns part of the drop into ice
It meets river water that flows along the floor of the cave

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **loses some of its carbon dioxide into the air** (מאבדת לאוויר חלק מהפחמן הדו־חמצני), הטיפה כבר לא יכולה להחזיק את כל הגיר המומס, ולכן היא משאירה מינרל.
explanation.en: When a drop **loses some of its carbon dioxide into the air**, it **can no longer hold all of the limestone it dissolved**.

items.context: Two history students discuss a reading about early sea voyages in a seminar.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent for both speakers. A: female graduate student, about 26, confident and precise, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). B: male graduate student, about 24, interested and quick to draw conclusions, moderate pace. A stresses 'Not really', 'centuries after', 'didn't make iron' and 'Well, not entirely'. A short pause at [pause].
script: A: The reading for today argues that Norse sailors reached North America about five hundred years before Columbus. What did you make of it?
B: I found it convincing, but I wondered why historians took so long to accept it. The old Norse sagas describe a voyage west to a land they called Vinland. Wasn't that enough?

A: Not really. The sagas were written down centuries after the events, and they mix travel with legend. For a long time, many scholars treated them as fanciful tales, interesting stories rather than reliable records.
B: So what changed their minds?

A: A site in Newfoundland, in eastern Canada. In the 1960s, archaeologists dug up the remains of several buildings there, and they were built in the Norse style, with walls of turf.   They also found iron nails and a spot where iron had been worked. The local people of that time didn't make iron, so the most likely explanation was Norse visitors.
B: And they dated the site?
A: Yes, to around the year one thousand, which fits the sagas quite well.
B: So the sagas weren't just legends after all.

A: Well, not entirely. The site proves that Norse sailors were there. It doesn't prove that every detail of the sagas is true. The stories needed hard evidence on the ground before historians could trust them.

questions.stem: According to the woman, why did historians doubt the sagas for many years?
options: They were written in an old language that few historians could read
They gave dates that clashed with the remains that were found in Canada
They were recorded long after the voyages and blended fact with myth
They spoke of iron tools that the Norse did not yet possess

explanation.he: ההיסטוריונים פקפקו בסאגות כי הן נכתבו מאות שנים אחרי האירועים (**written down centuries after the events**) ומערבבות תיאורי מסע עם אגדה (**they mix travel with legend**).
explanation.en: After **Not really**, she explains that **the sagas were written down centuries after the events, and they mix travel with legend**.

questions.stem: What point does the woman make at the end of the discussion?
options: The site shows that the sagas are correct down to the last detail
The site confirms the voyage but not each part of the stories
The site dates from a time long after the voyages in the sagas
Historians should trust written records more than finds in the ground

explanation.he: אחרי הצירוף **Well, not entirely** (טוב, לא לגמרי) בא המשפט **It doesn't prove that every detail of the sagas is true** (האתר לא מוכיח שכל פרט בסאגות נכון), ולכן האתר מאשר את המסע אך לא כל פרט.
explanation.en: **The site proves that Norse sailors were there**, but **it doesn't prove that every detail of the sagas is true**.

items.context: A chemistry lecturer talks about cleaning a greasy pan.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: male, about 35, lively and clear university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'although it doesn't actually break the grease down', 'two ends' and 'carry those drops away'.
script: Why can't plain water wash grease off a pan? Oil and water don't mix, so the water just slides over that obstinate film of grease. Soap solves the problem, although it doesn't actually break the grease down. Each soap molecule has two ends. One end is drawn to water, while the other is drawn to oil.   So the oily ends bury themselves in the grease and surround tiny drops of it, while the other ends face outward, and water can then carry those drops away.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, how does soap help water remove grease?
options: It breaks the grease down into parts that dissolve in water
Its water-loving ends sink deep into the grease and hold it in place
It coats the pan with a film that stops grease from sticking
It traps small bits of grease so that water washes them away

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **surround tiny drops of it** (מקיפים טיפות זעירות של השומן) והמשפט **water can then carry those drops away** (המים יכולים לסחוף את הטיפות), הסבון לוכד את טיפות השומן כך שהמים שוטפים אותן.
explanation.en: Soap does not break grease down; its oily ends **surround tiny drops of it**, so **water can then carry those drops away**.

items.context: An engineering lecturer talks about a feature of long bridges.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 45, clear and lively university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Light, inviting delivery on the opening sentence, a short pause at [pause], and slower, firmer delivery on the last two sentences, with stress on 'don't weaken' and 'move'.
script: When you drive across a long bridge, listen for a soft thump every so often. That sound comes from the joints, narrow, unobtrusive strips of metal that most drivers never notice. They look like a flaw in the road, but they're there on purpose. Steel and concrete grow slightly longer when they warm up and shorter when they cool.   Without these gaps, a bridge would push against itself on hot days and crack. So the joints don't weaken the bridge. They let it move safely.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what is the purpose of these joints?
options: To hold the bridge firmly in place when the weather turns hot
To make a regular noise that tells drivers they are crossing a bridge
To let the bridge stretch and contract as temperatures rise and fall
To mark weak spots where the bridge is likely to crack

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **grow slightly longer when they warm up** (הפלדה והבטון מתארכים מעט כשהם מתחממים) והמשפט **They let it move safely** (רצועות המתכת מאפשרות לגשר לזוז בבטחה), המרווחים נותנים לגשר מקום להתארך ולהתקצר.
explanation.en: Steel and concrete **grow slightly longer when they warm up**, and the joints **let it move safely** instead of letting it crack.

items.context: Two astronomy students talk about what they can see in the night sky.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural conversation rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
A: female astronomy student, about 20, curious and relaxed; a questioning lift on 'And a planet?'.
B: male astronomy student, about 22, calm and explanatory; gentle stress on 'isn't really', a short pause at [pause], and slower, firmer delivery on his last sentence, with stress on 'size' and 'not how bright'.
script: A: I assumed planets barely twinkle because they're brighter than stars.
B: Brightness isn't really the reason. A star is so far away that its light reaches us from a single tiny point, and that thin beam gets buffeted by the moving air above us, so it flickers.
A: And a planet?
B: A planet shows up as a small disk, so its light comes from many points at once, and their flickers average out.   So what matters is the size of the image, not how bright it is.

questions.stem: According to the man, why do planets shine more steadily than stars?
options: Their light comes from a small area rather than one point
Their light is too bright for its small changes to be noticed
Their light is made steadier by the moving air above us
Their light travels to us in a narrower beam than a star's

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **A planet shows up as a small disk** (כוכב לכת נראה כדסקה קטנה), האור של כוכב הלכת מגיע משטח קטן ולא מנקודה אחת, ולכן ההבהובים מתקזזים.
explanation.en: **A planet shows up as a small disk**, so **its light comes from many points at once** and the flickers **average out**.

items.context: An agriculture lecturer talks about an old farming practice.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 55, warm and steady university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A short pause at each [pause], a lift of interest on 'Now, here's the odd thing', stress on 'yet' in the next sentence, and slower, firmer delivery on the last two sentences.
script: For centuries, farmers in many parts of Europe followed a simple rule: if a field grew clover or beans one year, plant wheat there the next. The wheat came up taller and fuller. Those farmers were astute observers, but they had no idea why the rule worked.   The answer came in the late eighteen hundreds, and it lies underground. Every plant needs nitrogen to grow. Now, here's the odd thing. The air around us is mostly nitrogen, yet most plants can't use it in that form. Clover and beans get help. Their roots carry small swellings, and inside those swellings live bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can absorb. When the clover dies or is plowed back into the soil, that nitrogen stays behind for the next crop.   So the old rule wasn't luck. It was real science, found by practice long before anyone could explain it.

questions.stem: What does the lecturer mainly explain?
options: How farmers learned to grow clover and wheat side by side
Why the nitrogen in the air is of little use to most plants
How scientists replaced an old farming rule with a much better one
Why wheat grew better in a field that had just grown clover

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **they had no idea why the rule worked** (החקלאים לא ידעו מדוע הכלל עובד) והמשפט **the old rule wasn't luck** (הכלל הישן לא היה מזל), ההרצאה מסבירה מדוע חיטה גדלה טוב יותר אחרי שנה של תלתן.
explanation.en: The farmers **had no idea why the rule worked**, and the lecture shows that **the old rule wasn't luck**: clover leaves nitrogen for the wheat.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what do the bacteria in the root swellings do?
options: They carry nitrogen out of the soil and release it into the air
They change the air's nitrogen into a nutrient plants can use
They help the roots of the wheat reach deeper into the soil
They guard the clover's roots against insects in the ground

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can absorb** (חיידקים שהופכים חנקן מן האוויר לצורה שצמחים יכולים לקלוט), החיידקים ממירים את החנקן שבאוויר לחומר מזין לצמחים.
explanation.en: The swellings hold **bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can absorb**.

items.context: Two sociology graduate students discuss a classic study of how people find jobs.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural seminar-discussion rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
A: female sociology graduate student, about 26, curious and a little skeptical; a puzzled tone on 'That seems backwards to me' and a questioning lift on her last line.
B: male sociology graduate student, about 28, thoughtful and friendly; a short pause at [pause], stress on 'where' and 'not how much', and a measured, qualifying tone on 'I wouldn't go that far'.
script: A: I just read that classic study of how people found their jobs. Among those who heard about a job through someone they knew, most heard from people they saw only now and then, not from close friends. That seems backwards to me.
B: It surprised me too, at first. But think about who your close friends are. They usually know the same people you know and hear the same news you hear.
A: So by the time they hear about an opening, I've probably heard about it as well.

B: Exactly. A casual acquaintance moves in different circles, so that's who brings you news from outside your own group.   The salient point is where the information comes from, not how much the person cares about you.
A: Then close friends don't matter much for finding work?
B: I wouldn't go that far. Close friends may be more eager to help. The study just shows that distant contacts often carry news your friends never hear.

questions.stem: According to the man, why are distant contacts often useful in a job search?
options: They are more willing to help than close friends tend to be
They belong to other social groups and so hear different news
They share a person's circle and so hear the same news first
They have usually spent more years working than close friends have

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **A casual acquaintance moves in different circles** (מישהו שמכירים רק בשטחיות נע בחוגים חברתיים אחרים), אנשי קשר רחוקים שייכים לקבוצות אחרות ולכן מביאים חדשות שחברים קרובים אינם שומעים.
explanation.en: **A casual acquaintance moves in different circles**, so such contacts bring **news from outside your own group**.

questions.stem: What does the man say about close friends at the end of the conversation?
options: They are of little use, as they seldom hear about new jobs
They usually hear of more openings than distant contacts do
They tend to give poorer job advice than casual acquaintances do
They still matter, as they may be keener to lend a hand

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **I wouldn't go that far** (לא הייתי מרחיק לכת כל כך) והמשפט **Close friends may be more eager to help** (ייתכן שחברים קרובים להוטים יותר לעזור), חברים קרובים עדיין חשובים.
explanation.en: He answers **I wouldn't go that far** and adds that **Close friends may be more eager to help**.

items.context: A biology lecturer talks about the long journey of the salmon.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral UK accent. Lecturer: female, about 50, engaging and unhurried university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on 'So how does it find the way?', a short pause at each [pause], stress on 'two different senses' and on 'switch to smell', and slower, summing-up delivery on the last sentence.
script: Here's a puzzle that kept naturalists busy for a long time. A young salmon hatches in a small stream, swims down to the sea, and spends a few years in the open ocean, often thousands of kilometers from home. Then, when it's ready to breed, it makes a grueling journey back, swimming upstream against strong currents. And in most cases, it ends up in the very stream where it hatched. So how does it find the way?   It seems the fish relies on two different senses, one for each stage of the trip. Out in the open ocean, there are no landmarks, so researchers think salmon read the Earth's magnetic field, which differs slightly from place to place along the coast. That gets them to roughly the right stretch of coast. But to pick one stream out of hundreds, they switch to smell. Every stream carries its own blend of scents from the soil and plants along its banks, and young salmon memorize that blend before they leave. In a well-known series of experiments, researchers blocked the noses of some returning fish. Those fish chose streams almost at random, while fish that could still smell mostly returned home.   So the salmon's homing, which can seem almost unerring, depends on a kind of map for the long distance and a memory of smell for the last few kilometers.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, how do salmon find their way back?
options: They depend on one sense far out at sea and on another near home
They use smell to cross the ocean and the magnetic field near the coast
They follow familiar landmarks along the coast until they reach their stream
They are guided mostly by the warmth of the water in their home stream

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **one for each stage of the trip** (חוש אחד לכל שלב במסע) והמשפט **they switch to smell** (הדגים עוברים לחוש הריח), הסלמון נעזר בשדה המגנטי בים הפתוח ובריח ליד נחל הבית.
explanation.en: The fish uses **two different senses, one for each stage of the trip**: the magnetic field at sea, and then **they switch to smell**.

questions.stem: What did the experiment with blocked noses show?
options: Salmon can reach their own stream by the magnetic field without smell
Salmon that could still smell picked streams almost at random
Salmon rely on smell to pick out their own stream near the end
Salmon learn the smell of their home stream while living out at sea

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Those fish chose streams almost at random** (הדגים שאפם נחסם בחרו נחלים כמעט באקראי), בלי חוש הריח הסלמון מתקשה למצוא את נחל הבית, ולכן הריח נחוץ לבחירת הנחל בסוף המסע.
explanation.en: Fish with blocked noses **chose streams almost at random**, while those that **could still smell mostly returned home**.

items.context: Two ecologists discuss recordings of birdsong made in a city and in a forest.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural academic-conversation rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
A: female ecologist, about 38, precise and thoughtful; a careful, weighing tone on 'it may well be right. But there's a complication', a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'no louder' in her conditional sentence.
B: male ecologist, about 45, relaxed and at first confident in the usual story; a slower, realizing tone on 'So the higher pitch might be a side effect', and a measured, cautious delivery on his last turn.
script: A: I've finished going through the recordings. Birds of the same species sing at a noticeably higher pitch in the city parks than in the forest.
B: That fits the usual story, doesn't it? Traffic makes a low, steady din, so a higher song stands out against it. The birds are adjusting so they can be heard.

A: That's the obvious explanation, and it may well be right. But there's a complication. When birds sing louder, their songs naturally rise in pitch at the same time. And city birds have to sing louder just to be heard over the noise.
B: So the higher pitch might be a side effect of shouting, rather than a separate change.
A: Exactly. And that matters, because raising the pitch on its own may not help much. Singing louder could be doing most of the work.
B: Then how do we tell the two apart?
A: We'd have to measure loudness as well as pitch.   If city birds still sing higher when they're no louder than forest birds, then the pitch change is doing something on its own.
B: Getting reliable loudness readings in a busy park will be a formidable job, but I agree it's worth doing. Until then, I'd be careful about calling the higher pitch an adaptation.
A: Agreed.

questions.stem: What is the woman's concern about the usual explanation?
options: Traffic noise may be too high-pitched for higher songs to stand out
The city birds might belong to a different species from the forest birds
Singing more loudly may in fact lower the pitch of a song
The birds' louder singing might itself be pushing the pitch up

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **When birds sing louder, their songs naturally rise in pitch** (כשציפורים שרות חזק יותר, הצליל של שירתן עולה מעצמו), ייתכן שהצליל הגבוה בעיר נובע רק מכך שהציפורים שרות חזק יותר.
explanation.en: She notes that **When birds sing louder, their songs naturally rise in pitch**, so the change may be **a side effect of shouting**.

questions.stem: What do the researchers decide they need to do next?
options: Check how loud the songs are in addition to their pitch
Drop the pitch data and measure the songs' loudness instead
Record the same species in several more forests for comparison
Find out whether higher songs help the city birds attract mates

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **We'd have to measure loudness as well as pitch** (נצטרך למדוד את עוצמת הקול וגם את גובה הצליל), החוקרים צריכים למדוד את עוצמת השירה ולא רק את גובה הצליל שלה.
explanation.en: She says **We'd have to measure loudness as well as pitch**, and he agrees that **it's worth doing**.

items.context: An archaeology lecturer talks about what human remains can reveal.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 50, calm and precise university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, stress on 'never changes' and on 'by contrast', a short pause at [pause], and slower, balanced delivery on the last sentence, with stress on 'childhood' and 'later life'.
script: How can archaeologists tell whether someone buried in a village actually grew up there? Part of the answer lies in chemistry. Local rock leaves a faint chemical trace in the water and crops of each region, and that trace ends up in our bodies. Now, tooth enamel forms in childhood and never changes afterward. Bone, by contrast, is rebuilt in a slow, ceaseless cycle, so it reflects recent years.   Teeth, then, speak of childhood, and bone of later life.

questions.stem: Suppose a skeleton's bones match the local trace but its teeth do not. What would this suggest?
options: The person grew up in the area but spent later years elsewhere
The person moved to the area at some point after childhood
The person left the area as a child and did not come back
The person's teeth changed after they arrived in the area

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **tooth enamel forms in childhood and never changes afterward** (אמייל השן נוצר בילדות ואינו משתנה אחר כך) והמשפט **it reflects recent years** (העצם משקפת את השנים האחרונות), האדם הגיע לאזור אחרי ילדותו.
explanation.en: Enamel **forms in childhood and never changes afterward**, while bone **reflects recent years**, so the person arrived after childhood.

items.context: A linguistics lecturer talks about a pattern found in the words of many languages.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 45, lively but measured university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Slight stress on 'use most' and 'shortest', a light, amused delivery on the two examples (Omnibus, bus; telephone, phone), a short pause at [pause], rising intonation on 'Why?', and a slower, balanced last sentence with stress on 'more' and 'less'.
script: Here's a pattern found in almost every language that's been studied: the words people use most tend to be the shortest. And when a long word becomes common, speakers often cut it down. Omnibus turned into bus, and telephone into phone.   Why? Speakers are frugal with effort. They save it on the words they say all day, and spend it where a word is rare. In short, the more a word is used, the less of it we say.

questions.stem: Which of the following fits the lecturer's explanation?
options: Seldom-used words tend to hold on to their full length
Rarely heard words get cut down more often than common ones
Short words tend to fall out of use faster than long ones
Common words grow longer as speakers add detail to them

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **spend it where a word is rare** (משקיעים את המאמץ במילים נדירות), מילים שמשתמשים בהן לעיתים רחוקות נוטות לשמור על אורכן המלא.
explanation.en: Speakers save effort on frequent words and **spend it where a word is rare**, so seldom-used words keep their full length.

items.context: Two physics lab partners talk about why people slip on ice.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural lab-conversation rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
A: female physics student, about 22, curious and slightly surprised; a confident tone on her first turn and a puzzled, rising tone on 'Then why do people slip at all?'.
B: male physics student, about 23, calm and explanatory; stress on 'barely moves' and on 'of its own', a short pause at [pause], and a lighter, more tentative delivery on 'Still, the full picture is murky.'
script: A: I always thought ice was slippery because your weight melts a thin film of water under your shoes.
B: That's the textbook story, but the numbers don't support it. A shoe spreads your weight so widely that the melting point barely moves.
A: Then why do people slip at all?
B: Because ice seems to carry a watery layer of its own, even before anyone steps on it.   Moving feet add a little melting through friction. Still, the full picture is murky.

questions.stem: According to the man, what chiefly makes ice slippery?
options: Water melted by the weight of the people walking on it
A glassy surface too smooth for shoes to grip
Heat from friction, which melts the ice as feet slide over it
A thin wet coating present even when nobody is on the ice

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **ice seems to carry a watery layer of its own, even before anyone steps on it** (נראה שלקרח יש שכבה מימית משלו, עוד לפני שמישהו דורך עליו), הקרח חלקלק בעיקר בגלל ציפוי רטוב שקיים עליו גם כשאיש אינו דורך עליו.
explanation.en: He says **ice seems to carry a watery layer of its own, even before anyone steps on it**, while friction adds only **a little**.

items.context: A history of science lecturer talks about an early attempt to measure the Earth.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: male, about 55, warm, storytelling university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). Rising intonation on the opening question, a short pause at each [pause], stress on 'straight down' and on 'did cast', a slower, step-by-step delivery on the reasoning about parallel rays and 'a fiftieth', a candid tone on 'Honestly, we can't say', and stress on 'reasoning' and 'not the final number' at the end.
script: How do you measure the whole Earth without leaving home?   More than two thousand years ago, a scholar in Alexandria named Eratosthenes heard that at noon on the longest day of the year, the sun shone straight down a deep well in Syene, far to the south. In Alexandria, at the same hour, a tall column did cast a short shadow, so the light was arriving at a slightly oblique angle, about seven degrees. Now, the sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, so that small difference had to come from the curve of the Earth. Seven degrees is about a fiftieth of a circle, so the distance between the towns had to be a fiftieth of the way around the planet.   How close did he get? Honestly, we can't say, because nobody knows exactly how long his unit of distance was. What makes the work remarkable is the reasoning, not the final number.

questions.stem: Compared with the well at Syene, what did the shadow in Alexandria show?
options: The sun was nearer to Alexandria than to Syene
The sun was overhead at Syene but not at Alexandria
The sun's rays were spreading apart over long distances
The sun's light was bent by the air above Alexandria

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the sun shone straight down a deep well in Syene** (בסיינה השמש האירה ישר לתוך באר עמוקה) והמשפט **a tall column did cast a short shadow** (באלכסנדריה עמוד גבוה הטיל צל קצר), השמש עמדה ישר מעל סיינה בלבד.
explanation.en: In Syene **the sun shone straight down a deep well**, but in Alexandria **a tall column did cast a short shadow**, so only Syene had the sun overhead.

questions.stem: What is the lecturer's view of the estimate?
options: It came remarkably close, and that is why it is admired
It was too large, since his unit of distance was too long
Its logic was weak, though the figure turned out to be right
Its accuracy is unclear, but its logic is impressive

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **we can't say** (איננו יכולים לומר) והמשפט **What makes the work remarkable is the reasoning, not the final number** (מה שמרשים בעבודה הוא דרך החשיבה ולא המספר הסופי), הדיוק לא ידוע אך ההיגיון מרשים.
explanation.en: Asked how close he got, the lecturer says **we can't say**, and adds that **What makes the work remarkable is the reasoning, not the final number**.

items.context: A student visits her anthropology professor during office hours to ask about an idea from his lecture.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural office-hours rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
