A: female anthropology student, about 21, polite but skeptical and engaged; a doubtful tone on 'I'm still not sold', stress on 'timing' and 'much later', and a thoughtful, working-it-out delivery on 'So the fires might have been there all along'.
B: male anthropology professor, about 55, patient and even-handed; a step-by-step explaining tone on his first turn, a frank, conceding tone on 'I won't pretend otherwise', a short pause at [pause], and a calm, balanced delivery on 'plausible, not proven'.
script: A: Professor, I'm still not sold on the cooking idea from your lecture. How could heating food make our brains bigger?

B: Think about energy. The brain is costly to run: it uses about a fifth of our energy at rest. Cooked food is softer and easier to digest, so we get more energy from each meal, and the body can manage with a smaller gut. That spare energy could support a bigger brain.
A: But the timing bothers me. Brains and teeth changed nearly two million years ago, and the telltale signs of regular fire, like hearths, show up much later.

B: That's the strongest objection, and I won't pretend otherwise.   Supporters do have a rejoinder: ash and charcoal rarely survive that long, so the gap may reflect what gets preserved rather than what actually happened.
A: So the fires might have been there all along, and we just can't see them.
B: Possibly. But that isn't support, either. For now, the idea is plausible, not proven.

questions.stem: What makes the student doubt the idea?
options: Signs of habitual fire use come long after the body changed
Brain growth began long after people had learned to cook
The brain uses too little energy for diet to affect its growth
Cooked meals supply the body with less energy than raw food does

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **Brains and teeth changed nearly two million years ago** (המוח והשיניים השתנו לפני כמעט שני מיליון שנה) והצירוף **show up much later** (מופיעים הרבה יותר מאוחר), עדויות האש מאוחרות בהרבה מהשינוי בגוף.
explanation.en: She notes that **Brains and teeth changed nearly two million years ago**, while signs of regular fire **show up much later**.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the professor's final position?
options: The idea has been ruled out by the lack of early fire traces
The idea is supported by the fact that ash rarely survives
The idea is believable, but it still lacks firm confirmation
The idea explains the smaller gut but not the bigger brain

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **that isn't support, either** (גם זו אינה תמיכה) והמשפט **the idea is plausible, not proven** (הרעיון סביר אך לא הוכח), הפרופסור רואה ברעיון אפשרות סבירה שעדיין לא אוששה.
explanation.en: He says the preservation argument **isn't support, either**, and ends with **the idea is plausible, not proven**.

items.context: A botany lecturer talks about what happens when insects feed on plants.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 50, clear and engaging university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). A short pause at each [pause]; an amused, slightly incredulous rising tone on 'Talking trees?'; stress on 'often do prepare' and on 'calling for help'; a more careful, weighing delivery from 'should we call this communication?' onward, with stress on 'own distant leaves' and 'listening in', and a wry, summing-up tone on the last sentence.
script: When a caterpillar starts chewing on a leaf, the plant can't run away. But it isn't helpless either. Many plants respond by releasing airborne chemicals, some of the same compounds that give freshly cut grass its smell.   What happens next is the interesting part. In the early nineteen-eighties, a few researchers reported that trees near damaged trees seemed to strengthen their own defenses, as if they'd been warned. The claim was met with disdain. Talking trees? It sounded like wishful thinking, and the first studies were small. Since then, though, careful experiments have shown that undamaged plants exposed to these chemicals often do prepare, making their leaves harder to digest before any insect arrives. Some of the chemicals also attract wasps that lay their eggs inside caterpillars, so a plant beset by hungry insects is, in effect, calling for help.   Now, should we call this communication? I'd be cautious. It's hard to see what a plant gains by warning its competitors. A likelier story is that the signal evolved to reach the plant's own distant leaves, since air can carry it faster than the stem can. The neighbors, in other words, may simply be listening in. So yes, plants respond to each other's chemical alarms, but the word talking probably gives them too much credit.

questions.stem: What happened to the early reports about trees, according to the lecturer?
options: Welcomed at first, the claim later failed in more careful tests
Doubted at first, the claim was finally shown to involve real talking
Ignored at first, the claim came back through studies of wasps
Dismissed at first, the claim has since gained experimental support

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **It sounded like wishful thinking** (זה נשמע כמו משאלת לב) והמשפט **careful experiments have shown** (ניסויים קפדניים הראו), הטענה נדחתה בתחילה אך מאז קיבלה תמיכה ניסויית.
explanation.en: At first **It sounded like wishful thinking**, but **Since then, though, careful experiments have shown** that undamaged plants do prepare.

questions.stem: Why is the lecturer cautious about calling this communication?
options: The signal may have arisen to alert other parts of the same plant
The chemicals may be too weak to travel as far as nearby plants
The proof that neighbors respond rests on a few small, early studies
Plants that pick up the signal seldom change their own defenses in response

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the signal evolved to reach the plant's own distant leaves** (האיתות הכימי התפתח כדי להגיע לעלים הרחוקים של הצמח עצמו), השכנים כנראה רק קולטים איתות שנועד לצמח עצמו.
explanation.en: She suggests that **the signal evolved to reach the plant's own distant leaves**, so **The neighbors ... may simply be listening in**.

items.context: Two psychology students discuss a classic experiment in a seminar.
items.voiceDirection:
Neutral US accent for both speakers; natural seminar rhythm, about 150 words per minute.
A: female psychology graduate student, about 26, articulate and lively; a slightly weary tone on 'pure drudgery', a confident explaining tone on the usual explanation, a working-it-out delivery on 'So no inner tension', and a measured, concluding tone on her last line, with stress on 'but not, by itself, why'.
B: male psychology graduate student, about 27, relaxed and thoughtful; stress on 'one dollar' and 'twenty', a short pause at each [pause], a gently challenging tone on 'I'm not sure we need the discomfort at all', and an even, balanced delivery on 'each one fits different situations better'.
script: A: The study we read for today still surprises me. People spent an hour on pointless tasks, like turning pegs on a board, pure drudgery. Then they were paid to tell the next participant that it had been fun.
B: Right, and some got one dollar while others got twenty. Afterward, the one-dollar group rated the tasks as more enjoyable. That's the opposite of what you'd expect.

A: Not if you accept the usual explanation. Saying something you don't believe feels uncomfortable. If you were paid twenty dollars, the money explains the lie. But a meager dollar can't justify it, so the easiest way to ease the discomfort is to decide the task wasn't so bad after all.

B: That's the textbook account, but I'm not sure we need the discomfort at all.   Imagine watching a stranger praise a dull task for a single dollar. You'd conclude they must have liked it. Maybe the participants simply judged themselves the same way, by looking at what they'd just done.
A: So no inner tension, just people reading their own behavior the way an outsider would.
B: Exactly. Both accounts predict the same result, which is why the debate lasted so long.   Later studies suggest that each one fits different situations better.
A: Then the study shows that small rewards can shift attitudes, but not, by itself, why.

questions.stem: How does the man explain the result for the one-dollar group?
options: They felt uneasy about lying and changed their view to ease it
They wanted to please the researcher who had paid them so little
They judged their feelings by noticing what they had just said
They were paid too little to care about describing it honestly

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the participants simply judged themselves the same way, by looking at what they'd just done** (המשתתפים שפטו את עצמם כמו צופה מהצד, לפי מה שעשו זה עתה), הם הסיקו מה הם מרגישים ממה שאמרו.
explanation.en: He suggests that **the participants simply judged themselves the same way, by looking at what they'd just done**, as an onlooker would.

questions.stem: What conclusion does the woman reach at the end?
options: The discomfort account has now been shown to be mistaken
The experiment establishes the effect but not its cause
Larger payments do more to change what people come to believe
The observer account works better than the usual one in most cases

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **the study shows that small rewards can shift attitudes, but not, by itself, why** (המחקר מראה שתגמול קטן יכול לשנות עמדות, אך לא מדוע), הניסוי מוכיח את התופעה אך לא את הסיבה לה.
explanation.en: She concludes that **the study shows that small rewards can shift attitudes, but not, by itself, why**.

items.context: A statistics lecturer talks about a surprising pattern in everyday numbers.
items.voiceDirection: Neutral US accent. Lecturer: female, about 40, crisp and slightly playful university-lecture tone, moderate pace (about 150 words per minute). An inviting tone on 'Take a long list', a reasonable, expectant tone on 'You might expect', a short, firm 'It doesn't.', stress on 'a third' and 'one time in twenty', a short pause at [pause], and stress on 'far too evenly' and 'very evenness' at the end.
script: Take a long list of real-world numbers, say, the populations of towns or the sums in a company's accounts, and look only at the first digit. You might expect each digit from one to nine to lead about equally often. It doesn't. Ones lead nearly a third of the time, nines barely one time in twenty.   Curiously, people who concoct figures tend to spread those first digits far too evenly, and that very evenness is what auditors learn to notice.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer, what pattern in a set of figures might make an auditor suspicious?
options: Leading digits that are ones in close to a third of cases
Leading digits that occur with nearly identical frequency
Leading digits that become steadily rarer from one to nine
Final digits that are spread fairly evenly from zero to nine

explanation.he: לפי המשפט **people who concoct figures tend to spread those first digits far too evenly** (אנשים שממציאים נתונים נוטים לפזר את הספרות הראשונות באופן שווה מדי), ספרות פותחות בשכיחות כמעט זהה מעוררות חשד.
explanation.en: Real data favor ones, but **people who concoct figures tend to spread those first digits far too evenly**.

items.title: A Walk, a Dog and a New Kind of Fastener
paragraphs: In the 1940s, an engineer in Switzerland went for a walk in the hills with his dog. When they came home, both of them were covered with burrs, the small seed cases of a wild plant. The burrs were hard to pull off, and the engineer wanted to know why. Under a microscope, he saw many tiny hooks on each burr. The hooks had caught on the loops of thread in his clothes and on his dog's hair. This is useful for the plant: animals carry the burrs far away before they fall off, so the seeds can grow in new places.

The engineer decided to make a fastener with two strips of cloth, one covered with tiny hooks and the other with small loops. When the strips were pressed together, they would hold, and a strong pull would open them. The idea was simple, but making it work took about ten years. His first strips were made of cotton, and the cotton hooks soon became soft and weak. Nylon was much sturdier: nylon strips could be opened and closed thousands of times, and the hooks still held.

At first, few companies wanted the new fastener, and many clothing makers thought it looked cheap. Then it went into space. Astronauts used the strips to keep tools and food from floating away, and people began to see the fastener in a new way. Today it is used on bags, sports equipment and the shoes of small children who cannot tie their laces yet.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why burrs hold on so tightly to the fur of animals
How engineers have copied many different ideas from plants and animals
How a plant's seed cases led to a useful invention
Why the makers of clothing did not want to use nylon at first

explanation.he: הפסקאות עוברות מהצירוף **covered with burrs**, דרך הרצועות, אל הצירוף **Today it is used on bags**, ולכן הקטע עוסק בתרמילי זרעים של צמח שהובילו להמצאה שימושית (הצירוף **led to a useful invention**).
explanation.en: The passage moves from **covered with burrs** to the strips and **Today it is used on bags**, so it shows how a plant's seed cases led to a useful invention.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, how do the hooks help the plant?
options: They let animals take its seeds to new places.
They keep its seeds close to the parent plant.
They help its seeds take in water from the rain.
They stop birds from finding its seeds.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **animals carry the burrs far away before they fall off, so the seeds can grow in new places**, בעלי חיים לוקחים את הזרעים למקומות חדשים (הצירוף **new places**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 1 says **animals carry the burrs far away before they fall off, so the seeds can grow in new places**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what was the problem with the first strips?
options: Their two parts were too hard to pull apart.
Their loops were too small for the hooks to catch.
Their nylon hooks were too soft to hold.
Their hooks soon became too weak to hold.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the cotton hooks soon became soft and weak**, הווים של הרצועות הראשונות נחלשו מהר, ולכן הם היו חלשים מדי כדי להחזיק (הצירוף **too weak to hold**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says **His first strips were made of cotton, and the cotton hooks soon became soft and weak**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the word "sturdier" is closest in meaning to
options: harder to damage
softer to the touch
cheaper to make
simpler to use

explanation.he: אחרי הנקודתיים בא הסבר, הצירוף **could be opened and closed thousands of times, and the hooks still held**, ולכן המילה **sturdier** פירושה חזק ועמיד יותר (הצירוף **harder to damage**).
explanation.en: After the colon, **could be opened and closed thousands of times, and the hooks still held** shows that **sturdier** means harder to damage.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention astronauts in paragraph 3?
options: To show that the fastener was first made for use in space
To explain how the fastener came to be widely used
To explain why clothing makers thought it looked cheap
To explain why the engineer chose nylon over cotton

explanation.he: האסטרונאוטים באים בין הצירוף **few companies wanted the new fastener** לבין הצירוף **Today it is used on bags**, ולכן הם מסבירים איך ההמצאה הגיעה לשימוש רחב (הצירוף **widely used**).
explanation.en: The astronauts come between **few companies wanted the new fastener** and **Today it is used on bags**, so they explain how it came to be widely used.

items.title: Why Do Chameleons Change Color?
paragraphs: Many people believe that a chameleon changes its color to match the place where it sits. On a green leaf, they say, it turns green, and on a brown branch it turns brown. This is a popular idea, but it is mostly wrong. A chameleon's usual green or brown colors already help it hide among leaves and branches, so it does not need to change them for this purpose. Scientists now believe that its color changes have other jobs.

The changes happen in the skin. Under the top layer, many chameleons have special cells that contain very small crystals. When the animal is calm, the crystals are packed close together, and they reflect blue light. This blue mixes with a yellow color in the skin, so the chameleon looks green. When the animal becomes excited, the crystals move apart. Now they reflect yellow and red light, and in a few minutes the skin becomes bright.

Chameleons change color mostly to send messages to each other. When two males meet, each may turn bright to look strong, and the brighter male often wins, sometimes without a fight. The other male soon turns dark and dull, which shows that it is giving up. Color also helps with body temperature. In the cool morning, a chameleon may turn darker, because dark skin takes in more heat from the sun.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How crystals in a chameleon's skin reflect light
How and why chameleons really change color
Why chameleons change color to match what they sit on
How different animals use color to send messages

explanation.he: פסקה 1 דוחה רעיון נפוץ בצירוף **it is mostly wrong**, פסקה 2 מסבירה איך הצבע משתנה ופסקה 3 למה, ולכן הקטע עוסק באופן ובסיבה האמיתיים לשינוי הצבע (הצירוף **How and why chameleons really change color**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 1 calls the popular idea **mostly wrong**, and paragraphs 2 and 3 explain how and why chameleons really change color.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, why do chameleons not need to change color in order to hide?
options: They spend most of the day hidden under leaves.
Their skin changes color too slowly to help them hide in time.
Few other animals hunt them in the trees.
Their usual colors already help them hide among plants.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **usual green or brown colors already help it hide among leaves and branches**, הצבעים הרגילים של הזיקית כבר עוזרים לה להסתתר (הצירוף **already help them hide**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 1 says **usual green or brown colors already help it hide among leaves and branches, so it does not need to change them**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why does a calm chameleon look green?
options: Its crystals move apart and reflect yellow and red light.
Its skin takes in the green color of the leaves around it.
Blue light from its crystals mixes with yellow.
A green top layer of skin hides its other colors.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **This blue mixes with a yellow color in the skin, so the chameleon looks green**, האור הכחול מהגבישים מתערבב עם צבע צהוב (הצירוף **mixes with a yellow color**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says the calm crystals **reflect blue light**, and **This blue mixes with a yellow color in the skin, so the chameleon looks green**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the word "it" in "it is giving up" refers to
options: the male that is brighter
the fight between the two males
the bright color
the male that does not win

explanation.he: המילה **it** מתייחסת לנושא של המשפט, הצירוף **The other male**, כלומר לזכר שלא מנצח (הצירוף **the male that does not win**), כי הוא זה שנעשה כהה ומוותר.
explanation.en: The subject of the sentence is **The other male**, the one that does not win, so **it** refers to that male.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a chameleon that suddenly turns bright yellow and red?
options: It is probably reacting to another chameleon.
It is probably trying to match a bright flower.
Its crystals have probably moved closer together.
It probably wants to warm its body in the cool morning.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **When two males meet, each may turn bright**, צבע בהיר מופיע במפגש בין זיקיות, ולכן זיקית שנעשית בהירה כנראה מגיבה לזיקית אחרת (הצירוף **reacting to another chameleon**).
explanation.en: Bright colors come when the animal is **excited**, and **When two males meet, each may turn bright**, so it is probably reacting to another chameleon.

items.title: Why Is an Hour Sixty Minutes Long?
paragraphs: We count most things in tens. Our number system is built on ten, probably because people first counted on their ten fingers. Time is different, however. There are sixty seconds in a minute and sixty minutes in an hour. This unusual number comes from a very old way of counting.

More than four thousand years ago, people in Mesopotamia, the land between two great rivers in the Middle East, counted in groups of sixty. One possible reason is that sixty is easy to share. It can be divided by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, so a half, a third or a quarter of sixty is always a whole number. Ten, by contrast, can be divided only by 2 and 5.

This way of counting spread to other places. Much later, Greek scientists who studied the stars used it to divide circles into small parts. The word "minute" comes from a Latin phrase that means "small part," and "second" comes from the phrase for the second, even smaller, division. When clocks with minute hands appeared, the system of sixty was already old and familiar, so clocks used it too.

Not everyone has liked this system. In the 1790s, France tried decimal time, with ten hours in a day and one hundred minutes in each hour. Special clocks were made, but most people did not want to change their habits, and the plan was soon discarded. France kept other new measures, such as the meter, but time stayed in sixties.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why we count time in sixties rather than in tens
How people in ancient Mesopotamia did their counting
How people have measured time throughout history
Why France decided to keep the meter but not decimal time

explanation.he: הפסקאות עוברות מהצירוף **Time is different**, דרך מקור השיטה וניסיון לשנות אותה, אל הצירוף **time stayed in sixties**, ולכן הקטע מסביר למה סופרים זמן בשישים ולא בעשרות (הצירוף **in sixties rather than in tens**).
explanation.en: The passage moves from **Time is different** to **time stayed in sixties**, so it explains why we count time in sixties rather than in tens.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why may people in Mesopotamia have counted in sixties?
options: Sixty was the number of minutes in their hour.
Ten can be divided by more numbers than sixty can.
Sixty can be divided into many equal parts.
Large numbers were hard to write in groups of ten.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **One possible reason is that sixty is easy to share**, ולפי רשימת המספרים שאחריו, אפשר לחלק את שישים לחלקים שווים רבים (הצירוף **many equal parts**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says **One possible reason is that sixty is easy to share**, and it lists the many numbers that divide it.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, which of the following is true about the word "minute"?
options: It was first used by the people of ancient Mesopotamia.
It was taken from Latin words for a small part.
It was chosen because clocks had sixty marks.
It once meant a part of a second.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **The word "minute" comes from a Latin phrase that means "small part,"**, מקור המילה הוא צירוף לטיני שפירושו חלק קטן (הצירוף **a small part**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 says **The word "minute" comes from a Latin phrase that means "small part,"**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "discarded" is closest in meaning to
options: tested
made official
copied by others
given up

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **most people did not want to change their habits** והצירוף **time stayed in sixties**, התוכנית לא נשארה, ולכן המילה **discarded** פירושה שוויתרו עליה (הצירוף **given up**).
explanation.en: **most people did not want to change their habits**, and **time stayed in sixties**, so **discarded** means given up.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 4?
options: Decimal time may have failed because its clocks were hard to make.
A new system can succeed if special clocks are made for it.
A system that people use every day can be hard to replace.
Most people in France found it hard to count in tens.

explanation.he: התוכנית ננטשה כי רוב האנשים לא רצו לשנות את ההרגלים שלהם (**most people did not want to change their habits**), ומכאן שקשה להחליף שיטה שאנשים משתמשים בה כל יום (**can be hard to replace**).
explanation.en: The plan failed because **most people did not want to change their habits**, so a system used every day can be hard to replace.

items.title: Desire Paths: When Walkers Choose the Way
paragraphs: In many parks and on many university campuses, narrow lines of bare earth cut across the grass. Planners call them desire paths. Nobody builds them on purpose. They appear when many people choose the same shortcut, usually because the paved path takes a longer way around.

A desire path grows in stages. At first, only a few walkers cross the lawn, and the grass is just pressed down a little. Because a visible line is easier to follow than open grass, the next walkers tend to use it too. Soon the grass wears away completely. In this way, each person who takes the shortcut makes it more inviting for the next one.

For a long time, many planners saw these paths as a problem. They put up fences and signs, or they planted bushes in the way. Such efforts often fail, however. Walkers flout the signs and step around the bushes, and before long a new path appears close by.

Some designers now take the opposite approach. On several campuses, new lawns have been left without paths for a while, sometimes for a whole year. The paths were then paved where walkers had worn them down. Supporters say that this produces routes that people actually use, although the result may look less neat than a planned design.

glossary.he: להפר בגלוי (כלל או הוראה), להתעלם במופגן
glossary.en: to openly ignore a rule or an instruction

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why signs and fences often fail to keep walkers off the grass
How cities decide where to build new roads and parks
Why walkers should stay on the paths that planners build
How walkers' shortcuts form and how planners deal with them

explanation.he: הפסקאות עוברות מהצירוף **grows in stages** אל הצירוף **saw these paths as a problem** ואל הצירוף **the opposite approach**, ולכן הקטע עוסק בהיווצרות קיצורי הדרך ובתגובת המתכננים (הצירוף **deal with them**).
explanation.en: The paragraphs go from **grows in stages** to **saw these paths as a problem** and **the opposite approach**: how shortcuts form and how planners respond.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why do later walkers tend to use a path that has just begun to form?
options: The grass along it has already worn away.
A line that stands out is simpler to walk along.
Signs near the lawn point them toward the new shortcut.
The paved path nearby has been closed for repairs.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **Because a visible line is easier to follow than open grass**, קו בולט קל יותר ללכת בעקבותיו (הצירוף **a line that stands out**), ולכן ההולכים הבאים משתמשים בו.
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says **Because a visible line is easier to follow than open grass, the next walkers tend to use it too**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what often happens when bushes are planted in a desire path?
options: People walk around them, and a new path forms close by.
Walkers return to the paved path after a short time.
The bushes are pulled out by walkers who need the path.
Planners add signs to explain why the bushes are there.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **step around the bushes, and before long a new path appears close by**, אנשים עוקפים את השיחים ושביל חדש נוצר בקרבת מקום (הצירוף **a new path forms close by**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 says walkers **step around the bushes, and before long a new path appears close by**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the word "inviting" is closest in meaning to
options: hard to see
bare and muddy
tempting to use
flat and direct

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the next walkers tend to use it too**, כל הולך גורם לשביל למשוך עוד הולכים, ולכן המילה **inviting** פירושה מושך, מפתה (הצירוף **tempting to use**).
explanation.en: Each walker makes the next one more likely to use the path (**the next walkers tend to use it too**), so **inviting** means tempting to use.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about the designers who wait before paving paths?
options: They want lawns to stay free of paths for good.
They believe walkers' choices show where paths are needed.
They care more about neat designs than about walkers.
They have found that bushes keep walkers off better than fences do.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **paved where walkers had worn them down**, המעצבים סוללים שבילים במקום שבו ההולכים בחרו ללכת, ולכן הם מאמינים שבחירת ההולכים מראה איפה צריך שבילים (הצירוף **show where paths are needed**).
explanation.en: They pave the paths **where walkers had worn them down**, so they must believe walkers' choices show where paths are needed.

items.title: Why Our Fingers Wrinkle in the Bath
paragraphs: After a long bath or swim, the skin on our fingers and toes becomes covered in deep folds. In warm water, the fingertips can look wizened within about five to ten minutes, like the skin of an old apple. For many years, most people believed that the reason was simple: the outer layer of the skin takes in water and swells, so it has to fold, just as wet paper does.

However, this explanation has a serious problem. Doctors noticed long ago that when the nerves in a finger are damaged, the finger does not wrinkle, even after a long time in water. If water alone caused the folds, the nerves would not matter. In fact, some doctors once used a warm-water test to check whether a patient's nerves were working.

Today, scientists believe that the body itself produces the wrinkles. When the hands stay in water, the nerves send a signal that makes the tiny blood vessels under the skin constrict. As a result, the fingertip loses some of its volume, and the skin on top is pulled down into folds. This also explains why wrinkled fingers often look paler than usual.

But why would the body do this? One popular idea is that the folds work like the patterns on a car tire, which carry water away and help the tire grip a wet road. In one experiment, people with wrinkled fingers moved wet objects faster than people with smooth fingers. Other studies, however, have not found the same effect, so the question is still open.

glossary.he: מצומק וקמוט (בדרך כלל מזקנה או מהתייבשות)
glossary.en: dry, shrunken and full of wrinkles, often because of age

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main idea of the passage?
options: Doctors once checked whether a patient's nerves were working by placing the patient's hands in warm water.
Finger wrinkles form because the skin takes in water, and they probably help people grip wet objects.
Finger wrinkles are produced by the body rather than by water alone, but their purpose is still uncertain.
Wrinkled fingers are a warning sign of nerve damage and should be checked by a doctor as soon as possible.

explanation.he: משפטי הנושא עוברים מההסבר הישן אל הצירוף **the body itself produces the wrinkles** ואל הצירוף **the question is still open**, ולכן: הגוף יוצר את הקמטים, אבל מטרתם עדיין לא ברורה (**their purpose is still uncertain**).
explanation.en: The passage moves from **the body itself produces the wrinkles** to **the question is still open**: the body makes the folds, but their purpose is still uncertain.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what shows that water alone does not cause the wrinkles?
options: A finger whose nerves are damaged stays smooth in water.
Damaged nerves make the skin fold more quickly in water.
Doctors found that the outer layer of skin does not take in water.
Some doctors used warm water to damage the nerves in a finger.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **when the nerves in a finger are damaged, the finger does not wrinkle**, אצבע שהעצבים שלה פגועים נשארת חלקה (המילה **smooth**), ולכן המים לבדם לא יוצרים את הקמטים.
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says that **when the nerves in a finger are damaged, the finger does not wrinkle**, so water alone is not the cause.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what happens when the nerves send their signal?
options: The fingertip swells as it fills with water.
The fingertip becomes warmer, and its color grows darker than usual.
The nerves in the fingertip stop working for a short time.
The fingertip becomes smaller, and its skin is pulled into folds.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the fingertip loses some of its volume**, קצה האצבע נעשה קטן יותר, ולפי הצירוף **pulled down into folds** העור שמעליו נמשך לקפלים (הצירוף **becomes smaller**, נעשה קטן יותר).
explanation.en: After the signal, **the fingertip loses some of its volume, and the skin on top is pulled down into folds**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the word "constrict" is closest in meaning to
options: become wider
become narrower
fill with water
grow stronger

explanation.he: בעקבות האות קצה האצבע מאבד נפח, לפי הצירוף **loses some of its volume**, ונעשה חיוור יותר, ולכן המילה **constrict** פירושה להתכווץ, להיעשות צר יותר (הצירוף **become narrower**).
explanation.en: When the vessels **constrict**, the fingertip **loses some of its volume** and looks **paler**, so **constrict** means **become narrower**.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention a car tire in paragraph 4?
options: To show that the folds on fingers and on tires might form in the same way
To explain why later studies did not find the same effect as the first experiment
To compare how well wet fingers and dry fingers hold small objects
To illustrate one suggested reason why the body might produce finger wrinkles

explanation.he: הצמיג מובא כדי להסביר את הרעיון שבצירוף **One popular idea is that the folds work like the patterns on a car tire**, כלומר כדי להמחיש סיבה אפשרית לקמטים (המילה **illustrate**, להמחיש).
explanation.en: The tire explains **One popular idea**: the folds may **carry water away** like tire patterns, a possible reason for the wrinkles.

items.title: Earworms: Why Songs Get Stuck in Our Heads
paragraphs: Most people know the feeling. A short piece of music, often the chorus of a pop song or a jaunty tune from an advertisement, starts playing in the mind and will not stop. Such tunes are known as earworms. Surveys suggest that most people have one at least once a week, and that a single earworm can last for hours.

Earworms do not appear at random. They are usually songs that a person has heard recently or many times. They can also be brought back by a memory: a word, a place or even a face can remind us of a song connected with it. Interestingly, earworms tend to appear when the mind is not busy, for example while people are walking, showering or doing housework.

Some songs become earworms far more easily than others. Research suggests that such songs usually have a fairly fast beat and a simple melody that is easy to sing. At the same time, they often contain one or two surprising notes, which may help them stick in the memory. Usually, only a short part of the song gets stuck, so the same few seconds play again and again.

How can people get rid of an earworm? Trying hard not to think about the song often backfires, since the effort itself keeps the tune in mind. According to some studies, a better strategy is to work on a task that is moderately difficult, such as a word puzzle. Others find that chewing gum helps, perhaps because moving the jaw makes silent singing harder.

glossary.en: cheerful, lively and full of confidence

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To describe the musical features that make some songs easier to remember than others
To explain what earworms are, what causes them and how people can stop them
To compare the different ways in which music affects people's moods and memories
To warn readers that listening to pop songs and advertisements can harm their memory

explanation.he: הקטע עובר מהתופעה (**Such tunes are known as earworms**), דרך הגורמים, אל השאלה **How can people get rid of an earworm?**, ולכן מטרתו להסביר מה הן תולעי אוזן, מה גורם להן ואיך להפסיק אותן (**how people can stop them**).
explanation.en: It defines earworms, gives their causes and asks **How can people get rid of an earworm?**: what they are, their causes, how to stop them.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, when do earworms tend to appear?
options: When people are in a busy place, such as a crowded market or station
When people are working on a difficult task
When people see a face that they do not know
When people are doing something that needs little attention

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **when the mind is not busy**, והדוגמאות **walking, showering or doing housework**, תולעי אוזן מופיעות כשעושים דבר שדורש מעט תשומת לב (**needs little attention**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 2 says earworms appear **when the mind is not busy**, as in **walking, showering or doing housework**: activities that need little attention.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what is typical of songs that become earworms?
options: They are easy to sing but include a few unexpected notes.
They have a slow and steady beat that is easy to remember.
They are long songs that contain many different musical parts.
They are usually songs that people do not like.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **a simple melody that is easy to sing** והצירוף **one or two surprising notes**, השירים האלה קלים לשירה אבל כוללים כמה צלילים לא צפויים (**a few unexpected notes**).
explanation.en: Such songs have **a simple melody that is easy to sing**, but they also **contain one or two surprising notes**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "backfires" is closest in meaning to
options: is quickly forgotten
becomes a habit
has the opposite result
needs a lot of practice

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **since the effort itself keeps the tune in mind**, המאמץ לא לחשוב על השיר דווקא משאיר אותו בראש, ולכן המילה **backfires** פירושה פועל הפוך מהכוונה (**has the opposite result**).
explanation.en: The effort **keeps the tune in mind**, the opposite of what people want, so **backfires** means **has the opposite result**.

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 2 and 4, why might a word puzzle help to stop an earworm?
options: It keeps the mind busy, which makes the song less likely to return.
It probably teaches people to forget songs they have heard many times.
It keeps the jaw moving in the same way that chewing gum does.
It lets people sing the song silently until it finally stops.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **when the mind is not busy** תולעי אוזן מופיעות כשהמוח פנוי, ולכן משימה כמו תשבץ (**a word puzzle**) עוזרת כי היא מעסיקה את המוח (**keeps the mind busy**).
explanation.en: Earworms appear **when the mind is not busy**, so a task like **a word puzzle** helps because it keeps the mind busy.

items.title: Why People in Old Photographs Rarely Smiled
paragraphs: Look at almost any family photograph from the 1800s, and you will see the same thing: stiff, mirthless faces staring at the camera. Today, by contrast, it is hard to find a photograph of a person who is not smiling. Why did people in the past look so serious?

A popular answer is that early cameras were very slow. In the first years of photography, a person had to sit perfectly still for many seconds, sometimes even minutes, and few people can hold a natural smile for so long. This explanation is partly true, but it is not the whole story. By the 1880s, a photograph could be taken in a second or less, yet most people still did not smile.

Another reason has to do with tradition. Before photography, usually only the rich could pay for a painted portrait, and in such paintings a wide smile was often seen as foolish or rude. Early photographers and their customers followed these old rules. Moreover, a photograph was expensive, and for many people it was the only picture of themselves that they would ever have. Naturally, they wanted to look serious and respectable rather than silly.

This began to change in the early 1900s, when cheap, easy-to-use cameras appeared. Ordinary families could now take many pictures of holidays and celebrations, so a single photograph no longer seemed so special. Advertisements for these cameras also showed happy, smiling people, and over time the smile became the normal way to face the camera.

glossary.he: חסר שמחה, בלי שמץ של עליזות
glossary.en: without any joy or amusement

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Early cameras were so slow that people could not hold a smile while their picture was taken.
Photography changed the way people in the 1800s thought about art, about family and about the future.
Advertisements for cheap cameras were the first to show people smiling at the camera.
The serious faces in old photographs had several causes, of which slow cameras were just one.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **it is not the whole story** ההסבר הפופולרי לא מספיק, והקטע מוסיף סיבות של מסורת ומחיר, ולכן: לפרצופים הרציניים היו כמה סיבות, ומצלמות איטיות היו רק אחת מהן (**just one**).
explanation.en: The slow-camera answer **is not the whole story**; tradition and cost also mattered, so slow cameras were just one of several causes.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what shows that slow cameras do not fully explain the serious faces?
options: Few people could hold a natural smile for many seconds.
Faces stayed unsmiling even after cameras had become much faster.
Early cameras could take a picture in a second or less.
Early photographs often showed people with wide, natural smiles on their faces.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **a photograph could be taken in a second or less, yet most people still did not smile**, הפרצופים נשארו בלי חיוך גם כשהמצלמות נעשו מהירות (**Faces stayed unsmiling**).
explanation.en: **By the 1880s, a photograph could be taken in a second or less, yet most people still did not smile**.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, why did people want to look serious in their photographs?
options: Their cameras were too slow to record a natural smile.
They believed that a smile would probably make the photograph cost more.
They were paying a lot for what was often their only picture.
They were following new rules made by early photographers.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **a photograph was expensive** והצירוף **the only picture of themselves that they would ever have**, תמונה הייתה יקרה ולעתים קרובות התמונה היחידה של האדם (**their only picture**).
explanation.en: **a photograph was expensive**, and for many it was **the only picture of themselves that they would ever have**, so they wanted to look serious.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "This" in "This began to change" refers to
options: the custom of looking serious in photographs
the high cost of painted portraits
the slow speed of early cameras
the use of advertisements to sell new cameras

explanation.he: המילה **This** מתייחסת למה שתואר עד כה, הרצון להיראות רציניים בצירוף **wanted to look serious**, וסוף הפסקה, הצירוף **the smile became the normal way**, מאשר זאת: המנהג להיראות רציני (**the custom of looking serious**).
explanation.en: **This** points back to people who **wanted to look serious**; the paragraph ends with **the smile became the normal way to face the camera**.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the passage about the spread of smiling in photographs?
options: It began as soon as cameras could take a picture in a second or less.
It depended more on how people valued photographs than on camera speed.
It was probably started by painters, who began to paint smiling faces.
It happened because photographs became more expensive than painted portraits.

explanation.he: החיוך לא הופיע עם המצלמות המהירות (**yet most people still did not smile**) אלא כשתמונה כבר לא נראתה מיוחדת (**no longer seemed so special**), ולכן הוא תלוי ביחס לתמונות (**how people valued photographs**).
explanation.en: Fast cameras did not bring smiles (**yet most people still did not smile**); smiles came when a photograph **no longer seemed so special**.

items.title: Black, White and Puzzling: Why Zebras Have Stripes
paragraphs: The zebra's coat has long puzzled biologists. Bold stripes would seem to make an animal easy to spot on open grassland, yet a feature that makes an animal more visible to its enemies would be expected to disappear unless it brought some benefit. Several explanations have been proposed, and at first most of them sound reasonable.

The oldest idea is camouflage. Perhaps the stripes help a zebra blend into tall grass or the dappled light at the edge of a woodland, or perhaps a running herd becomes a confusing mass of lines from which a lion cannot easily pick out one animal. Recently, however, this explanation has lost much of its appeal. Lions hunt mainly at dusk and at night, and some studies suggest that in such dim light they can hardly see the stripes from more than a short distance.

A second idea concerns heat. Black stripes absorb more sunlight than white ones, and it has been suggested that the difference creates small air currents that cool the animal. Yet tests with barrels covered in striped and plain hides have produced mixed results, and any cooling effect appears to be small.

The explanation that now has the most support involves insects. Horseflies and other biting flies are importunate pests that spread disease and feed on the blood of large animals. In several experiments, flies approached striped coats as often as plain ones but landed on them far less often: instead of slowing down smoothly, they tended to fly past or bump into the coat. The stripes, it seems, thwart a fly's attempt to land. As a result, a striped animal may be bitten less often, which could explain why the zebras with the boldest stripes tend to live where biting flies are most active.
No single study has settled the matter, and the stripes may serve more than one purpose. Still, the zebra's coat shows how an obvious answer can give way to one that few people would have guessed.

glossary.en: marked with spots or patches of light and shade
annoyingly persistent; refusing to go away or stop asking

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how horseflies and other biting flies spread disease among the large animals they feed on
To argue that zebras' stripes help them hide from lions in tall grass and at dusk
To describe several explanations for the zebra's stripes and show which one the evidence now favors
To compare the various ways in which African animals protect themselves from their enemies

explanation.he: פסקאות 2–4 מציגות שלושה הסברים, ולפי הצירוף **now has the most support** אחד מהם מועדף, ולכן המטרה היא לתאר כמה הסברים לפסים ולהראות איזה מהם מועדף כיום (**which one the evidence now favors**).
explanation.en: Paragraphs 2-4 give three explanations, and the insect one **now has the most support**, so the purpose is to describe several explanations and show which the evidence favors.

questions.stem: Why has the idea that the stripes serve as camouflage lost much of its appeal?
options: Lions usually hunt when the light may be too dim for them to see the stripes.
Lions often hunt in bright daylight, when the stripes stand out clearly even from far away.
Zebras rarely spend time in tall grass or at the edges of woodlands.
Lions have been found to pick out single animals from running herds quite easily.

explanation.he: האריות צדים בעיקר בשעת בין ערביים ובלילה, לפי הצירוף **Lions hunt mainly at dusk and at night**, ואז הם כמעט לא רואים את הפסים, כי האור חלש מדי (**too dim**).
explanation.en: **Lions hunt mainly at dusk and at night**, when **they can hardly see the stripes**, so the light is **too dim** for the stripes to matter.

questions.stem: Which of the following is stated about the idea that the stripes help to cool the zebra?
options: It depends on white stripes taking in more sunlight than black ones.
It is the explanation that now has the most support among researchers.
It was put forward after the explanation involving insects had been rejected.
Tests of it have produced results that do not all agree.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **have produced mixed results**, הניסויים בחביות נתנו תוצאות מעורבות, כלומר תוצאות שאינן מתיישבות זו עם זו (**do not all agree**).
explanation.en: The barrel tests **have produced mixed results**, that is, results that **do not all agree**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "thwart" is closest in meaning to
options: direct
prevent
encourage
reveal

explanation.he: הזבובים מתקרבים אבל נוחתים הרבה פחות, לפי הצירוף **landed on them far less often**, ולכן המילה **thwart** פירושה לסכל, למנוע (המילה **prevent**).
explanation.en: Flies approached but **landed on them far less often**, so the stripes **thwart**, that is, **prevent**, a landing.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about zebras in places with few biting insects?
options: They probably rely on their stripes to stay cool more than zebras in other areas do.
They are more easily picked out of a running herd by hunting lions.
They probably have less bold stripes than zebras that live among many flies.
They tend to spend more of their time at the edges of woodlands.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the zebras with the boldest stripes tend to live where biting flies are most active**, היכן שיש מעט זבובים צפויים פסים פחות בולטים (**less bold stripes**).
explanation.en: Since **the zebras with the boldest stripes tend to live where biting flies are most active**, zebras among few flies probably have **less bold stripes**.

items.title: On the Tip of the Tongue: When a Familiar Word Will Not Come
paragraphs: Most people know the feeling. A speaker is about to name a film, a street or an old classmate, and the word simply will not come, even though the speaker is sure of knowing it. Psychologists call this a tip-of-the-tongue state. It is particularly galling because the missing word is usually a familiar one, not a rare term that the speaker barely knows.

Such a state is rarely a complete blank. In studies, people caught in one can often report the first letter of the missing word, roughly how many syllables it has, or another word that sounds similar. This partial knowledge suggests that the problem does not lie in meaning, since the speaker knows exactly what the word refers to. Instead, the link between the meaning of the word and its sounds seems to have weakened, so that only an inchoate outline of its form reaches awareness.

Several factors appear to make these states more likely. They tend to become more frequent with age, and they are especially common with proper names. One explanation is that a name such as Baker is tied to its owner by a single, arbitrary link, whereas the ordinary word "baker" is connected to many other words and ideas, such as bread, ovens and early mornings. Tiredness and stress may also play a part.

Oddly, trying harder seldom helps; it may even impede recall. A wrong word that comes to mind, such as a similar-sounding name, can block the right one, and each failed attempt may make the block stronger. Many people find that the missing word arrives on its own some time later, while they are thinking about something else entirely. Some studies even suggest that after one long search, a speaker is more likely to get stuck on the same word again, as if the mind had practiced the wrong path.

glossary.en: very annoying, especially because it seems unfair
only partly formed; not yet clear or complete

questions.stem: What is the passage mostly about?
options: The reasons why older people find it harder than younger people to remember proper names
A common failure to find a familiar word, and some of the factors behind it
The many different ways in which human memory can let people down in everyday conversation
A simple method that people can use to recall forgotten words more quickly

explanation.he: הקטע נותן שם לתופעה (**a tip-of-the-tongue state**) ומונה גורמים שמגבירים אותה (**Several factors**), ולכן הוא עוסק בכישלון נפוץ למצוא מילה מוכרת ובכמה מהגורמים שמאחוריו (**some of the factors behind it**).
explanation.en: The passage defines **a tip-of-the-tongue state** and its causes, so it is about a common failure to find a familiar word and the factors behind it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what can people in a tip-of-the-tongue state often do?
options: Spell the word correctly even though they are unable to say it aloud
Explain where and when they first learned the missing word
Give a clear definition of the word but not its first letter
Say which letter the word starts with or roughly how long it is

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **can often report the first letter of the missing word, roughly how many syllables it has**, אפשר לומר באיזו אות המילה מתחילה (**the first letter**) ולנחש את אורכה.
explanation.en: People **can often report the first letter of the missing word, roughly how many syllables it has**, so they can name the first letter or guess its length.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, are proper names a common source of these states?
options: A name usually has just one link to its owner, with no special logic.
Ordinary words usually have far fewer links to other words and ideas than names do.
Stress and tiredness affect names more strongly than they affect other words.
Names tend to be longer and harder to pronounce than most ordinary words.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **tied to its owner by a single, arbitrary link**, שם קשור לבעליו בקשר יחיד ושרירותי, כלומר בקשר אחד שאין מאחוריו היגיון מיוחד (**no special logic**).
explanation.en: A name **is tied to its owner by a single, arbitrary link**, that is, one link with **no special logic**.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "impede" is closest in meaning to
options: improve
measure
delay
replace

explanation.he: המאמץ כמעט לא עוזר (הצירוף **trying harder seldom helps**), ומילה שגויה חוסמת את הנכונה, ולכן המילה **impede** פירושה לעכב, להפריע (המילה **delay**).
explanation.en: Since **trying harder seldom helps** and a wrong word **can block the right one**, **impede** means **delay**.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the missing word in a tip-of-the-tongue state?
options: It is probably still stored in memory, although it cannot be reached.
It is probably a word whose meaning the speaker has partly forgotten.
It is more likely to be recalled easily the next time it is needed.
It is usually a rare term that the speaker learned long ago and barely knows.

explanation.he: הדובר בטוח שהוא מכיר את המילה, ולפי הצירוף **arrives on its own some time later** היא חוזרת מעצמה, ולכן היא כנראה עדיין שמורה בזיכרון (**still stored in memory**).
explanation.en: The speaker is **sure of knowing it**, and the word **arrives on its own some time later**, so it is probably still **stored in memory**.

items.title: Thinking Inside the Box: The Rise of the Shipping Container
paragraphs: Few inventions look as unremarkable as the shipping container, a steel box of standard size that can be moved from ship to train to truck without being opened. Yet this workaday object has arguably done more to shape modern trade than many far more complex machines. Before it appeared, the cost of moving goods by sea depended less on the distance traveled than on what happened in port.

For centuries, cargo was loaded by hand. Sacks, barrels and crates of every shape had to be lifted one by one into a ship's hold and fitted together like the pieces of a puzzle, then unloaded the same way at the other end. A ship could spend a week or more in port, and the wages of the dockworkers could cost more than the voyage itself. Goods were also often damaged or stolen while they waited on the docks.

Containers changed this because they turned many small loads into a few identical large ones. Goods were packed into the box at the factory and not touched again until they reached their destination. Cranes could lift a container from a truck onto a ship in minutes, so a ship that had once waited a week could be unloaded and reloaded in less than a day. As handling costs fell sharply, shipping goods across an ocean became so cheap that companies could make parts in one country and assemble them in another.

The change, however, was neither quick nor painless. Early containers came in many sizes, and the box became truly useful only after shipping companies agreed on a few standard dimensions, a process that took years. Many old ports, squeezed into narrow city centers, had no room for the huge cranes and storage yards that containers required. Laggard ports that hesitated to build them soon lost their traffic to new terminals elsewhere. For dockworkers, too, the gains came at a price, since far fewer workers were needed.

glossary.en: ordinary and everyday; not special or exciting
slower than others to act or make progress

questions.stem: Which of the following best sums up the passage?
options: Loading cargo by hand was slow and costly, and goods were often damaged or stolen.
Many inventions of the last century changed the way in which goods are made and sold.
Old ports in narrow city centers gained most of the traffic once containers came into use.
A standard steel box made shipping far cheaper, though not quickly or for everyone.

explanation.he: פסקה 3 מראה הוזלה חדה, ופסקה 4 מוסיפה את הצירוף **neither quick nor painless**, ולכן: קופסה תקנית הוזילה מאוד את השילוח, אבל לא מהר ולא לטובת כולם (**not quickly or for everyone**).
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 shows **handling costs fell sharply**, and paragraph 4 adds **neither quick nor painless**, so a standard box made shipping cheaper, but not quickly or for everyone.

questions.stem: What does the passage say about loading ships before containers were used?
options: It usually cost less than the voyage, although it took a long time.
Each item had to be carried and fitted into the ship's hold separately.
Dockworkers often packed the goods at the factory in order to save time.
Goods were rarely damaged, since workers handled them with great care.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **had to be lifted one by one into a ship's hold**, כל פריט הורם והותאם למקומו לבד, כלומר בנפרד (**separately**).
explanation.en: Goods **had to be lifted one by one into a ship's hold** and fitted together, that is, each item **separately**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why were companies able to make parts in one country and assemble them in another?
options: Ships began to travel much faster between distant countries than before.
Factories moved closer to the ports so that goods could be loaded onto ships directly.
Handling costs fell so much that sending goods overseas became very cheap.
Cranes allowed workers to open containers and check the goods in minutes.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **As handling costs fell sharply, shipping goods across an ocean became so cheap**, עלויות הטיפול ירדו עד כדי כך שהשילוח נעשה זול מאוד (**very cheap**).
explanation.en: **As handling costs fell sharply, shipping goods across an ocean became so cheap** that parts could be made in one country and assembled in another.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "them" refers to
options: cranes and storage yards
steel shipping containers
old and narrow city centers
the large shipping companies

explanation.he: נמלים שהיססו לבנות משהו איבדו את התנועה שלהם, ולפי הצירוף **the huge cranes and storage yards that containers required** מה שצריך לבנות הם המנופים ומגרשי האחסון (**cranes and storage yards**).
explanation.en: Ports hesitated to build **the huge cranes and storage yards that containers required**, so **them** means cranes and storage yards.

questions.stem: What is the role of the last paragraph in the passage?
options: It explains how the shipping container was first invented, and by whom.
It gives further examples of the savings that were described in paragraph 3.
It describes how modern ports load and unload their ships so quickly.
It shows that the change came slowly and left some groups worse off.

explanation.he: הפסקה נפתחת בצירוף **neither quick nor painless** ומתארת נמלים וסוורים שנפגעו, ולכן תפקידה להראות שהשינוי הגיע לאט והרע את מצבן של קבוצות מסוימות (**left some groups worse off**).
explanation.en: The paragraph opens with **neither quick nor painless** and describes ports and dockworkers who lost out, so it shows the change was slow and left some groups worse off.

items.title: Water from Thin Air: Harvesting the Fog
paragraphs: In a few of the driest places on Earth, rain may not fall for years, yet the air is far from empty. Along certain desert coasts, cool ocean currents produce thick fog that drifts inland on many mornings. Some plants and animals in these regions survive by catching tiny droplets from it, and in recent decades people have begun to do the same.

The method is surprisingly simple. A large net of fine plastic mesh, often several meters wide, is stretched between two poles and turned to face the wind. As fog moves through the diaphanous mesh, droplets strike the threads and cling to them. When enough droplets join together, they become heavy enough to run down into a gutter at the bottom of the net, and from there through a pipe into a storage tank. Because the system needs no fuel or electricity, it costs little to run.

Where conditions are right, the results can be impressive. A single large net may collect hundreds of liters on a foggy day, enough to provide drinking water for a small village or to water young trees. Some communities that once depended on deliveries by truck now receive at least part of their water from the fog.

Fog collection, however, is not an answer to drought everywhere. It works only where fog is frequent and the wind pushes it steadily through the nets, conditions found mainly on certain coasts and mountain slopes. Even there, the fog can be fickle, thick for weeks and then absent for a month, so most communities keep another source of water as well. The nets also need regular care: strong winds can tear them, and dust or algae can clog the mesh and reduce the amount of water collected.

glossary.en: so light and thin that you can almost see through it
changing often and suddenly, so that you cannot rely on it

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how nets can collect water from fog, and what limits their use
To show how desert plants and animals manage to survive for years without rain
To compare the different ways in which dry regions obtain their drinking water
To argue that fog nets could end water shortages in most of the world's dry regions

explanation.he: אחרי תיאור השיטה מגיעה הסתייגות, הצירוף **is not an answer to drought everywhere**, ולכן המטרה היא להסביר איך רשתות אוספות מים מערפל ומה מגביל את השימוש בהן (**what limits their use**).
explanation.en: Paragraphs 2-3 explain the method, and paragraph 4 says it **is not an answer to drought everywhere**, so the purpose is to explain how the nets work and their limits.

questions.stem: How does the water from the fog reach the storage tank?
options: A small electric pump draws the water out of the net and into a pipe.
The wind presses the droplets straight through the threads and into the tank.
Droplets gather on the threads until they are heavy enough to flow into a gutter.
The heat of the sun warms the droplets until they slide off the net into the tank.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **they become heavy enough to run down into a gutter**, הטיפות מצטברות על החוטים עד שהן כבדות מספיק כדי לזרום למרזב (**heavy enough to flow into a gutter**).
explanation.en: When droplets join together, **they become heavy enough to run down into a gutter**, and from there they flow into the tank.

questions.stem: Which of the following is stated about the water that fog nets collect?
options: It is usually sold to towns that lie far away from the coast.
It can supply part of the water used by some small communities.
It is used mostly by factories rather than by people in their homes.
It costs more to collect than water that is delivered by truck.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **now receive at least part of their water from the fog**, יש קהילות שמקבלות מהערפל חלק מהמים שלהן (**part of the water**).
explanation.en: **Some communities ... now receive at least part of their water from the fog**, so it supplies part of their water.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "clog" is closest in meaning to
options: tear
dry
stretch
block

explanation.he: האבק והאצות פוגעים ברשת וגורמים לכך שהיא אוספת פחות, לפי הצירוף **reduce the amount of water collected**, ולכן המילה **clog** פירושה לסתום (המילה **block**).
explanation.en: Dust or algae **clog the mesh and reduce the amount of water collected**, so **clog** means **block**.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a fog net set up in a sheltered valley where the air is usually still?
options: It would need more repairs than the nets that stand in windy places.
It would probably collect less water than a net on a windy coast.
It would collect more water, because its mesh would stay cleaner.
It would probably work well as long as the valley had thick fog.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **the wind pushes it steadily through the nets**, הרשת צריכה רוח, ולכן באוויר עומד היא תאסוף כנראה פחות מים (**collect less water**).
explanation.en: The nets work where **the wind pushes it steadily through the nets**, so in still air a net would probably **collect less water**.

items.title: Is That Really Me? The Puzzle of the Recorded Voice
paragraphs: Many people are dismayed the first time they hear a recording of their own voice, and some go to great lengths to avoid hearing it again. The speaker on the recording sounds thinner and higher than the voice they know, sometimes almost reedy, and they often wonder whether the equipment is faulty. It almost never is. The recording is, in fact, much closer to the voice that everyone else hears.

The difference arises because we hear ourselves in two ways at once. Like any other sound, our voice travels through the air and enters our ears from outside. At the same time, however, the vibrations of speech pass directly through the bones of the head to the inner ear. Bone tends to carry low tones better than high ones, so this inner route adds a deep, full quality to the voice we perceive, making it seem more mellifluous to us than to anyone else.

A recording captures only the sound that travels through the air, just as a listener across the room would hear it. When the inner route is removed, the low tones that we are used to hearing seem to vanish, and the voice appears to have lost its depth. Our own voice, in other words, is one sound that we never hear the way other people do.

Physics may not be the whole story, however. Some studies suggest that people judge their recorded voices more harshly than strangers do. In one kind of experiment, people who listened to several recorded voices without recognizing their own among them tended to rate it quite favorably. Perhaps, then, much of the discomfort comes from the surprise of hearing something unfamiliar in a sound that we thought we knew well.

glossary.en: high and thin in sound, not full or deep
smooth, sweet and pleasant to listen to

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
options: Recording equipment often makes voices sound thinner and higher than they really are.
People hear high tones better through the bones of the head than through the air.
Most people dislike their recorded voice because it is less pleasant than the voices of others.
Our recorded voice sounds strange to us because of how we hear and what we expect.

explanation.he: פסקאות 2–3 מסבירות שאנו שומעים את עצמנו בשתי דרכים (**in two ways at once**) ופסקה 4 מוסיפה את ההפתעה (**the surprise**), ולכן הקול המוקלט נשמע מוזר בגלל האופן שבו אנו שומעים ומה שאנו מצפים לשמוע (**what we expect**).
explanation.en: Paragraphs 2-3 explain how we hear ourselves, and paragraph 4 adds **the surprise of hearing something unfamiliar**, so the voice sounds strange because of how we hear and what we expect.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, does our own voice sound deeper to us than to others?
options: Sound reaching the inner ear through the skull carries low tones well.
The ears of other people are less able than ours to pick up the low tones of a voice.
The air inside the head makes high tones sound much louder than low ones.
We usually speak in a deeper voice when we are alone than when others are listening.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **Bone tends to carry low tones better than high ones**, הצליל שמגיע לאוזן הפנימית דרך העצמות מעביר היטב צלילים נמוכים (**carries low tones well**).
explanation.en: **Bone tends to carry low tones better than high ones**, so sound reaching the inner ear through bone **carries low tones well**.

questions.stem: What happens to the voice when it is recorded?
options: The equipment adds high tones that were not part of the original voice.
Its low tones are made louder so that it sounds clearer to listeners.
Only the part of the sound that moves through the air is captured.
The vibrations that pass through the bones of the head are recorded clearly.

explanation.he: לפי הצירוף **A recording captures only the sound that travels through the air**, ההקלטה קולטת רק את החלק של הצליל שעובר באוויר (**moves through the air**).
explanation.en: **A recording captures only the sound that travels through the air**, so the bone route is lost.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word "harshly" is closest in meaning to
options: quickly
critically
accurately
quietly

explanation.he: מי שלא זיהו את הקול שלהם דירגו אותו לטובה (הצירוף **rate it quite favorably**), ולכן המילה **harshly** פירושה בחומרה, באופן ביקורתי (המילה **critically**).
explanation.en: When they did not recognize their voice, people **tended to rate it quite favorably**, so judging it **harshly** means judging it **critically**.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the last paragraph about people's dislike of their recorded voice?
options: It may depend more on knowing the voice is theirs than on its actual sound.
It usually disappears once they learn why recordings sound different from what they hear.
It is shared by most strangers who listen to the same recording of their voice.
It probably shows that their voice really does sound unpleasant to other people.

explanation.he: אנשים שהאזינו לקולם בלי לזהות אותו (הצירוף **without recognizing their own**) דירגו אותו לטובה, ולכן הדחייה תלויה כנראה בידיעה שזה הקול שלהם (**knowing the voice is theirs**).
explanation.en: People who heard several voices **without recognizing their own** rated it **quite favorably**, so the dislike may depend on **knowing the voice is theirs**.

items.title: The Month That Matters: Birth Dates and Young Athletes
paragraphs: In many youth sports, children compete in groups defined by birth year, with a fixed cutoff date separating the groups. A child born just after that date may thus be nearly twelve months older than a teammate born just before it. At nine or ten, such a gap often brings real differences in height, strength and coordination. Studies of many sports have found that children born in the first months of the selection year are overrepresented on elite youth teams, a pattern known as the relative age effect.

The usual explanation is simple. Coaches choosing players for advanced squads tend to judge what they see on the day, and what they see reflects maturity as much as talent. The children selected then receive better coaching, stronger opponents and more practice, so that an advantage that was at first adventitious, a mere accident of the calendar, turns into a genuine difference in skill. Attrition, meanwhile, is highest among those born late in the year, many of whom are passed over before their bodies have had time to catch up.

The effect, however, is far from uniform. It tends to be strongest in sports that reward size and power and during the early teenage years, when physical differences are greatest; among adults it is much weaker. Some studies even point to a reversal at the top: late-born players who survive early selection appear somewhat more likely than their early-born peers to enjoy long professional careers, perhaps because years of competing against bigger children forced them to rely on technique and judgment rather than strength.

Several remedies have been proposed. One, meant to keep more late-born children in the game, is to move the cutoff date from season to season; another, tried by some clubs, is to group young players by physical maturity. None has yet been shown to remove the effect entirely, but such measures share a recognition that how well a callow player performs at ten is an uncertain guide to what that player might achieve at twenty-five.

glossary.he: מקרי, שנובע מנסיבות חיצוניות ולא מתכונה פנימית
glossary.en: happening by chance; coming from outside rather than from something's own nature

glossary.he: חסר ניסיון, צעיר ועדיין לא מגובש
glossary.en: young and lacking experience or maturity

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Several ways of limiting the influence of birth dates on selection have been suggested, with limited success so far.
Those born in the first months of the selection year are favored in youth sports, an advantage that usually stays with them well into their adult sporting careers.
Older children within an age group tend to be picked for top youth teams, an edge that says more about birth dates than about potential.
Children develop physically at different rates, and this affects how well they perform in many sports.

explanation.he: המבוגרים בקבוצה נבחרים יותר, אך לפי פסקה 4 הביצועים בגיל עשר הם מדד לא ודאי (**an uncertain guide**), ולכן: יתרון שמעיד יותר על תאריך הלידה מאשר על הפוטנציאל (**says more about birth dates than about potential**).
explanation.en: Early-born children are **overrepresented on elite youth teams**, yet early form is **an uncertain guide**, so their edge says more about birth dates than about potential.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens to the children chosen for advanced squads?
options: They build real skill through the extra training and tougher matches they receive.
They learn to rely on technique and judgment because their rivals are bigger.
They are given less practice than the others so that they do not tire out too early.
They tend to leave the sport sooner than children born late in the year.

explanation.he: הנבחרים מקבלים אימון טוב יותר, יריבים חזקים יותר ויותר תרגול (**better coaching, stronger opponents and more practice**), וכך היתרון הופך להבדל אמיתי במיומנות (**a genuine difference in skill**).
explanation.en: Those selected **receive better coaching, stronger opponents and more practice**, so their early edge becomes **a genuine difference in skill**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in which situation is the relative age effect likely to be most marked?
options: In sports that reward technique, once the players have become adults
In sports for young children, at about the age of nine or ten
In clubs that move their cutoff date each season, once players reach their twenties
In sports that favor size and strength, during the first years of adolescence

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 3 ההשפעה חזקה במיוחד בענפים שמתגמלים גודל וכוח (**sports that reward size and power**) ובשנות ההתבגרות המוקדמות (**the early teenage years**), ולכן התשובה היא ענפי גודל וכוח בתחילת גיל ההתבגרות.
explanation.en: The effect is strongest **in sports that reward size and power and during the early teenage years**, when bodies differ most.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "attrition" is closest in meaning to
options: being ignored by coaches
dropping out of the sport
growing more slowly than others
feeling unfairly treated

explanation.he: ההצעה הראשונה בפסקה 4 נועדה להשאיר ילדים במשחק (**keep more late-born children in the game**), ולכן המילה **attrition** פירושה נשירה מהענף (**dropping out of the sport**).
explanation.en: One remedy is **meant to keep more late-born children in the game**, so **attrition** here means dropping out of the sport.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that some of the late-born children who leave the sport early
options: usually leave because they prefer sports that reward technique
tend to be less talented than the children who are chosen for the top teams
might have done well as adults if they had stayed in it
are generally weaker in tactical judgment than early-born players

explanation.he: מי שנולדו מאוחר ושרדו מצליחים לעתים בצמרת (**long professional careers**), והביצועים בגיל עשר הם מדד לא ודאי (**an uncertain guide**), ולכן חלק מהנושרים היו עשויים להצליח (**might have done well**).
explanation.en: Late-born survivors may enjoy **long professional careers**, and early form is **an uncertain guide**, so some who left might have done well.

items.title: A Meal for a Ride: Plants That Rely on Ants
paragraphs: Plants cannot walk, yet many send their seeds away from the parent, which would otherwise compete with its young for light and water. Wind and fruit-eating birds can carry seeds a long way. A less familiar arrangement involves ants. Thousands of plant species produce seeds bearing a small, pale attachment rich in fats, and it is this attachment, rather than the seed itself, that the ants are after.

The sequence that follows is remarkably consistent. A worker ant that finds such a seed grips it by the attachment, which serves as a handle, and carries it to the nest. There the attachment, delectable to the colony though of no apparent use to the seed, is removed and fed to the young. The seed, with its hard coat, is too difficult to eat, so it is left whole, either in an underground waste chamber or on a refuse heap near the entrance. In effect, the plant has paid the ant to sow its seed.

These journeys are strikingly short. Ants seldom carry a seed more than a few meters, far less than a bird or the wind may move one. Why, then, should a plant spend its resources on food for ants? Several answers have been proposed, and they need not exclude one another. Seeds taken below ground are hidden from mice and birds that would otherwise eat them; where fires are frequent, a buried seed is shielded from the heat; and a nest's waste may enrich the soil around it. On this view, it matters less how far a seed travels than where it ends up.

The arrangement has a weak point, however. A plant that relies on ants is beholden to whichever species happen to live around it, and not all ants behave alike. In some regions where an introduced ant has pushed out the native species, the newcomers have been seen eating the attachment on the spot and leaving the seed on the surface, and fewer seedlings of ant-dependent plants have reportedly appeared there.

glossary.en: very pleasant to taste; delicious

glossary.he: תלוי במישהו או מחויב לו, נתון לחסדיו
glossary.en: depending on someone, or owing them something

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Ants introduced into new regions often eat the food on seeds without carrying the seeds away.
Many plants pay ants in food to move their seeds to favorable spots, a deal that depends on which ants are present.
Ants spread the seeds of many plants over long distances, which in turn keeps the young plants from having to compete with their parents.
Plants have developed a number of different ways of spreading their seeds, relying on wind, birds and insects.
