explanation.he: הצמח משלם לנמלה במזון (**paid the ant to sow its seed**), התועלת היא במקום שהזרע מגיע אליו (**where it ends up**) ויש נקודת תורפה, ולכן: עסקה שתלויה בנמלים שבסביבה (**depends on which ants are present**).
explanation.en: The plant has **paid the ant to sow its seed**, the gain lies in **where it ends up**, and the deal depends on which ants are present.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens to a seed once an ant has carried it to the nest?
options: It stays in a storeroom until the young ants are old enough to eat it.
It gets broken open so that the colony can feed on the nutrients inside.
It is often eaten by mice that visit the nest in search of food.
It loses its fatty part to the young but is otherwise left undamaged.

explanation.he: התוספת מוסרת ומוגשת לצעירים (**removed and fed to the young**), והזרע קשה מדי לאכילה ולכן נשאר שלם (**left whole**), כלומר הוא מאבד רק את החלק השומני.
explanation.en: The attachment is **removed and fed to the young**, and the seed, **too difficult to eat**, is **left whole**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following has been proposed as a benefit for plants whose seeds are taken by ants?
options: Their seeds may be spared the heat of fires by lying under the soil.
Their seeds may be carried farther than the wind would take them.
Their seeds may be guarded by native ants against the newcomers.
Their seeds may be moved on by birds that search the ants' refuse heaps.

explanation.he: בפסקה 3 נאמר שבמקומות שיש בהם שריפות רבות זרע קבור מוגן מהחום (**a buried seed is shielded from the heat**), ולכן אחת התועלות היא שהזרע ניצל מחום השריפה כשהוא מתחת לאדמה.
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 says that **where fires are frequent, a buried seed is shielded from the heat**.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "exclude" is closest in meaning to
options: depend on
agree with
rule out
build on

explanation.he: אחרי הצירוף **need not exclude one another** הכותב מונה שלוש תשובות שיכולות להיות נכונות יחד, ולכן המילה **exclude** כאן פירושה לשלול (**rule out**).
explanation.en: After **they need not exclude one another**, three answers are listed that can all be true at once, so **exclude** means rule out.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that seeds left on the surface by the introduced ants
options: are more likely to be eaten than seeds taken into a nest
usually sprout sooner because they are exposed to light
end up farther from the parent than seeds moved by native ants
probably lose their hard coats once the attachment has been eaten

explanation.he: זרעים מתחת לקרקע מוסתרים מעכברים ומציפורים (**hidden from mice and birds**), ולכן זרעים שנשארו על פני הקרקע חשופים יותר לאכילה (**more likely to be eaten**).
explanation.en: **Seeds taken below ground are hidden from mice and birds**, so seeds left on the surface are more likely to be eaten.

items.title: Signals on the Skyline: The Optical Telegraph
paragraphs: Long before electric wires crossed the land, some European governments could send a message hundreds of kilometers in a matter of hours, using little more than wood, rope and telescopes; a rider needed several days for the same journey. The optical telegraph, which spread across parts of Europe from the 1790s, was a chain of towers placed on hilltops and other high points, each within sight of the next and often ten to twenty kilometers apart.

On top of each tower stood a frame with movable wooden arms that an operator could set in dozens of distinct positions. Each position stood for a letter, a number or, in later codes, an entire word or phrase listed in a numbered codebook. An operator watched the neighboring tower through a telescope, copied each position onto his own frame, and waited for the next station to do the same. Because nothing physical had to travel, a short message could cross a country at a speed that no courier on horseback, however unflagging, could approach.

The system's weaknesses, however, were as plain as its speed. It worked only in daylight and only when the air was clear, so that fog or heavy rain could stop a message partway along the line; in regions with mercurial weather, stations might sit idle for days at a time. Every tower also needed trained operators working in shifts, and a single careless copy could garble a message for every station beyond the one where the mistake was made. Partly because building and staffing a line was so expensive, the towers were reserved mostly for official business, and private messages were generally not accepted.

Not until electric telegraphs spread in the 1840s did the towers begin to fall silent, and within a few decades most lines had been abandoned. The new system was faster still, but its real advantages lay elsewhere: a wire worked at night and in any weather, needed far fewer workers, and could be strung cheaply beside the new railways.

glossary.he: בלתי נלאה, שאינו מתעייף ואינו נחלש
glossary.en: never tiring or losing energy

glossary.he: הפכפך, משתנה במהירות ובאופן בלתי צפוי
glossary.en: changing suddenly and unpredictably

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how operators used telescopes and codebooks to pass signals from tower to tower
To argue that the optical telegraph failed because its codes were too hard for operators to learn
To trace the history of long-distance communication from riders on horseback to modern wires
To describe how a chain of signal towers carried messages, and why a newer system replaced it

explanation.he: הקטע מתאר שרשרת מגדלים (**a chain of towers**), את חולשותיה ואת יתרונות החוט החשמלי, ולכן: לתאר איך המגדלים העבירו הודעות ולמה מערכת חדשה החליפה אותם (**why a newer system replaced it**).
explanation.en: The passage describes **a chain of towers**, its **weaknesses**, and the electric system's **real advantages**: how the towers worked and why a newer system replaced them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why could a message travel so quickly along the line?
options: Codebooks let operators send several messages along the line at once.
Signals were passed on by sight, so nothing had to be carried.
Operators worked in shifts, so the line could run day and night.
Messages were sent beside the railways by trained operators.

explanation.he: המשפט **Because nothing physical had to travel** (כי שום דבר מוחשי לא היה צריך לעבור את הדרך) מסביר את המהירות: האותות עברו במבט, ולא היה צריך לשאת דבר (**nothing had to be carried**).
explanation.en: The clue is **Because nothing physical had to travel**: signals were passed on by sight, so nothing had to be carried.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following was one of the real advantages of the electric telegraph?
options: It used codebooks in which one sign could stand for a phrase.
It was faster, and this was the chief reason it took the towers' place.
It went on working after dark and whatever the weather was like.
It needed more workers along the line, so mistakes were caught sooner.

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 4 היתרונות האמיתיים לא היו המהירות (**its real advantages lay elsewhere**), אלא למשל שהחוט פעל בלילה ובכל מזג אוויר (**worked at night and in any weather**).
explanation.en: Speed was not the point: **its real advantages lay elsewhere**, for **a wire worked at night and in any weather**.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "garble" is closest in meaning to
options: scramble
shelve
expose
duplicate

explanation.he: העתקה רשלנית (**a single careless copy**) יוצרת טעות שעוברת הלאה (**where the mistake was made**), ולכן המילה **garble** פירושה לשבש, לערבל (**scramble**).
explanation.en: **a single careless copy** creates a mistake that is passed on, so **garble** means scramble.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, other things being equal, an optical telegraph line probably carried fewer messages
options: on clear days than on foggy or rainy ones
for government offices than for private citizens
after codebooks came into use than before
in the winter months than in the summer months

explanation.he: הקו פעל רק באור יום (**It worked only in daylight**), והימים בחורף קצרים יותר, ולכן בחודשי החורף עברו פחות הודעות (**in the winter months**).
explanation.en: The line **worked only in daylight**, and winter days are shorter, so it probably carried fewer messages in the winter months.

items.title: Old Violins, New Ears: Putting a Legend to the Test
paragraphs: A handful of violins made in a few illustrious Italian workshops in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries now sell for millions of dollars, and many players regard their tone as beyond the reach of any modern maker. Makers and scientists have offered many explanations for this supposed superiority, from a lost recipe for varnish to chemical treatments of the wood to unusually dense timber grown during a run of cold decades.

Until recently, however, the belief had rarely been tested in a way that ruled out the influence of expectations. Players who know they are holding a famous instrument may find its tone more dulcet simply because they expect to. In experiments carried out over the past two decades, experienced soloists played a mix of old and high-quality new violins while wearing modified goggles that kept them from seeing which was which. Most could not reliably tell the old instruments from the new ones, and in one study a majority chose a new violin as the one they would most like to take home.

Listeners have been tested as well. In trials held in concert halls, audiences heard old and new violins played behind a screen, so that no one could see which instrument was in use. New violins were often judged to project better, a quality that matters to a soloist who must be heard over a full orchestra in a large hall, and listeners on the whole did no better than chance at picking out the old instruments.

Defenders of the old violins have raised trenchant objections. A player, they argue, needs weeks to learn the subtleties of an unfamiliar instrument, whereas the tests allowed an hour or so, and the old violins available may not have been the finest examples. The researchers accept some of these limits. Even so, the results are hard to dismiss: if experts cannot single out the old violins without knowing which is which, part of the instruments' fame may lie in the listener rather than in the wood.

glossary.en: famous and much admired because of past achievements
sweet and pleasant to hear
sharp, forceful and direct in expression

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Blind tests suggest that famous old violins may sound no better than fine new ones, though the tests have their critics.
Several explanations, from varnish to dense wood, have been offered for the tone of old Italian violins.
Blind tests have shown that new violins sound better than the old ones, a result that even the defenders of the old instruments now accept.
In many fields, experts' judgments of quality often depend more on expectations than on the objects themselves.

explanation.he: בבדיקות עיוורות הנגנים לא הבחינו בעקביות בין ישן לחדש (**could not reliably tell**), אך יש טענות נגד (**trenchant objections**), ולכן: ייתכן שהישנים אינם עדיפים, אף שלבדיקות יש מבקרים (**the tests have their critics**).
explanation.en: In blind tests players **could not reliably tell** old from new, yet defenders raised **trenchant objections**: old violins may sound no better, though the tests have critics.

questions.stem: What did the experiments with soloists find?
options: Most players preferred the old violins once they had played them for an hour.
Players needed several weeks to tell the old violins from the new ones.
Players could not dependably pick out which of the violins were the old ones.
Players could tell old from new by the feel of the instrument, but not by its sound.

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 2 רוב הנגנים לא הצליחו להבחין באופן עקבי בין הישנים לחדשים (**could not reliably tell the old instruments from the new ones**), כלומר לא זיהו בעקביות את הישנים.
explanation.en: Most soloists **could not reliably tell the old instruments from the new ones**, so they could not dependably pick out the old violins.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is one objection raised by defenders of the old violins?
options: The soloists chosen for the tests may have lacked experience with violins.
The tests may not have included the very best of the famous violins.
The audiences had been told beforehand which violin was which.
The tests went on for weeks, which left the players too tired to judge.

explanation.he: בפסקה 4 המגינים טוענים שהכינורות הישנים שעמדו לרשות הבודקים אולי לא היו המשובחים ביותר (**may not have been the finest examples**), כלומר ייתכן שבבדיקות לא נוגנו הכלים הטובים ביותר.
explanation.en: Defenders argue that **the old violins available may not have been the finest examples**.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "project" is closest in meaning to
options: appear clearly on a screen
plan carefully for the future
sound sweet to the player's ear
carry well to distant listeners

explanation.he: ההסבר שבא אחריה, הצירוף **must be heard over a full orchestra in a large hall**, מראה שהמילה **project** כאן פירושה להגיע היטב למאזינים רחוקים (**carry well to distant listeners**).
explanation.en: The phrase **must be heard over a full orchestra in a large hall** shows that **project** means carry well to distant listeners.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the high prices paid for the old violins
options: are likely to fall now that the blind tests have been published
may owe something to reputation rather than to sound alone
show that buyers can hear differences that experts miss
probably reflect the cost of the rare wood used to make them

explanation.he: לפי הקטע חלק מהתהילה של הכינורות נמצא אצל המאזין (**may lie in the listener rather than in the wood**), ולכן המחיר הגבוה נובע אולי גם מהמוניטין ולא רק מהצליל (**owe something to reputation**).
explanation.en: Part of their fame **may lie in the listener rather than in the wood**, so their high prices may owe something to reputation, not sound alone.

items.title: Riding on Vapor: Why Water Skates on a Very Hot Pan
paragraphs: Anyone who has flicked water onto a heated pan may have noticed something odd. On a pan that is merely hot, the drops hiss and vanish within a second or two. On a much hotter pan, however, they gather into shiny beads that glide about for a minute or more. That a hotter surface should make water last longer seems to confound common sense, yet the behavior has been described for over two centuries.

The explanation lies beneath each drop. Once the metal passes a certain temperature, often put at roughly 200 degrees Celsius for water, the underside of a drop boils the instant it lands, and the vapor forms a thin cushion that holds the rest of the drop above the surface. Because vapor carries heat far less well than direct contact with metal would, the drop is largely shielded from the heat below and shrinks only slowly. With almost nothing to rub against, it also slides freely, so a slight tilt or a breath of air can send the errant bead skating across the pan.

What counts as very hot, though, depends on the liquid. Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, so for it even an ordinary kitchen floor is extremely hot. Spilled drops of nitrogen therefore do not spread over the tiles but roll across them, riding on their own vapor just as water does on a pan. What matters, in other words, is not the temperature of the surface as such but how far it exceeds the boiling point of the liquid.

The effect has practical consequences. Some cooks test a pan by flicking water onto it: drops that skate show that the pan is hot enough to sear meat. In industry, by contrast, the same layer can be the bane of metalworkers. When hot steel is plunged into water to harden it, a film of vapor may form around the metal and slow its cooling just when speed matters most, which is one reason the water is often stirred.

glossary.en: to surprise or puzzle by going against what is expected
wandering or straying from the expected course
a constant cause of trouble or annoyance

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Cooks can tell when a pan is ready for searing meat by flicking water onto it and watching whether the drops skate.
A very hot surface can make a drop last longer by holding it up on vapor, which helps in some tasks and hinders others.
Water lasts longer on a hotter pan because the steam it gives off cools the metal to below the point at which water boils.
Liquids tend to behave in unexpected ways when they are heated, and scientists are still trying to explain why.

explanation.he: פסקה 2 מסבירה שכרית אדים (**a thin cushion**) מגינה על הטיפה ופסקה 4 מוסיפה תועלת ונזק, ולכן התשובה: משטח לוהט מאריך את חיי הטיפה בעזרת אדים, וזה מועיל או מזיק (**helps in some tasks and hinders others**).
explanation.en: A **thin cushion** of vapor keeps drops alive on a very hot pan, and paragraph 4 adds that this helps cooks but is **the bane of metalworkers**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a drop on a very hot pan take so long to disappear?
options: Its shiny surface sends back most of the heat that rises from the metal below.
It keeps sliding, so it rarely stays in one spot long enough to heat up.
Most of the water turns to vapor the moment the drop first lands.
A layer of vapor lets little of the metal's heat get through to the drop.

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 2 האדים מעבירים חום גרוע הרבה יותר ממגע עם המתכת (הצירוף **vapor carries heat far less well**), ולכן שכבת האדים מעבירה לטיפה מעט חום (**lets little of the metal's heat get through**).
explanation.en: The drop is shielded because **vapor carries heat far less well than direct contact with metal would**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do spilled drops of liquid nitrogen roll across a kitchen floor instead of spreading?
options: The tiles are far warmer than the point at which nitrogen boils.
The tiles are too smooth for the drops to spread out on them.
The nitrogen freezes the moment it touches the cold tiles.
Nitrogen needs a higher temperature than water does in order to boil.

explanation.he: החנקן רותח בטמפרטורה של כמינוס 196 מעלות, ולכן אפילו רצפה רגילה לוהטת בשבילו (**even an ordinary kitchen floor is extremely hot**), כלומר האריחים חמים בהרבה מנקודת הרתיחה שלו.
explanation.en: Nitrogen **boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius**, so **even an ordinary kitchen floor is extremely hot** for it.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the phrase "as such" is closest in meaning to
options: for that reason
in the same way
considered in itself
at that particular moment

explanation.he: הצירוף **as such** בא בתוך ניגוד: לא הטמפרטורה של המשטח עצמה אלא בכמה היא עולה על נקודת הרתיחה (הצירוף **how far it exceeds**), ולכן פירושו כשלעצמו (**considered in itself**).
explanation.en: In **not the temperature of the surface as such but how far it exceeds**, the phrase sets the temperature in itself against the gap.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that if water flicked onto a pan hisses and vanishes at once, the pan
options: probably needs more heating before meat is seared in it
is probably too hot and should be left to cool before use
is already covered by a thin cushion of vapor
has passed roughly 200 degrees Celsius

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 1 טיפות שרוחשות ונעלמות מעידות שהמחבת רק חמה (**merely hot**), ולפי פסקה 4 טיפות שמחליקות הן הסימן שהיא מוכנה, ולכן היא כנראה צריכה עוד חימום (**needs more heating**).
explanation.en: Drops that **hiss and vanish** mean a pan that is **merely hot**, while **drops that skate** show it is ready, so it probably needs more heating.

items.title: Thirteen and Seventeen: The Arithmetic of Periodical Cicadas
paragraphs: Most insects live by an annual rhythm, but a few cicada species in eastern North America keep a stranger calendar. Their young, or nymphs, spend thirteen or seventeen years underground, feeding on sap from tree roots. Then, in a single spring, the nymphs of a brood emerge within days of one another, by some estimates more than a million to an acre, mate, lay their eggs and die within weeks. To a human observer, so interminable a wait seems out of all proportion to so brief an adult life.

The least disputed part of the explanation concerns sheer numbers. Far from hiding from predators, the cicadas appear in such masses that birds and other animals gorge themselves and still leave most of the brood untouched. A cicada that emerged alone, or a year early, would enjoy no such protection, which may be why stragglers seldom give rise to lasting populations. Synchrony, in other words, is less a curiosity than a defense.

Harder to explain is the length of the cycles, above all the arresting fact that both thirteen and seventeen are prime numbers. One hypothesis holds that a prime-numbered cycle seldom coincides with the shorter, regular cycles of predators. A brood that appeared every twelve years would meet any enemy whose numbers peaked every two, three, four or six years, whereas a seventeen-year brood would meet a five-year enemy only once every eighty-five years. A related idea is that prime cycles keep broods of different lengths from emerging together and interbreeding.

Neither idea has gone unchallenged. No predator with a matching multi-year cycle has been found, critics point out, and an advantage over enemies that may never have existed is hard to test. Few would gainsay, however, that the cicadas keep time with remarkable precision, though how they do so is unclear. One experiment suggests that nymphs count the yearly cycles of their host trees rather than the years themselves: nymphs on trees made to shed and regrow their leaves twice within a year emerged a year early.

glossary.he: בלתי נגמר, ארוך ומייגע עד שנדמה שלא יסתיים

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Appearing in huge numbers protects the cicadas, and their prime-numbered cycles have been shown to keep them well clear of predators with shorter cycles.
Periodical cicadas may keep time by counting the yearly cycles of the trees on whose roots they feed.
Emerging in vast numbers at once protects the cicadas, but why their cycles run to a prime number of years is still debated.
Many animals rely on safety in numbers, which explains why their life cycles tend to follow a fixed rhythm.

explanation.he: פסקה 2 קובעת שההופעה ההמונית היא הגנה (**less a curiosity than a defense**) ופסקאות 3–4 מציגות השערות שנויות במחלוקת, ולכן התשובה: ההמונים מגינים, אבל אורך המחזור הראשוני עדיין שנוי במחלוקת (**is still debated**).
explanation.en: Mass emergence is **less a curiosity than a defense**, but for the prime cycles **Neither idea has gone unchallenged**, so their length is still debated.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a cicada that came out of the ground a year before the rest of its brood would most likely
options: lose the protection that comes from appearing in vast numbers
run short of the root sap it needs before it could mate
mate with cicadas from a brood that follows a different cycle
escape the notice of predators that do not expect cicadas that year

explanation.he: פסקה 2 אומרת שציקדה שיוצאת לבד או שנה מוקדם לא תיהנה מהגנה כזו (**would enjoy no such protection**), כלומר היא מאבדת את ההגנה שבהמונים (**lose the protection**).
explanation.en: A cicada that emerged **alone, or a year early, would enjoy no such protection**, the protection of vast numbers.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one objection to the idea that prime cycles help the cicadas avoid predators is that
options: prime-numbered cycles are also common among insects that live above ground
broods of different lengths have often been seen emerging together in the same year
the cicadas keep time less precisely than the idea would require
the enemies the idea depends on have not been shown to exist

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 4 המבקרים מציינים שלא נמצא טורף בעל מחזור מתאים (**No predator with a matching multi-year cycle has been found**), כלומר לא הוכח שהאויב שההשערה נשענת עליו קיים.
explanation.en: Critics note that **No predator with a matching multi-year cycle has been found**, so the enemy the idea needs is unproven.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the phrase "gorge themselves" is closest in meaning to
options: crowd into narrow valleys
eat greedily and heavily
eat sparingly and selectively
compete fiercely for the food

explanation.he: המילה **still** בצירוף **and still leave most of the brood untouched** (ובכל זאת משאירים את רוב הלהקה) מראה שהטורפים אוכלים הרבה, ולכן הצירוף **gorge themselves** פירושו לזלול כמה שאפשר (**eat greedily and heavily**).
explanation.en: Predators **gorge themselves and still leave most of the brood untouched**: they eat as much as they can, yet most cicadas survive.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention a brood that appeared every twelve years?
options: To report that some broods of cicadas once followed a cycle that lasted for twelve years
To argue that a twelve-year cycle would help keep broods of different lengths from interbreeding
To explain why the numbers of many predators rise and fall at regular intervals of a few years
To show, by an imagined case, that a cycle that is not prime would meet enemies more frequently

explanation.he: הצירוף **would meet any enemy** (הייתה פוגשת כל אויב) מציג להקה דמיונית, והצירוף **whereas a seventeen-year brood** מעמיד מולה מחזור ראשוני, כדי להראות שמחזור לא ראשוני מביא יותר מפגשים עם אויבים.
explanation.en: The twelve-year brood is imagined (**would meet any enemy**) and set against **a seventeen-year brood** to show what a cycle that is not prime would cost.

items.title: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
paragraphs: Few questions sound more naive than why the sky is dark at night, yet for centuries it posed a genuine puzzle. Suppose, as many astronomers once did, that the universe is infinite in extent, unchanging in time and evenly filled with stars. Then every line of sight, extended far enough, should end on the surface of a star, much as someone deep in an impenetrable forest sees trunks in every direction. On this reasoning the whole sky ought to blaze, and the dark gaps between the stars demand an explanation.

The obvious objection, that distant stars look fainter, does not dispose of the puzzle. The light of any single star does weaken with distance, but the number of stars at a given distance grows at just the rate needed to make up for that loss, so each distant shell of sky should be as bright as a nearby one. Nor does dust between the stars help, though it was once a favored answer: dust that absorbed so much light would itself heat up until it glowed like the stars behind it. An infinite, unchanging universe, in short, would be uniformly incandescent, by night as by day.

The answer now generally accepted lies in the assumptions rather than the arithmetic. On current evidence, the universe had a beginning some fourteen billion years ago, and light travels at a finite speed. We can therefore see only stars whose light has had time to reach us. Stars, moreover, do not shine forever. The expansion of space also stretches the light of remote galaxies toward wavelengths the eye cannot detect, though its contribution is thought to be the smaller one.

Curiously, one of the first to sketch this solution is often said to have been not an astronomer but a writer of poems and tales, in a speculative essay that scientists of his day largely ignored. Seldom has so puerile a question carried so much weight: the darkness that falls each evening is, in effect, a sign that the universe has not existed forever.

glossary.he: שאי אפשר לעבור דרכו או לראות דרכו
glossary.en: impossible to pass or see through

glossary.he: זוהר באור חזק מרוב חום; בוהק

childish and silly

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Dust between the stars fails to explain the dark sky, since it would grow hot and glow almost as brightly as the stars.
The night sky is dark because the light of distant stars grows too faint to be seen from the Earth with the naked eye.
Simple everyday observations, rather than costly instruments, have settled most of the great questions about the origin of the universe.
Long a genuine puzzle, the dark night sky is now explained largely by the limited age of the universe and the speed of light.

explanation.he: פסקאות 1–2 מציגות חידה שההסברים הישנים לא פתרו ופסקה 3 מסבירה אותה, ולכן התשובה: החושך מוסבר בעיקר בגיל המוגבל של היקום (**the limited age of the universe**) ובמהירות האור.
explanation.en: Paragraphs 1 and 2 build the puzzle, and paragraph 3 solves it: the universe **had a beginning** and **light travels at a finite speed**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does the faintness of distant stars fail to account for the dark sky?
options: Their light has not yet had time to reach the Earth, however bright the stars may be.
There are more of them at greater distances, which offsets the weaker light of each one.
Dust between the stars dims the light of nearby stars as much as that of distant ones.
Distant stars are generally larger and hotter than the stars that lie closer to the Earth.

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 2 מספר הכוכבים גדל עם המרחק בדיוק בקצב שמפצה על החלשות האור (הצירוף **the rate needed to make up for that loss**), ולכן יש יותר כוכבים רחוקים, וזה מקזז את האור החלש (**offsets the weaker light**).
explanation.en: The number of stars grows at **just the rate needed to make up for that loss**, so more distant stars offset each one's weaker light.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is one reason the night sky is dark?
options: Dust between the stars soaks up much of their light.
The light of distant stars is too faint to reach the Earth.
Stars eventually burn out and stop giving off light.
Light gradually loses speed on very long journeys through space.

explanation.he: בפסקה 3 ההסבר המקובל כולל גם את העובדה שכוכבים לא מאירים לנצח (**Stars, moreover, do not shine forever**), ולכן אחת הסיבות היא שכוכבים כבים בסופו של דבר ומפסיקים להפיץ אור.
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 adds that **Stars, moreover, do not shine forever**, so stars that burn out help keep the sky dark.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "sketch" is closest in meaning to
options: outline in broad terms
draw a picture of
work out in full detail
argue strongly against

explanation.he: הפתרון הוצע במסה השערתית (**in a speculative essay**) בידי מי שלא היה אסטרונום (**not an astronomer**), ולכן המילה **sketch** פירושה להציג בקווים כלליים (**outline in broad terms**).
explanation.en: A solution offered **in a speculative essay** by someone **not an astronomer** was only outlined in broad terms, not worked out in detail.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the scientists who largely ignored the essay
options: had already reached the same conclusion through their own work
rejected it because it relied on dust between the stars
passed over an early version of the explanation accepted today
were probably right to doubt it, as later evidence showed

explanation.he: הצירוף **sketch this solution** מפנה להסבר המקובל היום בפסקה 3, ולכן המדענים שהתעלמו מהמסה החמיצו גרסה מוקדמת שלו (**passed over an early version**).
explanation.en: The essay was **one of the first to sketch this solution**, the one **now generally accepted**, so the scientists who ignored it passed over an early version of it.

items.title: Reading in Silence: Did the Ancients Only Read Aloud?
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, many scholars held that readers in ancient Greece and Rome almost always read aloud, even when alone. Silent reading, on this view, was a rare accomplishment that became widespread only in the Middle Ages. Much of the case rested on a famous account, written around AD 400, in which the author describes his astonishment at seeing a learned man read with his eyes alone, his voice silent and his lips still.

The theory drew further support from the look of ancient books. Most texts were written without spaces between words and with little punctuation, and some historians argued that such pages could hardly be made sense of without being sounded out, if only in a sibilant whisper. On this account, it was medieval copyists, who began to separate words with spaces, who made silent reading easy and therefore common.

More recent work has cast doubt on this picture. Scholars have gathered passages from ancient plays and other writings in which characters read letters to themselves rather than declaim them, and nobody on stage treats this as remarkable. Experienced readers, moreover, seem to have managed unspaced text with little trouble, much as skilled readers today take in familiar words at a glance. Seen in this light, the famous account may record surprise not at silent reading itself but at a host who read silently while visitors waited, leaving them no share in the text.

Why, then, was reading aloud so common? The answer seems to lie less in necessity than in custom. Books were scarce and costly, many people were unlettered, and literature was often enjoyed in company: a trained reader might perform a work for guests at dinner, and authors tried out new writing before invited audiences. Few historians now doubt that silent reading existed in antiquity, although they still disagree about how widespread it was.

glossary.he: שורק ולוחש, בעל צליל של ס או ש
glossary.en: making or having a hissing sound

glossary.he: להקריא או לנאום בקול רם ובאופן דרמטי

glossary.en: unable to read; poorly educated

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The old belief that ancient readers rarely read silently has been challenged, though reading aloud stayed common for social reasons.
Recent studies have shown that people in the ancient world read in silence just as often as we do today, so the older view was simply wrong.
Words in ancient texts ran together without spaces, so most readers had to sound them out in order to follow them.
Ancient authors preferred to hear their work performed because they distrusted readers who took in a text in silence.

explanation.he: פסקה 3 מערערת על התפיסה הישנה ופסקה 4 מייחסת את הקריאה בקול למנהג (**custom**), ולכן התשובה: התפיסה הישנה עורערה (**has been challenged**), אבל הקריאה בקול נשארה נפוצה מסיבות חברתיות.
explanation.en: Paragraph 3 has **cast doubt on this picture**, and paragraph 4 traces reading aloud to custom, **less in necessity than in custom**.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did some historians conclude from the way ancient books were written?
options: Copyists had made the texts difficult to read in silence on purpose.
Punctuation had been added to guide those who were reading aloud.
Readers would have had to voice the words to make sense of them.
Few people could afford to own the books that they wanted to read.

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 2 היסטוריונים טענו שאת הדפים הללו כמעט אי אפשר להבין בלי להשמיע אותם (**could hardly be made sense of without being sounded out**), כלומר הקוראים נזקקו להשמיע את המילים (**voice the words**).
explanation.en: Historians argued that such pages **could hardly be made sense of without being sounded out**, so readers had to voice the words.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what may the author of the famous account really have found surprising?
options: That a learned man could read with his voice and lips quite still
That a host read to himself while guests waited, leaving them out
That the page before him had no spaces between its words
That his visitors had been asked to read the text aloud in turn

explanation.he: לפי פסקה 3 ייתכן שההפתעה לא הייתה מהקריאה השקטה עצמה, אלא ממארח שקרא בשקט בזמן שאורחיו חיכו (**a host who read silently while visitors waited**), כלומר מכך שהאורחים נשארו מחוץ לטקסט.
explanation.en: The account may record surprise **not at silent reading itself but at a host who read silently while visitors waited**.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word "managed" is closest in meaning to
options: was in charge of
made copies of
read out loud
dealt well with

explanation.he: הצירוף **with little trouble** (בלי קושי רב) וההשוואה לקוראים שקולטים מילים במבט אחד (**take in familiar words at a glance**) מראים שהמילה **managed** פירושה כאן להתמודד היטב (**dealt well with**).
explanation.en: **with little trouble** and the comparison with readers who **take in familiar words at a glance** show that **managed** means dealt well with.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that reading aloud in the ancient world
options: was a sign that a reader had not yet fully learned to read
often let people who never learned their letters enjoy a text
was needed chiefly to make sense of pages written without spaces
was usually done by authors presenting their own new work

explanation.he: פסקה 4 מונה בין הסיבות לקריאה בקול את העובדה שאנשים רבים לא ידעו קרוא וכתוב (**many people were unlettered**) ושספרות נהנו ממנה בחברה, ולכן הקריאה בקול אפשרה גם להם ליהנות מהטקסט (**enjoy a text**).
explanation.en: Since **many people were unlettered** and literature **was often enjoyed in company**, reading aloud let those who could not read share in it.

items.stem: Before the swimming lesson starts, the children take a shower and put on their caps.
options: The children take a shower and take off their caps before they start the swimming lesson.
The children take a shower and put on their caps, and then the swimming lesson starts.
After the children take a shower and put on their caps, they swim in groups of four.
The children take a shower and put on their caps after the swimming lesson.

explanation.he: הצירוף **Before the swimming lesson starts** (לפני שהשיעור מתחיל) מציב את המקלחת ואת הכובעים לפני השיעור, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הסדר בעזרת הצירוף **and then the swimming lesson starts** (ואחר כך השיעור מתחיל).
explanation.en: **Before the swimming lesson starts** puts the shower and the caps first, and the correct answer keeps this order with **and then the swimming lesson starts**.

items.stem: The soup was cooked by my father, and the bread was baked by my sister.
options: My father made the soup and the bread.
The soup was cooked for my father, and the bread was baked for my sister.
My father baked the bread, and my sister cooked the soup.
My father cooked the soup, and my sister baked the bread.

explanation.he: המילה **by** (על ידי) מראה מי עשה את הפעולה, והתשובה הנכונה הופכת את המשפט לפעיל ושומרת על התפקידים בצירוף **My father cooked the soup** ובצירוף **my sister baked the bread**.
explanation.en: **by** shows who did what, and the correct answer keeps the roles in the active voice: **My father cooked the soup**, **my sister baked the bread**.

items.stem: Ruth does not eat meat, and she does not drink milk either.
options: Ruth eats no meat and drinks no milk.
Ruth eats no meat.
Ruth eats no meat, but she drinks milk.
Ruth does not eat meat, and her sister does not drink milk either.

explanation.he: המילה **either** (גם לא) מצרפת שלילה שנייה לשלילה הראשונה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שתיהן בצירוף **eats no meat and drinks no milk** (לא אוכלת בשר ולא שותה חלב).
explanation.en: **either** adds a second negative to the first one, and the correct answer keeps both with **eats no meat and drinks no milk**.

items.stem: The café near my school sells hot drinks in winter and cold drinks in summer.
options: In winter, the café near my school sells hot drinks.
The café near my school sells cold drinks in winter and hot drinks in summer.
In winter, the café near my school sells hot drinks, while in summer it sells cold drinks.
In winter, the café near my school sells hot drinks and soup, while in summer the café sells ice cream and cold drinks.

explanation.he: הצירוף **hot drinks in winter** והצירוף **cold drinks in summer** מקשרים כל עונה לסוג המשקה שלה, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שני הקשרים בעזרת המילה **while** (בעוד ש-).
explanation.en: **hot drinks in winter** and **cold drinks in summer** link each season to its drinks, and the correct answer keeps both links with **while**.

items.stem: It was a little windy on Sunday, so Ella and her brother flew their kite in the park.
options: Ella and her brother flew their kite in the park on Sunday because there was a bit of wind.
It was a bit windy on Sunday, so Ella and her brother stayed at home and played games together.
Ella and her brother flew their kite on Sunday, so it was a little windy.
It was very windy on Sunday, so Ella and her brother flew their kite in the park.

explanation.he: המילה **so** (לכן) מראה שהרוח הקלה היא הסיבה להטסת העפיפון, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הקשר ועל הדרגה בעזרת המילה **because** (כי) והצירוף **a bit of wind** (קצת רוח).
explanation.en: **so** makes the light wind the reason for flying the kite, and the correct answer keeps the link and the degree with **because** and **a bit of wind**.

items.stem: The train was late this morning because there was a problem with the signals.
options: The problem with the signals was caused by the late train this morning.
Tomorrow morning, a problem with the signals will make the train late.
A problem with the train made the signals late this morning.
A problem with the signals made the train late this morning.

explanation.he: המילה **because** (כי) מראה שהבעיה באיתות היא הסיבה לאיחור, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על הסיבה ועל התוצאה בעזרת הפועל **made** (גרם ל-).
explanation.en: **because** makes the problem with the signals the reason for the delay, and the correct answer keeps reason and result with **made the train late**.

items.stem: Few of the students in my class have a pet, but most of them would like one.
options: A few of my classmates own a pet, while most of the others would like to have one.
Most of my classmates want a pet, but not many people in my class have one.
Most students in my class own a pet, but few of them want another one.
In my class, few students have a pet, and most of them do not want one.

explanation.he: המילה **Few** (מעטים) והצירוף **most of them** (רובם) קובעים כמה מחזיקים חיית מחמד וכמה רוצים, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת על שתי הכמויות בסדר הפוך בצירוף **Most of my classmates** ובצירוף **not many people** (לא הרבה אנשים).
explanation.en: **Few** and **most of them** give the two quantities, and the correct answer keeps both in reverse order with **Most of my classmates** and **not many people**.

items.stem: The pictures in the school magazine were taken by students, but they were chosen by the teacher.
options: The teacher took the photos in the school magazine, and students picked them.
The pictures in the school magazine were taken by students.
Students took the pictures in the school magazine, but the teacher chose them.
The teacher and the principal chose the pictures that students took for the school magazine.

explanation.he: המילה **but** (אבל) מציגה שני תפקידים שונים, והתשובה הנכונה שומרת עליהם בצירוף **Students took** (התלמידים צילמו) ובצירוף **the teacher chose them** (המורה בחר בהן).
explanation.en: **but** sets two different roles side by side, and the correct answer keeps both with **Students took** and **the teacher chose them**.

items.stem: Last summer, my cousin spent two weeks on a farm, where she learned to milk cows.
options: Last summer, my cousin stayed on a farm for two weeks and learned how to milk cows there.
Next summer, my cousin will spend two weeks on a farm and learn to milk cows.
